  Velocity template, large body) over HTTP and HTTPS/HTTP-2.
- growth.js: a sustained constant-load run at the default 100k maxLogEntries that
  surfaces "increases over time" regressions (e.g. the #2329 O(n) log-eviction
  CPU climb) via CPU/heap/latency end/start slope ratios.
- JMH MatchingBenchmark: gc.alloc.rate.norm + ns/op as an absolute, hardware-
  noise-immune backstop the rolling baseline cannot provide.

How it gates:
- A dedicated, pinned (c5.4xlarge), on-demand, scale-to-zero (min_size 0) Buildkite
  perf queue gives reproducible numbers; results persist to a new
  mockserver-ci-perf-results S3 bucket (versioned history).
- perf-test-compare.sh pulls the last N prior runs and flags a regression when a
  metric crosses a rolling median+MAD threshold (growth slopes also get an
  absolute floor). Notify-only: posts a Buildkite annotation table and always
  exits 0.
- A daily schedule fires the run; a cheap commit guard on the trigger queue
  dynamically dispatches the heavy steps only when there is a new commit, reusing
  the last-successful-commit helper extracted from generate-pipeline.sh.

Includes Terraform for the perf queue, S3 results bucket + IAM, and the daily
schedule, plus docs across performance-tuning, ci-cd, aws-infrastructure,
build-system, metrics, and the k6 README.

fix(perf): gate the daily regression run on the last ACTUAL run, not lint passes

The commit guard keyed "have we run since the last commit?" off the last
*successful perf-test build*. But that pipeline passes on its lint step on every
push, so the last successful build is almost always HEAD — meaning the guard
would skip the heavy regression run forever, even after real commits land.

Fix: perf-test-run.sh now records `perf_regression_ran_commit` in the build's
Buildkite meta-data when the run actually executes, and the guard resolves the
most recent such value (new `last_perf_run_commit` helper) and dispatches when
HEAD differs. Lint builds never set the meta-data, so they can't poison the
signal. First run (no meta-data) and API failures fall through to running.

The sibling `last_successful_commit` helper (last passed build) is unchanged and
still used by generate-pipeline.sh for path-based change detection.

feat(perf): add [perf-run] message marker to force-trigger the daily perf regression

API/UI builds with '[perf-run]' in the message now dispatch the heavy
run/microbench/compare steps via the guard, and forced runs (UI source or
[perf-run] marker) always dispatch even on the same commit as the last run.
Scheduled runs keep the existing 'new commit since last run' gate, so the
daily-only, commit-gated design is preserved (orchestrator/commit builds never
carry the marker).

docs(test): explain why the test-only trust-all/hostname-skip TLS is safe (CodeQL #56/#57)

Two CodeQL alerts flagged test helpers:
- java/insecure-trustmanager — Http3ServerTest.trustAllManager()
- java/unsafe-hostname-verification — WebhookServerTest.createConnection()

Both are test-only client code that connects to a test server's ephemeral
self-signed certificate on loopback, where trust-all / hostname-skip is the
standard way to talk to the in-JVM server and carries no production risk
(MockServer's runtime TLS trust is config-governed; the real k8s webhook is
verified by the kube-apiserver via the configured caBundle).

The alerts are dismissed in code-scanning as "used in tests"; this adds an
in-source note at each site explaining the justification for future auditors.
Comment-only change — no behaviour change.

fix(perf): make k6 output dir world-writable so non-root k6 can write results

The k6 container runs as uid 12345; mktemp -d created the shared /out bind-mount

the result-assembly jq with a missing regression-http.json. chmod 0777 the
per-run output dir (k6 result files only, no secrets) so the unprivileged
container user can write its artifacts.

fix(aws-build): make hardening terraform apply cleanly

Two defects in the IAM/CloudTrail hardening (commit 1c111d3b8) blocked a
clean `terraform apply` of terraform/buildkite-agents:

- main.tf passed freshly-created `aws_iam_policy.*.arn` values into each
  elastic-ci-stack module's `managed_policy_arns`. Those ARNs are computed
  (unknown until apply), so the module's internal
  `for_each = toset(var.managed_policy_arns)` failed at plan time with
  "Invalid for_each argument" on a clean state. Construct the ARNs from the
  statically-known policy `.name` + account id via a `locals` map so the
  for_each keys resolve at plan time, while still referencing the resource
  to preserve creation ordering.

  event selector with `resources.type = AWS::SecretsManager::Secret`, which
  the CloudTrail API rejects (InvalidEventSelectorsException) — Secrets
  Manager is not a data-event resource type. GetSecretValue is a management
  event, already captured by the ManagementEvents selector. Remove the
  invalid selector and document where secret access is audited.

harden(buildkite): migrate pipelines + agents onto the Default cluster

Buildkite is deprecating unclustered (organization-level) agents and has
removed the org-level agent-token UI, so the legacy token could no longer be
rotated. Migrate everything onto the pre-existing Default cluster:

- clusters.tf: data source for the Default cluster; create the four cluster
  queues (default, trigger, release, perf) matching the agents' buildkite_queue
  keys; mint a cluster agent token; publish it to the SSM SecureString
  /buildkite/buildkite/agent-token.
- pipelines.tf: assign all 16 pipelines to the cluster via cluster_id.
- run.sh: load the agent token from SSM into TF_VAR_buildkite_agent_token
  before init/plan/apply (the variable doc claimed this already happened, but
  run.sh never did it — the token was coming from inline tfvars). The inline
  token is removed from the gitignored terraform.tfvars, closing the audit
  finding that the agent token lived in plaintext on local disk.

Applied (both stacks converge, no drift): pipelines stack 6 add / 16 change;
agents stack rolled the new cluster token into the 4 elastic-ci-stack SSM
params. Verified live: 4 queues present, all pipelines show cluster=Default
cluster, cluster agent token active. Cutover is clean — agents are
scale-to-zero, so the next build launches a fresh agent on the cluster token.

fix(buildkite): set 'default' as the cluster default queue

Each pipeline's bootstrap step (`buildkite-agent pipeline upload`) carries no
explicit agents queue tag, so it runs on the cluster's default queue. After the
cluster migration that default was still the auto-created "default-queue", which
has no agents — so every build would have hung at the upload step. Point the
cluster default queue at our "default" queue (served by the elastic-ci-stack
default agents). Applied + verified live: cluster defaultQueue is now 'default'.

feat(perf): attach dependency-cache policy to default + release agent roles

Completes the dependency-cache 'add': the bucket + IAM policy now exist (created
with the cluster/hardening apply), but the policy was attached to no agent role,
so agents couldn't use the cache. Re-attach buildkite-dependency-cache to the
default and release queues via the new local.policy_arn map (keeps the for_each
keys static/known at plan time). Applied: 2 attachments, 0 changed, 0 destroyed;
plan now clean.

harden(buildkite): give the Terraform provider its own management token

The Buildkite provider previously read mockserver-build/buildkite-api-token —
the same secret the trigger/cleanup CI scripts read on build agents. Scoping
that token down to CI build-control (read_builds/write_builds) for least
privilege broke the provider, which needs read_pipelines + write_pipelines +
graphql to manage pipelines and the cluster.

Point the provider at a dedicated mockserver-build/buildkite-tf-token instead
(read_pipelines, write_pipelines, graphql). That secret is read only by local
admin running Terraform and is NOT granted to any build queue, so build agents
can no longer rewrite pipelines or manage the cluster. Verified: terraform plan
succeeds and converges to no changes.

harden(buildkite): change-detection uses a read-only API token

Defence-in-depth on top of the management-token split: last-successful-commit.sh
(the change-detection / perf-guard library, GET /builds only) now defaults to the
read-only token mockserver-build/buildkite-api-token-readonly instead of the
write token. The build-control scripts (trigger-pipeline.sh, cleanup-closed-pr-
builds.sh) keep the write token; the Terraform provider keeps its own management
token. So the change-detection code path physically cannot create/cancel/delete
builds, even though the agent still holds the write token for its other steps.

- build-secrets.tf: data source for the out-of-band read-only secret + a
  read_buildkite_api_token_readonly GetSecretValue policy; refreshed the
  queue->secret mapping comment.
- main.tf: attach the read-only policy to the default, trigger, and perf queues
  (the queues that run change detection).

Applied (4 add / 0 change / 0 destroy, converges clean). Verified: the read-only
token returns the builds array (read works) and gets HTTP 403 on create-build
(write blocked). review-final PASS.

harden(buildkite): split Docker Hub credentials snapshot vs release

The default queue runs untrusted PR code on every master build but read the same
Docker Hub credential used for release image pushes. Split them so the default
queue cannot obtain the release-designated token:

- docker-login.sh selects the secret via DOCKERHUB_SECRET_ID (default
  mockserver-build/dockerhub = snapshot; release callers set
  mockserver-release/dockerhub), with a release-queue fallback.
- docker-push-release.sh and scripts/release/components/docker.sh export the
  release secret id. Snapshot callers (java-docker-push-snapshot.sh,
  maven-image-push.sh) fall through to the snapshot secret.
- build-secrets.tf: read_dockerhub_release_secret policy over the (out-of-band)
  mockserver-release/dockerhub secret; main.tf swaps the release queue's grant
  to it so the release queue reads ONLY the release token and the default queue
  reads ONLY the snapshot token.

Applied (2 add / 1 destroy — release detaches the snapshot secret; converges
clean). Verified: both tokens authenticate (HTTP 200), all 4 docker-login.sh
callers route to the correct secret.

NOTE: Docker Hub PATs cannot be repo/tag-scoped on the current plan, so both
tokens share the same push rights; the win is credential separation (independent
rotation/revocation + audit) and the AWS guarantee that the default queue cannot
read the release token.

fix(test): cap maxLogEntries in test JVMs to prevent event-log OOM

The release build (mvn clean install) ran the full test suite and the
mockserver-core / integration forks died with OutOfMemoryError, then GC-thrashed
until the CI Maven Central step hit its wall-clock timeout (the JVM never exits,
so a longer timeout does not help).

Root cause: maxLogEntries defaults to min(heapAvailable/8, 100000), so in a test
fork it resolves to 100000 and every MockServerEventLog pre-allocates a disruptor
RingBuffer of nextPowerOfTwo(100000)=131072 LogEntry objects. The 7.0.0 cycle
added many tests that each spin up event logs; in the reused sequential fork these
huge ring buffers accumulate and exhaust the heap.

Fix: set mockserver.maxLogEntries=1000 via Surefire/Failsafe systemPropertyVariables
so test ring buffers are 1024 slots instead of 131072. Production sizing is
unchanged (a real server still sizes its single ring buffer from real heap).

Validated locally: full clean build+test, 0 OutOfMemoryError, mockserver-core
5685+694 tests green (was OOMing before).

fix(ci): run the JetBrains gradle build in an in-container /tmp copy

The gradle + IntelliJ Platform build runs as root in Docker and wrote build/,
.gradle/, .kotlin/ and .intellijPlatform/ into the mounted workspace as root.
The buildkite-agent user then can't git-clean them on the next build, so the
editors pipeline's checkout deterministically hung ~10 min and exited 128 (a
known buildkite elastic-stack root-owned-files issue). Building under /tmp keeps
the mounted workspace pristine so it stays cleanable.

harden(ci): run build containers non-root, drop caps, withhold the Docker socket from PRs

Hardens CI against untrusted PR code (the default queue runs PR builds):
- run-in-docker.sh runs containers as the host agent UID by default (HOME=/tmp,
  $HOME-relative caches), with a --root opt-out. Non-root means a breakout is
  unprivileged and nothing root-owned is left in the checkout (also fixes the
  prior git-clean poisoning + JetBrains soft-fail at the source).
- L4: --security-opt no-new-privileges + --cap-drop ALL by default, with a
  --cap-add passthrough.
- L3: the Docker socket (-s) is refused on PR builds (host-root breakout path);
  the Testcontainers integration steps that need it now run --root, master-only.
- Step fixes for non-root: PHP uses composer:2 (no apt-get/root); python uses
  `python -m pytest`; the JetBrains build drops the /tmp workaround; the
  Playwright browser test disables the Chromium setuid sandbox (container is the
  boundary) instead of needing SYS_ADMIN.

Validated locally non-root: Go, Rust, Node, .NET, PHP, Python; remaining heavy
pipelines (maven/java) validate on CI (corporate proxy blocks local download).

harden(ci): make container hardening opt-in via --harden (default = legacy behaviour)

The all-non-root default broke existing pipelines on CI in ways that don't
reproduce locally (no log access to diagnose remotely). Revert to a safe,
incremental model:
- run-in-docker.sh: default keeps the legacy behaviour (root, full caps);
  --harden opts a step into non-root (host UID, HOME=/tmp) + no-new-privileges
  + cap-drop=ALL. Steps adopt --harden once validated non-root on CI.
- L3 stays ALWAYS-ON: the Docker socket is withheld from PR builds regardless
  of --harden (the highest-value untrusted-PR protection, and a safe skip).
- go-unit-test adopts --harden (proven non-root on CI). php uses composer:2,
  jetbrains keeps the /tmp-copy (root, no workspace pollution); both convert to
  --harden later. Browser test disables the Chromium sandbox (harmless as root).

harden(ci): redefine --harden as cap-drop only (agents already userns-remap)

The build agents already run Docker with user-namespace remapping
(DOCKER_USERNS_REMAP=true on every queue, the elastic-ci-stack default), so
container-root is already an unprivileged host UID — a breakout is not host-root.
That is the 'map container-root to a non-root host user' protection, already in
place fleet-wide.

Adding --user on top double-remaps the UID so it no longer matches the workspace
owner, which is exactly why per-step non-root passed locally (no userns-remap on
a dev Mac) but broke writes on CI. So --harden no longer adds --user; it now adds
only the userns-remap-compatible defense-in-depth: cap-drop=ALL +
no-new-privileges (+ --cap-add passthrough). L3 (socket withheld from PRs) is
unchanged and always-on.

harden(agents): set IMDS hop-limit to 1 so PR-build containers can't steal agent creds

The elastic-ci-stack launch template hardcodes the IMDS response hop limit to 2
(no module variable), which lets a build container — one hop from the host —
reach 169.254.169.254 and read the agent instance-role credentials. userns-remap
and the PR socket block don't cover this.

Add a boot script (hosted in a new mockserver-ci-bootstrap bucket, run via the
module's bootstrap_script_url on every queue) that calls
modify-instance-metadata-options to set the hop limit to 1: the agent runs on the
host (hop 0, keeps IMDS) while build containers (hop 1+) are blocked. Grants each
instance role s3:GetObject on the script + ec2:ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions on
in-account instances. Applied + converged; 0 destroys.

fix(core): initialise secret-redaction fields before reading the property file (#2338)

ConfigurationProperties failed to initialise — NoClassDefFoundError: Could not
initialize class org.mockserver.configuration.ConfigurationProperties — whenever a
mockserver.properties file (or the Helm chart's app.config.properties) contained
entries. The PROPERTIES static initialiser runs readPropertyFile() during <clinit>,
which redacts sensitive values via isSensitivePropertyName() reading the
SENSITIVE_SUBSTRINGS set; that set (and REDACTED_VALUE) were declared ~3000 lines
later, so they were null during class initialisation and the per-property log loop
threw a NullPointerException.

Move REDACTED_VALUE + SENSITIVE_SUBSTRINGS above the PROPERTIES initialiser (with a
guard comment) so they are non-null when readPropertyFile() runs.

Add ConfigurationPropertiesInitializationTest, which loads ConfigurationProperties in
an isolated child-first classloader (serving the property file via getResourceAsStream
so it touches no global state) and asserts clean initialisation against a populated
property file including a sensitive key. Verified red on the buggy code and green after
the fix; the full 181-test config package passes.

test(ui): inline @mui/material in vitest so its ESM directory import resolves

Inline @mui/material via test.server.deps.inline so Vite transforms it and resolves the
import. Verified with the full suite green on both 9.0.1 (current) and 9.1.0 (the bump):
84 files / 956 tests, plus lint and the tsc-strict build.

fix(core): make object-mapper Swagger coupling optional so the client can exclude the parser

ObjectMapperFactory registered its Swagger/OpenAPI-coupled serializers (the schema
serializers and the OpenAPI-derived HttpRequestsPropertiesMatcher serializer)
unconditionally, so initialising the object mapper loaded io.swagger.v3.oas.models.*
even on a client that never produces those objects. That forced mockserver-client-java
to keep the whole Swagger/OpenAPI parser on a consumer's classpath.

- Isolate the Swagger-coupled serializers in a new SwaggerSerializers helper, registered
  only when swagger-core is on the classpath (SWAGGER_PRESENT probe via Class.forName).
  JVM lazy class-loading means the helper and its swagger references are never resolved
  when the guard is false.
- Replace the single com.github.fge (json-tools) JacksonUtils.prettyPrint call on the
  client-reachable path with a small JsonPrettyPrinter (no behavioural change; output is
  logged and re-parsed).
- Declare jackson-datatype-jsr310 as a direct mockserver-core dependency. The object
  mapper registers JavaTimeModule directly but the artifact previously only arrived
  transitively via the Swagger parser (surfaced by a swagger-absent runtime test).
- mockserver-client-java now also excludes io.swagger.parser.v3:swagger-parser and
  org.mozilla:rhino. A client-only consumer's swagger-derived dependencyConvergence
  conflicts drop from 13 to 0 (3 unrelated non-swagger conflicts remain; the BOM pins
  those).

Verified: 718 core serialization/OpenAPI/matcher tests and 155 client tests pass with
swagger present; a standalone project depending only on the slim client (swagger
genuinely absent) round-trips expectations and OpenAPI expectations with no
NoClassDefFoundError. Server behaviour is unchanged (swagger-core is always present there).

feat: add interactive request breakpoints (hold/modify/resume)

Add backend mechanism for Charles/Fiddler-style interactive breakpoints
that pause outbound proxied requests for inspection, modification, or
abort before forwarding to the upstream. Default OFF.

Core components:
- BreakpointRegistry: singleton holding paused exchanges in a
  ConcurrentHashMap with configurable max-held DoS cap (default 50)
  and per-exchange timeout auto-continue (default 30s)
- BreakpointDecision: CONTINUE/MODIFY/ABORT resolution model
- PausedExchange: holds captured HttpRequest + CompletableFuture

Intercept point: inside handleUnmatchedProxyForward in HttpActionHandler,
within the scheduler.submit lambda (worker thread, NOT the event loop).
Gated to async mode only (synchronous/embedded mode skips breakpoints).

Control-plane endpoints (behind controlPlaneRequestAuthenticated):
- GET/PUT /mockserver/breakpoint - list paused exchanges
- PUT /mockserver/breakpoint/continue - resume with original request
- PUT /mockserver/breakpoint/modify - resume with replacement request
- PUT /mockserver/breakpoint/abort - return abort response without forwarding

Config (4-form: static + instance + DTO):
- breakpointEnabled (default false)
- breakpointTimeoutMillis (default 30000)
- breakpointMaxHeld (default 50)

Reset: BreakpointRegistry.reset() added to HttpState.reset().

fix: eliminate thread-blocking in request breakpoints, fix JSON injection + reset race

CRITICAL: refactor breakpoint intercept from blocking .get() to async
CompletableFuture chaining (thenAcceptAsync on scheduler executor). The old
code blocked scheduler worker threads for up to 31s per paused exchange;
with CallerRunsPolicy, exhausting the pool caused the next submit to run
inline on the Netty event-loop thread, producing a self-inflicted DoS from
normal traffic. Now no thread is held while a breakpoint is pending.

The forward-and-respond logic is extracted into executeUnmatchedForward()
so the async continuation can reuse it. The breakpointMaxHeld cap is now
purely a memory/DoS bound, not a thread bound.

Additional fixes:
- JSON injection (MAJOR): breakpoint success responses in HttpState
  (continue/modify/abort) used string concatenation to embed the
  caller-supplied id into JSON, allowing a malicious id to break the
  response. Now uses Jackson ObjectMapper.createObjectNode() consistently.
- Reset race (MINOR): BreakpointRegistry.reset() used explicit
  held.clear() after completing futures, but the whenComplete callback
  already removes entries, so clear() could orphan exchanges added
  mid-reset. Replaced with a drain loop that relies on the callback.

Documentation + OpenAPI (MAJOR):
- Added breakpointEnabled/TimeoutMillis/MaxHeld to consumer config docs,
  configuration-reference.md, and mockserver.example.properties.
- Added GET/PUT /breakpoint, PUT /breakpoint/continue|modify|abort to
  the OpenAPI spec (mockserver-openapi.yaml).
- Created docs/code/breakpoints.md architecture note.

Non-blocking concurrency test: pauses poolSize+5 concurrent exchanges on a

exhausted), all async continuations fire on resolution, and the pool
remains usable after all completions.

feat(chaos): add scheduled multi-stage chaos experiments

Introduce ChaosExperimentOrchestrator — a singleton that runs an ordered
sequence of chaos stages, each applying service-scoped chaos profiles for
a configurable duration before automatically advancing to the next stage.

Endpoints (behind control-plane auth, mirroring serviceChaos pattern):
  PUT    /mockserver/chaosExperiment — start an experiment
  GET    /mockserver/chaosExperiment — poll current status
  DELETE /mockserver/chaosExperiment — stop and clear chaos

Key design decisions:
- Non-blocking: uses a single-thread ScheduledExecutorService (daemon)
  for stage advancement; never blocks the Netty event loop.
- C1 auto-halt integration: if ChaosAutoHaltMonitor clears the registry
  mid-experiment, the next stage advance detects the empty registry and
  halts the experiment with status "halted_by_auto_halt".
- Safety limits: max 50 stages, max 24h per stage, one active experiment
  at a time, stopping is idempotent.
- Reset: orchestrator.reset() is wired into HttpState.reset().
- Endpoint-driven config: experiments are defined via the REST payload,
  not static ConfigurationProperties.

Tests use a controllable AtomicLong clock and advanceNow() for
deterministic stage transitions with zero wall-clock sleeps.

feat: add forwarded-stream frame breakpoints (hold/modify/drop SSE+chunked)

in a StreamFrameBreakpointRegistry, and resolved via new control-plane
REST endpoints. Fully non-blocking (event-loop safe), with backpressure
(requestMore paused while a frame is held), ordered frame resolution,
stream-close eviction (DROP to prevent out-of-order writes), timeout
auto-continue, and DoS cap. Gated by breakpointStreamEnabled (default
false, zero overhead). Scoped to HTTP/1.1; gRPC/HTTP-2/WebSocket are
explicit follow-ups (A1d/A1e).

fix(node): remove unrecognised tar --no-absolute-filenames flag

The on-demand launcher passed `--no-absolute-filenames` to tar on Linux,
but GNU tar 1.34/1.35 (the CI image) does not recognise that long option,
so extraction aborted with exit 64 — breaking the node launcher
integration tests on every build since 215.

behaves the same, so the H3 path-traversal protection is unchanged. This
restores the plain `tar -xf <archive> -C <dir>` extraction that the prior
known-good builds used, with SHA-256 verification still gating extraction.

fix(ruby): clear rb/polynomial-redos ReDoS in binary launcher asset_url

The trailing-slash strip in BinaryLauncher.asset_url used
base.sub(%r{/+\z}, ''), whose /+\z sub-expression can restart at every
'/' and backtrack quadratically on a base URL with a long slash run that
does not end in '/' (relevant on Ruby < 3.2, which lacks the regex match
cache). The base URL is operator-supplied via MOCKSERVER_BINARY_BASE_URL,
so real-world exploitability is low, but the regex is now anchored with a
negative look-behind (%r{(?<!/)/+\z}) to make the strip linear.

preservation and a 100k-slash pathological input.

feat(breakpoints): matcher-driven breakpoints, remove global flags

BREAKING: removes the breakpointEnabled, breakpointResponseEnabled,
breakpointStreamEnabled and breakpointInboundEnabled config flags.

Breakpoints are now driven by a request matcher (identical to expectation
request matchers) plus a set of phases (REQUEST, RESPONSE, RESPONSE_STREAM,
INBOUND_STREAM). A forwarded/proxied exchange whose request matches a
registered breakpoint pauses at the selected phase(s).

- New org.mockserver.mock.breakpoint.{BreakpointPhase, BreakpointMatcher,
  BreakpointMatcherRegistry} (single CopyOnWriteArrayList; allocation-light
  findMatch with empty-registry fast path, safe on the Netty event loop).
- All 11 forward hold-point gate checks now consult the matcher registry
  instead of a global flag. Inbound-frame handlers evaluate the matcher at
  construction time (channelRead0 has no HttpRequest) and skip entirely when
  no matcher matches, preserving the zero-allocation fast path.
- REST: PUT /mockserver/breakpoint/matcher (register), GET|PUT
  /mockserver/breakpoint/matchers (list), PUT /mockserver/breakpoint/matcher/remove,
  PUT /mockserver/breakpoint/matcher/clear; registry cleared on reset.
- Retains breakpointTimeoutMillis + breakpointMaxHeld rails. Existing
  continue/modify/abort + stream-frame resolution endpoints unchanged
  (WS-callback resolution lands in a later unit).
- Internal + consumer docs and OpenAPI updated; flags purged everywhere.

feat(breakpoints): interactive resolution over the callback WebSocket

A breakpoint matcher can carry an optional owner clientId. When set, a
matching forwarded REQUEST or RESPONSE exchange is dispatched to that
connected callback-WebSocket client (the same /_mockserver_callback_websocket
channel forwardObject/responseObject clients use) for interactive resolution;
the client replies with a modified request (forward), a response (abort/
replace), or the original (continue). When no clientId is set, the existing
REST poll/continue/modify/abort flow is used unchanged (additive, non-breaking).

- New BreakpointCallbackDispatcher reusing WebSocketClientRegistry primitives;
  cleanup centralised in a single whenComplete so every completion route
  (reply, timeout, disconnect, reset, send-failure) unregisters handlers,
  cancels the timeout, and clears the in-flight entry.
- BreakpointMatcher gains optional clientId; registry register overload +
  removeByClientId; REST register/list carry clientId.
- All 4 forward hold points branch clientId -> WS dispatch vs REST-park
  (attemptResponseBreakpoint helper dedupes the 3 response sites).
- WebSocketClientRegistry.unregisterClient removes the client's breakpoints and
  auto-continues its in-flight dispatches.
- Shares breakpointTimeoutMillis + breakpointMaxHeld rails. REST resolution
  endpoints retained until the dashboard becomes a callback client (later unit).

feat(breakpoints): per-frame streaming resolution over the callback WebSocket

RESPONSE_STREAM (outbound) and INBOUND_STREAM (client->server) breakpoints
resolve interactively over the callback WebSocket when the matcher carries a

feat(breakpoints): fire REQUEST/RESPONSE breakpoints on matched forwards, mock responses, and unmatched 404s

Previously interactive breakpoints only paused unmatched/anonymous proxy
forwards. Matched forward expectations could not pause at the REQUEST phase,
and matched mock RESPONSE expectations and unmatched-404 responses could not
pause at all — so a breakpoint matcher registered against those paths silently
had no effect.

Extend coverage:
- REQUEST phase via a shared attemptRequestBreakpoint gate, applied to the six
  matched FORWARD* dispatch cases (dispatchForwardWithBreakpoint), the mock
  RESPONSE/RESPONSE_TEMPLATE/RESPONSE_CLASS_CALLBACK cases
  (dispatchMockResponseWithBreakpoint), and the unmatched-404 dispatch.
- RESPONSE phase inside writeResponseActionResponse (gated by action type so the
  shared writer's LLM/gRPC/WebSocket/SSE callers are not intercepted) and inside
  returnNotFound for the 404 path.

CONTINUE/MODIFY/ABORT semantics and the non-blocking async continuation mirror
the existing unmatched-proxy REQUEST breakpoint; breakpoints remain fully skipped
in synchronous (WAR) mode. Adds HttpActionHandlerBreakpointTest (registered in
both Surefire phases) and updates docs and the demo banner.

perf(ui): memoize dashboard rows + stabilize store refs to cut click/update lag

The dashboard re-rendered every row of all four panels on each once-per-second
WebSocket push because applyMessage replaced the entity arrays wholesale with
freshly-parsed objects, giving every row a new reference each tick. With no
row memoization this meant a full re-render storm that kept the main thread
busy and made panel interactions feel sluggish.

- store: reconcileByKey preserves the previous object reference for entries
  whose content is unchanged (matched by stable key, structural JSON compare),
  so memoized rows and their useMemo([item.value]) hooks stay valid across
  pushes. Whole entries are reused, so a log group's nested entries are stable
  for free.
- JsonListItem, LogEntry: wrapped in React.memo so unchanged rows skip
  re-rendering entirely, including the expensive expanded JsonViewer subtree.
- RequestPanel: extracted a memoized RequestRow and moved traceparent
  extraction into a useMemo keyed on the item, out of the parent's .map()
  where it re-ran for every item on every render.

Local expand state is preserved across both reference reuse and content
changes (React key is item.key in all cases).

fix(ui): make the Sessions Call graph button toggle open/closed

fix(ui): keep breakpoints registered across tab changes (don't drop the callback WS)

Leaving the Breakpoints tab unmounted the panel, whose effect called
client.disconnect() — closing the callback WebSocket, nulling the server-assigned
clientId, and so dropping every breakpoint matcher registered under it. Returning
reconnected with a fresh clientId, leaving the old matchers orphaned, so the
breakpoints appeared lost.

Fix: the callback client is an app-lifetime singleton — stop disconnecting on
unmount, and make connect() idempotent (no-op when already connected/connecting to
the same server) so a re-mount preserves the connection, clientId and server-side
matchers. The panel now also seeds wsState/clientId from the live client on mount.

fix(ui): reconnect dashboard WebSocket on StrictMode remount

The connection-status chip could stay stuck (e.g. on a stale state) after a
page load in dev, only recovering once an action lazily reconnected (such as
switching to a tab that sends a request filter).

Root cause: App gated the mount-time connect({}) behind a useRef 'once' guard.
Under React StrictMode the initial mount is immediately unmounted (which runs
useWebSocket's cleanup and closes the socket) and then remounted — but the ref
was still set, so the remount skipped the reconnect and left the socket dead.

The connect effect's dependency (connect) is already stable, so the guard was
unnecessary; removing it lets StrictMode's remount re-establish the connection.
useWebSocket still tears the socket down on real unmount, and closeWebSocket's
deferred-close handles the still-CONNECTING socket from the discarded mount, so
exactly one live socket remains.

perf(ui): defer expanded JSON body so row expand feels instant

Clicking a request/expectation/log row to expand it built the heavy
@uiw/react-json-view tree synchronously in the same render, stalling the click
before any visual feedback appeared.

Gate the expanded body on a useDeferredValue(expanded) instead of expanded
directly: the chevron and row layout still react to the urgent flag (instant
feedback) while the expensive JSON subtree builds in a non-blocking follow-up
render. Applied in both expand sites (JsonListItem, LogEntry).

perf(ui): skip off-screen dashboard rows with content-visibility

Long dashboard panels (up to 100 rows each across four panels) paid full
layout/style/paint cost for every row, even rows scrolled out of view —
contributing to sluggish view-switching and scrolling.

Add a shared listRowSx (content-visibility: auto + contain-intrinsic-size:
auto 44px) to each row in the Log, Active Expectations, Received and Proxied
panels. The browser now skips layout/paint for off-screen rows while keeping
them in the DOM, and reuses each row's last-rendered height as its placeholder
so expanded rows don't cause scrollbar jumps. Unsupported browsers ignore the
properties and render as before.

This stands alongside the upcoming windowing: windowed (on-screen) rows are
unaffected, while the render-all fallback path still benefits.

fix(ui): give Live Exchanges/Streams a stable sort by arrival timestamp

Each paused item now captures a receivedAt timestamp once, at arrival, and both
the Live Exchanges and Live Streams lists are explicitly sorted by it (with the
monotonic key as a tiebreaker). This guarantees a deterministic, stable order so
items keep a fixed chronological position instead of reshuffling as new pauses
arrive — a newly paused exchange/stream slots in by time rather than perturbing
the existing rows.

perf(ui): virtualize dashboard panel lists with lifted expand state

The Log, Active Expectations, Received and Proxied panels mounted every row
(up to 100 each) whenever the dashboard was shown, then kept them all in the
DOM. Combined with MUI/emotion per-row styling this made switching into the
dashboard and scrolling sluggish.

Add a reusable VirtualList (backed by @tanstack/react-virtual) that windows
each list to roughly the visible rows, using the enclosing Panel's scroll
container — published via PanelScrollContext — as the scroll element. Row
heights are measured, so expanding a row reflows correctly. When the viewport
isn't measurable (pre-layout, or a non-layout environment like jsdom) it falls
back to rendering all rows wrapped in listRowSx, so behaviour degrades
gracefully and unit tests still see the full list.

Because windowed rows unmount when scrolled off-screen, per-row expand/open
state is lifted out of JsonListItem/LogEntry/LogGroup into the panel via a
useExpansion() hook (a Set of expanded keys with a stable toggle), so a row
expanded then scrolled away stays expanded when scrolled back. The row
components accept controlled expanded/open + onToggle props and keep an
uncontrolled internal-state fallback for standalone use and tests.

Adds a VirtualList test that mocks viewport geometry to exercise both the
render-all fallback and the windowed path.

feat(breakpoints): carry request receive-timestamp through all phases for stable ordering

Adds a stable per-request receive-timestamp so the dashboard can sort Live
Exchanges by the ORIGINAL request time instead of WS dispatch-arrival time — a
late RESPONSE-phase pause now sorts next to its request rather than at the bottom.

Server:
- RequestDefinition gains a transient receivedTimestamp (Long), @JsonIgnore,
  excluded from equals/hashCode (mirrors logCorrelationId); clone/shallowClone
  copy it. HttpState.handle() stamps it once (EpochService.currentTimeMillis,
  idempotent) where logCorrelationId is set, so REQUEST and RESPONSE phases of the
  same exchange share the value.
- BreakpointCallbackDispatcher sends it as the X-MockServer-RequestTimestamp header
  (REQUEST + RESPONSE), and strips the internal dispatch headers (correlation,
  breakpointId, timestamp) from a continued/modified request so they don't leak
  upstream. PausedStreamFrame/DTO + StreamFrameCallbackDispatcher gain a nullable
  requestTimestamp (frame call sites pass null for now → client falls back to
  arrival time; fully backward compatible).

Client: parse the header/field into PausedItem/PausedStreamFrame and sort by
requestTimestamp ?? receivedAt (older servers keep working).

Backward compatible — purely additive; no other language client needs changes
(they route by breakpointId/correlationId and ignore the extra header). Verified:
mockserver-core test-compile + BreakpointCallbackDispatcherTest pass; client
eslint + 42 breakpoint tests pass. Docs: breakpoints.md updated.

perf(ui): replace dashboard windowing with progressive background rendering

The @tanstack/react-virtual windowing regressed the dashboard: it rendered the
full list then re-rendered windowed (slower initial paint), and its JS-driven
per-scroll re-measuring/re-positioning made scrolling janky. content-visibility
likewise deferred off-screen layout, so scrolling still did layout work.

Replace both with ProgressiveList: it mounts an initial batch of rows (roughly
what's visible) on the first paint, then appends the remaining rows in batches
during browser idle time (requestIdleCallback, setTimeout fallback). The end
state is the whole list fully laid out, so the browser does no per-scroll
mounting or repositioning and native scrolling stays smooth, while spreading
the initial mount across idle ticks keeps the first frame fast.

Removes @tanstack/react-virtual, VirtualList, PanelScrollContext and listRowSx,
and reverts Panel to its plain scroll container. The lifted expand state
(useExpansion + controlled props) is kept — harmless now that rows stay
mounted. ProgressiveList.test.tsx covers the initial batch and idle growth.

docs(ui): document dashboard rendering-performance techniques

Record the net rendering design in the dashboard UI doc: reference-stable store
reconciliation, row memoization, deferred expand body, progressive rendering,
and lifted expand state — plus a note on why true windowing was tried and
reverted.

fix(ui): keep the dashboard on Get Started instead of auto-jumping to Dashboard

applyMessage auto-advanced the view from 'get-started' to 'dashboard' the first
time a non-empty payload arrived. With a server that already has data, the very
first WebSocket snapshot tripped this, so the dashboard jumped straight past the
Get Started landing view on load. (The recent StrictMode reconnect fix made the
first snapshot arrive reliably, exposing this.)

Remove the auto-switch: applyMessage no longer touches the view. The store still
starts on 'get-started' and a reset still returns there, but the user now stays
on Get Started until they navigate away themselves. Tests and the dashboard-ui
doc updated to assert the sticky behaviour.

fix(breakpoints): preserve request timestamp through a continued/modified request

A REQUEST-phase breakpoint that is continued/modified echoes the request back over
the WebSocket; the server deserializes it into a fresh object that has LOST the
transient receivedTimestamp (it is @JsonIgnore). The forwarded request therefore
reached the RESPONSE-phase breakpoint with no timestamp, so the response sorted to
the bottom of Live Exchanges instead of next to its request.

Re-apply the ORIGINAL held request's receivedTimestamp onto the cleaned/modified
request in the forward-callback handler, so the whole REQUEST -> RESPONSE chain of
one exchange shares the same value and groups together in the dashboard sort.
Extended requestPhase_modify test to assert the timestamp survives. 16/16 pass.

feat(http3): interactive INBOUND breakpoints for gRPC bidi streaming over HTTP/3

Extends INBOUND_STREAM breakpoints to bidirectional gRPC streaming over HTTP/3
(QUIC) — the analogue of the HTTP/2 gRPC-bidi inbound path. Http3MockServerHandler
resolves an INBOUND_STREAM matcher once at HEADERS time (default-off) and wires the
matched breakpoint into Http3GrpcBidiStreamHandler, which parks each inbound gRPC
DATA frame in the StreamFrameBreakpointRegistry/StreamFrameCallbackDispatcher before
decoding and resolves it over the callback WebSocket (continue/modify/drop/inject/close).

Event-loop safe (decisions marshalled onto the QUIC stream event loop, never blocked);
no ByteBuf retained (the driver copies to byte[] and releases the frame before onData,
so the QUIC flow-control window is never pinned); per-frame ordering preserved by
dispatching one frame at a time and buffering the rest (bounded by maxRequestBodySize),
with stream-close eviction and the shared timeout/max-held rails. Completes interactive
breakpoints across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3.

Adds Http3GrpcBidiInboundBreakpointTest and updates internal docs (http3.md,
breakpoints.md), consumer docs (interactive_breakpoints.html), and the changelog.

test(http3): end-to-end gRPC-bidi INBOUND breakpoints with a real QUIC client

Adds three integration tests driving a real native-QUIC HTTP/3 gRPC-bidi client
through an INBOUND_STREAM breakpoint resolved over the callback WebSocket (Java
client handler): DROP suppresses the matched request's response, CONTINUE is
transparent (both responses returned in order), and MODIFY rewrites the inbound
request frame so the modified bytes reach the rule matcher. Verifies the full
cross-transport path (QUIC inbound frame -> TCP callback WS decision -> resumed
QUIC stream) end-to-end.

Fix #2347: compute dashboard Content-Length from UTF-8 byte length

The dashboard static assets (JS/CSS/HTML) are always written to the wire
as UTF-8 (the Content-Type carries charset=UTF-8), but the Content-Length
header was computed with the JVM default charset via content.getBytes().
On a platform whose default charset is not UTF-8 (e.g. Windows, legacy
default windows-1252), any asset containing multi-byte characters got a
Content-Length shorter than the actual body, so the browser truncated the
bundle and the dashboard rendered a white page. A JAR built on macOS
(UTF-8) therefore worked there but failed on Windows.

Content-Length is now computed from content.getBytes(UTF_8).length,
matching the bytes actually sent. Adds a regression test asserting the
declared Content-Length equals the UTF-8 byte length for a multi-byte
asset.

fix(website): add Subresource Integrity to highlight.js CDN scripts

fix(dashboard): adversarial-review correctness fixes (batch 1)

Five defensive fixes from a full adversarial review of the dashboard UI:

- BreakpointsPanel: cap the paused-exchange list (drop oldest beyond 500)
  and clear it on callback-WebSocket disconnect. A broad breakpoint matcher
  (e.g. path `.*`) previously grew the list unbounded until the tab ran out
  of memory, and held items reference a clientId the server replaces on
  reconnect (so they can never be resolved from the UI again).
- llmTraffic.parseSseStream: normalise CRLF/CR to LF before splitting so
  real on-the-wire SSE handles the `[DONE]` sentinel correctly and does not
  leak stray carriage returns into reassembled streaming text.
- prometheusParser: skip non-finite (NaN/+Inf/-Inf) sample values so they
  cannot poison chart auto-scaling or numeric formatting. No MockServer
  metric value is legitimately infinite (histogram `le="+Inf"` is a label,
  not a value).
- ServiceChaosPanel: decrement the TCP and gRPC service-chaos TTL countdowns
  against their own poll timestamps instead of the HTTP poll's timestamp,
  which kept advancing while those sections were collapsed and their data
  frozen, making the countdowns drift.
- TrafficInspector: wrap the detail pane in a new ErrorBoundary so a parser
  exception on a malformed captured body shows an inline error instead of
  unmounting the whole inspector.

Tests updated for the new parser behaviour; full UI gate green (lint, 1153
vitest tests, strict tsc build).

fix(website): return 404 not 403 for missing pages on archive version subdomains

The 9 archived documentation subdomains (5-10..7-0.mock-server.com) front
private OAC S3 buckets, so S3 returns 403 for any missing object. Unlike the
main www/apex distribution, the per-version 'site' distributions had no
custom_error_response, so deleted/partial archive URLs answered with a bare
403 ('Blocked due to access forbidden') or soft-404. Google Search Console
keeps such URLs queued instead of dropping them.

Mirror the main distribution's mapping (403 -> 404, /error403.html) on the
archive distributions. error403.html exists on every archive bucket (verified
live, returns 200) and meta-refreshes to www, so users land on current docs
while crawlers see a clean 404 and drop stale URLs.

fix(release): bootstrap JDK 21 for binary bundles + hard-gate their presence

The release `binary` step builds JVM-less per-OS bundles with `jlink`, which
needs a JDK 21. The release-queue agent's AMI may only ship the Maven build
JDK (17), and the step is `soft_fail`, so the old hard `exit 1` when 21 was
absent silently dropped every bundle asset — exactly why 7.0.0 shipped with
no assets and every client launcher 404'd at runtime.

- Add shared helper `scripts/lib/ensure-host-jdk21.sh` that reuses an on-agent
  JDK 21 or bootstraps Temurin 21 on demand (jlink only; the Maven build stays
  on 17 via a per-invocation JAVA_HOME). Diagnostics go to stderr so stdout
  carries only the resolved JDK home.
- binary.sh: replace the hard-fail with the on-demand bootstrap; pass
  JAVA_HOME + --jdk-version 21 to build-all-bundles.sh.
- java-publish-snapshot-bundles.sh: use the same shared helper (was a
  near-identical inline block) so the two paths cannot drift.
- verify.sh: flip the binary-bundle liveness check from soft to HARD so a
  missing bundle fails the release (the verify step is a hard gate) instead
  of shipping silently broken clients.

feat(templates): load templates from a file and template response body files

Answers discussion #2350: combine externally stored response bodies
(FileBody, issue #2163) with response templating.

Two related additions:

- httpResponseTemplate / httpForwardTemplate accept a new `templateFile`
  field (classpath-or-filesystem path) as an alternative to the inline
  `template`. HttpTemplate.getTemplateContent() returns the inline template
  when present, otherwise reads the file; the three template action handlers
  now resolve via getTemplateContent(). Inline template wins when both set.

- A static httpResponse whose body is a FILE body can set `templateType`
  (VELOCITY or MUSTACHE): the file contents are rendered as a template
  against the request before being returned, while status/headers/contentType
  still come from the static response. Implemented via a new raw-text
  TemplateEngine.renderTemplate(template, request) on the text engines;
  JavaScript is unsupported for body files (its templates return a full
  response object, not text) and routes users to httpResponseTemplate.

Includes DTO/serializer/deserializer wiring, JSON + OpenAPI schema updates,
unit tests, and consumer + architecture docs.

- Add a MetricsLock @ClassRule (a shared ReentrantLock) to the metrics-mutating

feat(verify): match upstream responses in verification (core foundation)

Verification can now optionally match the response of a recorded
request-response exchange, not just the request. The presence of an
httpResponse matcher on a Verification (or an index-aligned httpResponses
list on a VerificationSequence) switches verification from counting
requests received to counting recorded request-response pairs whose
response matches — by status code, reason phrase, headers, and body
(reusing the existing request body matchers). When no response matcher is
supplied, behaviour is byte-for-byte identical to before.

- Verification.withResponse / VerificationSequence.withResponses
- new HttpResponseMatcher reusing body/header matcher primitives; body
  matcher construction extracted to BodyMatcherBuilder so request matching
  is unchanged
- MockServerEventLog.verify branches to a response-aware path for both the
  single and sequence cases, with "Response not found" failure messages
- VerificationDTO / VerificationSequenceDTO + JSON schemas + validators
- embedded OpenAPI model updated to keep the server contract consistent
- schema keeps expectationId/httpRequest mutual exclusivity while allowing
  httpResponse orthogonally (httpRequest+httpResponse is valid)

Clients, external OpenAPI spec, dashboard UI and consumer docs follow as
separate units.

docs(openapi): document httpResponse in verify / verifySequence schemas

Mirror the embedded server OpenAPI model in the external spec: the

expectationId(s)/httpRequest(s) mutually exclusive while allowing the
response matcher orthogonally.

- verify(HttpResponse, VerificationTimes) / verify(HttpResponse)
- verify(Verification) / verify(VerificationSequence) pass-throughs for
  building request+response (and response-sequence) verifications fluently

A response matcher counts recorded request-response pairs whose response
matches (by status, reason phrase, headers, body), optionally also matching
the request. Existing verify methods are unchanged. The two-arg
verify(RequestDefinition, HttpResponse) form is intentionally omitted to
avoid overload ambiguity with verify(RequestDefinition, VerificationTimes)
when the second argument is null — use the three-arg form or verify(Verification).

Adds proxy integration tests covering request+response, response-only,
body-matcher, verify(Verification), and response-sequence verification.

docs(verify): document response verification (consumer + event-system)

feat(clients): response verification across 7 client libraries

Add response-aware verification to the Node, Python, Ruby, Go, .NET, Rust
and PHP clients, mirroring the Java client: a response matcher can be passed
to verify (and an index-aligned list of responses to verifySequence),
serialized as httpResponse / httpResponses per the frozen wire format.

All additions are backward compatible — existing verify/verifySequence calls
serialize byte-identically. Response-only verification omits httpRequest from
the JSON entirely (the server schema rejects a present-but-null httpRequest);
each client uses its idiomatic omit-when-absent mechanism. In response
sequences, a position with no request matcher serialises as an empty {}
request, which is a valid "match any request" matcher.

Idiomatic per language: new methods in Node/Go/.NET/Rust/PHP, keyword args in
Python/Ruby. Tests added and run green in every client (Node verified against
a freshly built server jar).

fix(release): harden sync_to_origin_master to reset to FETCH_HEAD

`git fetch origin master` then `git reset --hard origin/master` lands on the
origin/master remote-tracking ref. In a normal clone that ref is updated by the
fetch, but in a shallow/CI clone whose configured refspec doesn't cover the
branch the fetch may only move FETCH_HEAD, leaving the tracking ref stale — so
the reset silently lands on an old commit. Reset to FETCH_HEAD (the ref just
fetched) instead, which always points at the fetched master tip.

Verified locally: in a clone/remote scenario with a commit pushed after the
clone, fetch + reset --hard FETCH_HEAD advances to the new tip.

fix(release): containerize Go client publish + add retry helper

The Go/Rust/.NET client + testcontainers publishes silently skipped on the
release agent: they probed `command -v <tool>` on the host, but the release-queue
AMI ships only Java/Maven/Docker, so the tool was absent and the step exited 0
with a WARNING — green build, nothing published.

Foundation for fixing the whole class:
- Add GO_IMAGE/RUST_IMAGE/DOTNET_IMAGE pins (the other toolchains — maven, node,
  ruby, python — were already pinned and containerized; these three were the gap).
- Add a retry() helper (exponential backoff, set -e-safe, propagates the real
  exit code) for transient network/registry failures.

Rework client-go.sh as the template: run `go vet` + the proxy-indexing nudge in
the pinned golang container (no host `go`), tag+push via host git wrapped in
retry, and HARD-fail on real errors. pkg.go.dev indexing is eventually-consistent
so the indexing nudge is retry-then-tolerate (surfaced, not swallowed); the
tag-push publish itself is hard.

Verified locally: retry() unit-tested (eventual success, exhaustion returns the
real code, set -e safe); `go vet` runs green in golang:1.21-bookworm against the
real module.

fix(release): containerize Rust + .NET client/TC publishes (hard-fail + retry)

Same fix as the Go client, applied to the Rust and .NET publishes that also
silently skipped (host `command -v cargo`/`dotnet` missing on the release agent
→ exit 0 + WARNING, nothing published):

- client-rust / tc-rust: run cargo check + cargo publish in $RUST_IMAGE; token via
  -e CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN (cargo reads it from env); retry the publish; HARD-fail
  on real errors; keep dry-run + idempotent "already on crates.io" skip;
  crates.io visibility is retry-then-tolerate (eventually-consistent).
- client-dotnet / tc-dotnet: run restore/build/pack/push in $DOTNET_IMAGE (scoped
  to the src project — the tc test project targets net10.0, unsupported by SDK 8);
  retry the push; HARD-fail; NuGet visibility retry-then-tolerate.

Adversarial review caught a secret leak: `--api-key "$KEY"` sat in the container
command args, which run-in-docker.sh does NOT redact (only -e values are). Fixed
by passing the key via -e and dereferencing it inside a single-quoted `sh -c`
body, so the literal key never appears in the logged command.

Verified locally (Docker): cargo check passes in rust:1-bookworm for both crates;
dotnet restore/build/pack succeed in sdk:8.0 for both projects (corp CA mounted).

fix(release): stop verify.sh crashing on the PHP/Packagist check

fix(release): resolve infinispan clustered-image deps in post-maven builds

The Docker Image step aborted in post-maven build #51:
  Could not find artifact org.mock-server:mockserver-core:jar:7.1.1-SNAPSHOT

docker.sh syncs origin/master, so the tree is at the in-dev SNAPSHOT version.
`mvn -pl mockserver-state-infinispan dependency:copy-dependencies` must resolve
the reactor tree (incl. mockserver-core at that SNAPSHOT) before -DexcludeGroupIds
drops it; in post-maven the Maven Central `install` was skipped, so the SNAPSHOT
core is neither in .m2 nor on Central → resolution fails. (Full releases worked
because Central's install populated .m2; #50 worked because master wasn't yet
bumped to the next SNAPSHOT.)

Run `mvn -DskipTests -Djacoco.skip=true -pl mockserver-state-infinispan -am
install` unconditionally before copy-dependencies so .m2 has core at the current
version. -Djacoco.skip=true is REQUIRED: mockserver-core binds jacoco:check to
verify, which install runs, and it fails with no coverage data under -DskipTests.
The image still ships the RELEASE_VERSION module JAR from Central (the install is
only to satisfy dependency resolution).

Verified locally (Docker, tree at 7.1.1-SNAPSHOT, corp CA in JDK cacerts): both
maven steps exit 0; 147 transitive libs copied (infinispan-core/jgroups/
protostream...), no mockserver-* leaked.

fix(release): rust --allow-dirty + .NET MCR pre-pull (build #51 publish failures)

- Rust (client + tc): `cargo publish` aborted with "files in the working

  re-pull.

fix(ci): derive Playwright image tag from lockfile (de-drift node browser tests)

The client-node browser tests ran in a hardcoded mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:
v1.60.0-noble image, but @playwright/test in package-lock.json is 1.61.0. Playwright
1.61 needs Chromium build 1228, absent from the 1.60.0 image, so every browser test
failed at launch ("browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist at
.../chromium_headless_shell-1228/...") — this had reddened mockserver-node for many
builds (predates and is unrelated to the recent npm/security changes).

Derive the image tag from the @playwright/test version in package-lock.json so the
bundled Chromium always matches; a future Dependabot bump can't re-drift it.
Verified: derived tag = v1.61.0-noble, and that image ships chromium-1228 /

fix(ci): clean vscode node_modules in-container to unblock editors checkout

mockserver-editors builds failed at checkout with "unlinkat .../mockserver-vscode/
node_modules/keytar/build/Release/keytar.node: permission denied" -> "cloning git
repository: exit status 128". Under the elastic-ci-stack's userns-remap, files the
node:20 container writes into the bind-mounted workspace are owned by a remapped UID
the buildkite-agent user can't delete, so the native keytar.node (pulled by
@vscode/vsce) left in node_modules blocked the NEXT build's git checkout/clean.

Add `trap "rm -rf node_modules" EXIT` to the in-container command so the container
(which owns those files) removes them on the way out, leaving the workspace cleanly
removable. The npm cache (--cache npm) is mounted separately and untouched.
(jetbrains-test.sh already sidesteps this by building in /tmp, not the workspace.)

fix(release): repair build #53 failures (cosign digest, crates.io UA/idempotency, NuGet prefix)

Build #53 (post-maven 7.1.0) got further than #52 — .NET client, Rust client,
PHP, VS Code and JetBrains all published — but 3 jobs still failed. Root causes
and fixes:

docker: cosign signing resolved the image digest with
`imagetools inspect --format '{{.Digest}}'`, but `.Digest` is not a field on
imagetools' template input (`.Manifest.Digest` is). `2>/dev/null` hid the
template error, so every digest came back empty and ALL signing failed, aborting
the release. Use `{{.Manifest.Digest}}`, capture stderr to a temp file so a
benign warning can't corrupt the digest, and surface the error instead of
swallowing it.

tc-rust / client-rust: the crates.io "already published?" pre-check curled
without a User-Agent; crates.io returns 403 to UA-less requests, so the check
silently failed and `cargo publish` hard-failed with "already exists on
crates.io index" on the already-published crate. Add a User-Agent to every
crates.io curl (pre-check + visibility, both crates) and wrap `cargo publish`
with run_idempotent so an already-published version is treated as success.
verify.sh's check_http/check_http_soft get the same User-Agent.

tc-dotnet: `Testcontainers.MockServer` sits under NuGet's reserved
`Testcontainers.*` ID prefix (owned by the Testcontainers org), so the push
403s regardless of the API key. Rename the published PackageId to
`MockServer.Testcontainers` (the package was never published — no consumers).
The assembly/namespace stay `Testcontainers.MockServer`, so consumer code is
unchanged: `dotnet add package MockServer.Testcontainers` then
`using Testcontainers.MockServer;`. Updates the csproj, the release + verify
scripts (nupkg filename + lowercased flat-container URLs), the module README,
the consumer docs page, the NuGet secret-setup runbook, and the cross-link

fix(release): resolve cosign image digest from plain imagetools output (version-portable)

Build #54's Docker job still failed at cosign signing: the digest came back
empty for every image ("skipping cosign sign ()" — empty parens, empty stderr).
Root cause: `docker buildx imagetools inspect --format '{{...}}'` template field
names are NOT portable across buildx versions. Locally `.Digest` errors and
`.Manifest.Digest` works; on the release agent `.Manifest.Digest` yields an
EMPTY string with no error — so neither template is safe everywhere.

Parse the `Digest:` line from imagetools inspect's PLAIN output instead
(`awk '/^Digest:/{print $2; exit}'`). The first `^Digest:` line is the
index/manifest-list digest — exactly what cosign signs — and that output format
has been stable across buildx versions for years. Stderr is captured to a temp
file (not merged into the digest, not swallowed) so a genuine failure (auth,
missing image) is surfaced; `|| true` keeps pipefail from aborting on a non-zero
inspect. Validated locally for both the success and missing-image paths.

fix(release): unbreak MCP publish (validate cmd) and node_modules checkout leak

Two independent post-maven release failures:

MCP Registry: mcp.sh called `mcp-publisher validate`, but the pinned CLI
v1.2.3 has no validate subcommand (only init/login/logout/publish), so the
step hard-failed with 'Unknown command: validate'. Bump the pin to v1.7.9
(first line with validate; login/publish flags unchanged) and fix the
download URL — the release asset-name scheme changed at v1.7.0 to drop the
version from the filename (mcp-publisher_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz). Dry-run now
validates server.json against the live registry schema and exits 0.

Binary Bundles (and any job sharing the agent): failed at git checkout with
'unlinkat .../mockserver-vscode/node_modules/.../keytar.node: permission
denied' -> 'exit status 128'. Under the elastic-ci-stack userns-remap, an
in-container npm ci/npm i in the bind-mounted workspace leaves node_modules
owned by a remapped UID the host agent cannot delete, breaking the next
job's clean. Commit 7e26ac3c2 fixed this for the editors test pipeline but
not the release components. Add a shared clean_workspace_node_modules helper
(removes node_modules from inside a container, which owns the files) and
register it as an EXIT trap in the three in-workspace npm components:
vscode.sh, tc-node.sh and npm.sh.

fix(release): add MCP label to published Dockerfile + make finalize idempotent

Two more post-maven release failures (build #56):

MCP Registry: the registry rejected the server.json publish with 400
'OCI image docker.io/mockserver/mockserver:7.1.0 is missing required
annotation io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name'. The published image is
built from the docker/local buildx context, but the LABEL only existed in
the top-level docker/Dockerfile (which the release does not use) — so the
live image had no such label. Add the LABEL to docker/local/Dockerfile (the
context docker.sh actually builds + pushes as mockserver/mockserver:<ver>)

Finalize: finalize.sh bumps the pom RELEASE_VERSION -> NEXT_VERSION via
update_pom_versions, which hard-fails if no pom contains the old version. On
a re-run where a prior build's finalize already bumped+pushed the pom to
NEXT_VERSION, there is no RELEASE_VERSION left and the step died with 'no
pom.xml contained <version>7.1.0</version>'. Since the commit is finalize's
last step (after mvn deploy), a pom at NEXT_VERSION on master means the
deploy already succeeded. Add a read-only poms_contain_version helper and an
idempotency guard that skips the bump/deploy/commit when already finalized.

fix(deps): stop leaking vulnerable commons-beanutils to consumers (#1981)

velocity-tools-generic:3.1 (the latest release) hard-declares
commons-beanutils:1.9.4 and pulls commons-digester3:3.2 which declares
commons-beanutils:1.8.3 — both affected by GHSA-wxr5-93ph-8wr9
(CVE-2025-48734). The build already pinned 1.11.0 in the parent pom's
dependencyManagement, but dependencyManagement is not transitive, so
downstream consumers of mockserver-core still resolved the vulnerable
versions (as observed in #1981 via kotest).

Exclude commons-beanutils from velocity-tools-generic in mockserver-core
(pruning the whole vulnerable subtree, including the digester3 edge) and
declare commons-beanutils directly at the managed 1.11.0 so velocity-tools
and digester3 keep beanutils on the classpath and the fixed version
propagates to consumers via Maven nearest-wins.

Verified: mockserver-core dependency:tree resolves commons-beanutils:1.11.0
only (no 1.9.4/1.8.3); 42 velocity templating tests pass.

feat(core): numeric comparison operators for header/cookie/query matching

feat(core): expose scenario state to response templates

A new `scenario` template helper lets Velocity/JavaScript/Mustache response
templates read and write the live ScenarioManager state — scenario.get(name),
scenario.set(name,state), scenario.matches(name,state) — so a value captured in
one request can drive a later response (stateful scenario mocking). The helper
resolves the live manager per call via the CrossProtocolEventBus singleton that
HttpState already publishes, so template writes and matcher state transitions
see each other. New scenario test classes are pinned to the sequential test
phase and serialized with a shared lock (they mutate the global singleton).

feat(core): declarative capture rules into scenario state

An expectation can carry a list of capture rules { source, expression, into }

under 'into' (resolved via the live CrossProtocolEventBus singleton), so a later
request's response template can read it via the WS2.1 scenario helper — enabling
auth->resource->confirm journeys with no manual scenario triggers. Fires once per
matched expectation before the response is built; missing/malformed expressions
are skipped (never throw, never overwrite). XPath uses the XXE-hardened parser.
Round-trips via JSON (CaptureRuleDTO + schema). mvn verified: CaptureProcessorTest
+ serialization + guards green.

alongside the existing client-credentials grant. Served as generated
HttpClassCallback expectations; cross-request state in a new OidcAuthorizationStore
singleton (registerProvider made atomic; reset wired into HttpState.reset).
mvn verified: OidcProviderGeneratorTest (28) + global-state guards green.

fix(editors): make the expectation schema root IntelliJ-navigable so completion and validation work

The bundled expectation JSON Schema had a root oneOf (single expectation OR
array). IntelliJ's JSON-schema engine cannot offer completion or validation
through a root oneOf reached only via $ref, so the JetBrains plugin gave no
autocomplete or error highlighting on *.mockserver.json files (VS Code, whose
engine expands the oneOf, worked).

Rebuild the root as a concrete object/array union: type [object, array] with the
expectation's properties + additionalProperties + anyOf inlined for the object
form and items + minItems for the array form. Semantically equivalent for valid
and invalid documents (verified with a Draft-07 validator), but IntelliJ can now
navigate it. Regenerated both editors' schemas from the generator.

Also add captureRule to REFERENCE_FILES (the committed schema was stale and
missing the declarative capture rule that expectation.json references), and add
a generator self-check that fails if the root ever regresses to a oneOf.

feat(core): expectation namespacing / multi-tenancy

Let multiple teams or test-suites share ONE MockServer without their
expectations colliding. Each Expectation can carry an optional namespace
(null = global); a request's namespace is read from a configurable header
(matchNamespaceHeader, default X-MockServer-Namespace; env
MOCKSERVER_MATCH_NAMESPACE_HEADER). Matching is scoped: a request matches
expectations in its own namespace plus global (null) ones, never another
tenant's. A request with no namespace header sees only global expectations
(true isolation by construction).

Control plane is namespace-aware: clear?namespace=T clears only T's
expectations (event log left intact), retrieve?type=active_expectations&
namespace=T returns tenant+global, reset stays a full reset. The Java client
gains clearByNamespace(String) and retrieveActiveExpectations(req, namespace).
Expectation.withNamespace trims blank to null; namespace round-trips through
the DTO/JSON/schema/OpenAPI model and is omitted when null (no payload churn).
A DEBUG diagnostic explains a namespace-gated non-match.

Fully additive and backward-compatible: the no-namespace hot path is unchanged
(no extra allocation, single cheap header lookup, INFO behaviour identical).

feat(core): mockable HTTP response trailers (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, Servlet)

Previously only gRPC responses could carry trailing headers. HttpResponse now
has an optional trailers field with builders mirroring headers
(withTrailers/withTrailer, getTrailers/getTrailerList/getTrailerMultimap),
emitted as protocol-appropriate trailing headers:

- HTTP/1.1: forces chunked transfer-encoding and an announcing Trailer header,
  dropping any Content-Length (trailers and Content-Length are mutually exclusive
  per RFC 7230 3.3.1); trailers ride the final LastHttpContent.
- HTTP/2: Netty converts the LastHttpContent trailing headers to a trailing
  HEADERS frame (endStream) on both the default and gRPC-multiplex pipelines.
- HTTP/3: a trailing Http3HeadersFrame is emitted after the data frame(s).
- Streaming bodies and the Servlet/WAR path also emit trailers.

gRPC responses are unaffected (they build their own grpc-status trailing frame
and do not read this field). Trailers round-trip through the DTO/JSON/schema/
OpenAPI model and are omitted when empty. Backward compatible: with no trailers
the response is byte-identical to before (single FullHttpResponse). ByteBuf
ref-counting verified leak-free across every branch including exception/abort.

  makes no changes (read-only/investigation/review) — no work runs in the bare
  checkout. Helper subagents still share the spawning session's worktree so the
  review gate sees uncommitted in-flight work; spec section 8.3 is reconciled so
  the independent session (not every agent) is the isolation unit.

- Delegate-to-subagent is the near-universal default for implementation AND
  investigation; the orchestrator's primary job is to coordinate subagents,
  which is where model/temperature/effort are selected — the main lever for
  managing inference cost and determinism.

- Reasoning effort is now a first-class, audited routing variable: explicit
  effort on every .claude/agents definition, threaded through the spec and the
  control-surface rules (control-integrity, risk-authority, evaluation-harness,
  decision-log) so effort-routing changes are gated, eval-gated, and logged.

docs: surface HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 in key feature summaries

Make HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support visible in the user-facing capability summaries
where it was missing or understated (the root README and Docker Hub readme
already cover it). Website homepage headline + meta description + protocol
bullet, Helm chart description, MCP server.json description, VS Code marketplace
keywords, and the JetBrains plugin marketplace blurb now mention HTTP/1.1,
HTTP/2 and experimental HTTP/3 (QUIC). Accurate about scope: HTTP/1.1+HTTP/2
(h2/h2c)+HTTPS share the auto-detected unified port; HTTP/3 (QUIC) is
experimental on its own UDP port.

feat(core): stream-level error injection for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

Extend the HttpError action with an optional streamError code so a matched
expectation resets the stream instead of returning a response — for resilience
testing of clients that must handle mid-stream resets. Well-known codes via a
StreamErrorCode enum (HTTP/2 RFC 7540 7: NO_ERROR..HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED; HTTP/3
RFC 9114 8.1: H3_NO_ERROR..H3_VERSION_FALLBACK), a raw long setter, and
withStreamErrorCodeName(name).

- HTTP/2: RST_STREAM via Http2ConnectionHandler.resetStream (default path) or a
  DefaultHttp2ResetFrame on the multiplex stream channel — sibling streams and
  the connection stay alive.
- HTTP/3: resets the QUIC stream (shutdownOutput) via a transport-neutral
  StreamErrorWriter seam so QUIC types stay out of mockserver-core.
- HTTP/1.1: no stream concept, falls back to dropping the connection.
- streamError takes precedence over dropConnection when both are set.

Security: the internal x-http2-stream-id is now trusted only when the request
genuinely arrived over HTTP/2 — for h2c the unified-port handler sets a
server-side negotiated-protocol channel attribute, so a plain HTTP/1.1 client
cannot forge a stream id into the request model/logs.

streamError round-trips through the DTO/JSON/schema/OpenAPI (int64) model and is
exposed on the Node, Python and Ruby clients; omitted when null; existing
HttpError behaviour byte-identical when unset. review-final PASS. mvn: core +
netty H2/H3 integration (H3 on real QUIC) + client model tests all green.

feat(core): match and verify requests by negotiated protocol (incl. HTTP/3)

Add HTTP_3 to the Protocol enum and let users match expectations on, and verify
recorded requests by, the protocol a request actually arrived over. The request
matcher already evaluated protocol; this closes the gaps:

- HTTP/3 requests are now tagged protocol=HTTP_3 (the h3 ALPN id is server-
  trusted, so it cannot be spoofed by a header).
- HttpRequestPrettyPrintedDTO (the default JSON retrieval format) previously
  omitted protocol entirely, so retrieved/recorded requests lost it for HTTP/2
  too — now it round-trips, enabling verify(request().withProtocol(...)) and
  retrieveRecordedRequests to carry the protocol.
- HTTP_3 added to the JSON schema, OpenAPI models, and bundled editor schemas;
  HarConverter maps HTTP_3 -> "HTTP/3".
- NettyHttpClient warns and falls back to ALPN when asked to forward an
  HTTP/3-tagged request over TCP (QUIC can't ride a TCP connection).

Backward compatible: protocol is optional; an expectation with no protocol
matches a request regardless of how it arrived. review-cheap PASS. mvn: matcher
+ serializer + HAR + guard tests and a live HTTP/3 verify integration test (real
QUIC) all green.

test(jetbrains): guard the JSON-schema provider wiring with a headless platform test

Adds MockServerSchemaWiringTest (BasePlatformTestCase) asserting that

This guards the extension-point registration bug that silently disabled
