Blast radius is limited to the Java client: an expectation sent over the
REST API with a blank specUrlOrPayload is deserialised as a plain
request, since RequestDefinitionDTODeserializer only builds an
OpenAPIDefinitionDTO when the spec is non-blank. A spec that fails to
parse was already safe - the matcher list is assigned an empty ArrayList
before parsing, so it ends up empty rather than null.

fix(azure): round-trip metadata keys above U+00FF instead of corrupting them

encodeKey escaped non-alphanumerics with String.format("%02x", (int) c),
which silently widens to four hex digits for any code point above 0xFF,
while decodeKey always consumed exactly two. A metadata key of 中文 was
therefore stored as _4e2d_6587 and read back as N2de87, and emoji-✓ came
back as emoji-'13 - a silently corrupted key, with no error anywhere.

Escapes are now a fixed four hex digits, which covers the whole UTF-16
range; characters outside the BMP are encoded as their two surrogate
code units and recombine on decode. A leading digit is now escaped as
well, which keeps the encoded key starting with a letter or underscore
as Azure requires and removes the previous _00 guard prefix - that
prefix is ambiguous against a four-digit escape, which can itself begin
_00. Decoding also validates that all four characters are hex rather
than relying on parseInt to throw, since parseInt accepts a leading sign
and would otherwise decode _-12f as an escape.

Keys written by an earlier version that contain escaped characters will
not decode correctly. The two formats cannot be distinguished
unambiguously (_4e2d is either one four-digit escape or _4e followed by
a literal 2d), so no compatibility shim is possible; blob metadata is
ephemeral mock state, so clear the container if this matters.

The bug survived because the only coverage was the shared
BlobStoreContract fixture, which used ASCII keys exclusively, and there
was no direct test of encodeMetadataKeys/decodeMetadataKeys at all. Both
gaps are closed: a direct round-trip test that needs no Docker, and a
new shared contract case covering non-ASCII keys for every backend.

The contract asserts "never silently corrupt" rather than "always
round-trip", because the backends genuinely differ in what they can
represent and refusing an unrepresentable key is correct behaviour.
Azure, GCS, filesystem and in-memory round-trip these keys; S3 rejects
them with a 400, since it carries metadata in x-amz-meta-* HTTP headers
whose field names are ASCII tokens. Which camp a backend is in is
declared per backend via supportsNonAsciiMetadataKeys(), and the
rejecting backend must also assert the rejection is a genuine invalid
request - S3 pins S3Exception with status 400 and asserts the blob did
not land. A blanket catch of RuntimeException was deliberately avoided:
it would also pass for a stopped container, an expired credential or a
connection reset, making the S3 arm of the contract permanently green
regardless of behaviour.

No backend was found in the third camp - accepting the write and
returning a different key. Azure was the only such case.

fix(oidc): validate presented tokens instead of fabricating success

The mock OIDC provider reported success without checking what it was given, so
tests asserting that an application rejects a bad token passed while proving
nothing.

- /introspect ignored the token entirely for JWT providers (the default) and
  reported `active` from static configuration, so any string - garbage, expired,
  tampered, or issued by another provider - introspected as active. It now
  verifies the token against the provider's signing key and validity window, and
  fails closed.
- /revoke returned 200 and did nothing, so a revoked token kept introspecting as
  active. Revocations are now recorded and honoured (RFC 7009).
- /userinfo was a static response returning the subject and every configured
  claim to any caller, with no Authorization header inspection at all. It is now
  an OAuth2 protected resource returning 401 per RFC 6750, and the challenge
  distinguishes missing credentials from an invalid token.
- Inactive introspection responses carried sub/iss/aud/scope and every additional
  claim; they now carry `active:false` and nothing else (RFC 7662 section 2.2).
  A request with no token parameter returns 400 invalid_request.
- The issuer was hardcoded to http://localhost:1080 and never derived from the
  request, so a provider on a random or container-mapped port advertised an
  issuer no conformant client would accept (OIDC Discovery section 4.3). It is
  now derived per request from the Host header, honouring X-Forwarded-Proto
  through an http/https allow-list; an explicit issuer still wins.
- Discovery advertised response types that /authorize rejects.
- A JWT with no exp claim was treated as valid; exp is now required.
- /token, /introspect, /revoke and /userinfo send Cache-Control: no-store.

Token validation for /introspect and /userinfo is a single shared path
(OidcTokenResolver) so the two endpoints cannot drift apart. Conformance is
asserted with the independent nimbus oauth2-oidc-sdk at test scope rather than
against MockServer's own objects, which is how these defects survived: every
existing test asserted the happy path against a pre-baked response.

Each fix is covered by a test proven to fail when the fix is degraded.

fix(streaming): answer WebSocket control frames, order GraphQL subscription frames, preserve CR in SSE data

Three defects sharing one shape - a stream that looks healthy and delivers
nothing - the same family as issue #2419.

WebSocket control frames (RFC 6455 5.5.1 / 5.5.2)
  The handshake is performed by hand via WebSocketServerHandshaker.handshake,
  which installs only the frame codec and contributes no control-frame
  behaviour; WebSocketServerProtocolHandler appears nowhere in the codebase.
  Mocked WebSockets therefore never answered a PING and never echoed a CLOSE,
  so every keepalive-based client (browsers, OkHttp pingInterval,
  Java-WebSocket's connection-lost detector) eventually tore the session down
  mid-test. Six control-plane handlers answer PING correctly; only the single
  user-facing path did not, which is why it went unnoticed. Server-initiated
  closes now send 1000 rather than an empty frame that left clients reporting
  1005 "no status received".

GraphQL subscription frame ordering
  pushNextSequence recursed through the payload list without waiting for each
  frame to be sent, then wrote the terminal `complete` immediately. With any
  delay configured, `complete` reached the wire before every `next`, and both
  Apollo and graphql-ws discard post-terminal messages - so the subscription
  delivered nothing at all. Each `next` is now chained off the previous frame's
  send completion, which also makes per-message delays cumulative rather than
  all firing from the same instant.

  Why this survived: the test fake recorded `next` frames into a private list
  while `complete` went to the channel, so the two were asserted from separate
  sinks and their relative order on the wire was structurally unobservable. The
  fake now writes to the channel and genuinely defers a delayed frame, so wire
  order is a real observation.

Legacy graphql-ws subprotocol
  Accepted at handshake but never implemented, so a legacy client's `start` was
  silently ignored. Now handles start/stop/connection_terminate, emits `data`
  rather than `next`, and uses the single-object error payload shape.

SSE lone carriage return
  data was split on LF only, so a bare CR was emitted raw inside a `data:` line.
  Per WHATWG an event stream splits on CRLF, CR or LF, so a real client treats
  it as a line terminator and drops everything after it. id and event were
  already sanitised; data was not.

WebSocket text matcher
  The text comparison was guarded by `frame instanceof TextWebSocketFrame`, so a
  PING, PONG or BINARY frame skipped it entirely and fell through to a match,
  firing the matcher's responses on client keepalive traffic. Reachable when the
  frame type is set after the text; the text setters otherwise pin it to TEXT.

Every fix was proven by degrading it and confirming the tests go red.

test(streaming): verify WebSocket and SSE conformance with third-party clients

Adds Java-WebSocket 1.6.0 and okhttp-sse 5.3.2 at test scope, following the
precedent already set by the test-scoped gRPC client. Both are implementations
of the same RFCs independent of Netty - the library MockServer itself is built
on - so they do not share the server's assumptions.

This closes the gap that let the issue #2419 family ship: conformance had only
ever been asserted against MockServer's own objects, so handler-level tests
stayed green while mocked WebSockets answered no PING, echoed no CLOSE, and SSE
silently truncated at a bare carriage return.

The close-echo assertion reads raw wire bytes rather than going through a
client library, because neither Java-WebSocket nor OkHttp surfaces the received
close frame's payload: both report the locally-sent code when no echo arrives,
so neither can distinguish a proper echo from the server dropping the TCP
connection. Reading the bytes is the only observation that discriminates.

GraphQL subscription ordering is deliberately covered at unit level only, and
the reason is recorded in the test file: the feature cannot currently be
configured on a running server at all. HttpWebSocketResponseDTO types
graphqlSubscriptionFilter as GraphQLBodyDTO, which has all-final fields, no
no-arg constructor and no @JsonCreator, so no control-plane JSON parses; and no
client gets that far anyway, because GraphQLBody always emits a "type"
discriminator that the JSON schema rejects under additionalProperties:false.
Both are separate serialization defects.

Records both dependencies and their transitive set in docs/operations/security.md,
since that table is the manual triage surface when a CVE lands. okhttp-sse pulls
okhttp-jvm, okio-jvm and kotlin-stdlib, all test scope in one module.

fix(wasm): ship the chicory interpreter so WASM rules work in released artifacts

The chicory WASM interpreter was declared <optional>true</optional> in
mockserver-core. Maven keeps an optional dependency on its declaring module's
own classpath but does not propagate it to consumers, so mockserver-netty --
the module the jar-with-dependencies, brew-tar and every Docker image are
assembled from -- never received it.

Every shipped artifact therefore carried the nine org/mockserver/wasm classes
with no interpreter behind them. Uploading a module and registering a WASM body
matcher both succeeded, then every match failed closed on a
NoClassDefFoundError, so a documented, advertised feature silently never
matched. Verified by inspecting the built artifact: 9 wasm classes, 0 chicory
classes; and end-to-end against the fat jar, where a matching request returned
404 in 12ms with a WARNING naming the missing class.

The failure was already fail-closed and correctly bounded -- callMatch catches
Throwable and callWithinBudget rethrows an unwrapped Error (efc0d256c), so it
did not hang or drop connections. Only the packaging was wrong.

Ship chicory rather than degrade gracefully. GraalJS is the precedent for a
genuinely optional engine -- unbundled, its own image variant, a classpath
probe and an actionable error -- but its rationale is size and that does not
transfer: GraalVM is ~262 MB, chicory ~365 KB. Measured cost on the standalone
jar is +360,376 bytes (+0.35%). WASM stays gated off by default via
wasmEnabled=false so the bundled interpreter is inert until opted into, and
mockserver-client-java's existing exclusion keeps it off the client.

The guard must live in mockserver-netty, a consumer of core. An equivalent test
in core is structurally incapable of failing, because an optional dependency is
present on its declaring module's own test classpath -- still observable there
for polyglot, js and slf4j-jdk14. This bug class has precedent: issue #2097 lost
the shaded jar's SLF4J provider by the same mechanism.

test(control-plane): pin the mTLS trust anchor per-server and cover the OIDC denial path

The control-plane mTLS negative test used the process-global ConfigurationProperties
store as a client-configuration vehicle: it set the CA chain to ca.pem, started the
server, then rewrote the same global store to separateca/ purely to build a client
signed by a different CA. That relied on the server having frozen ca.pem at bootstrap.

Since the authentication handler became derived from the live configuration, it no
longer is. A Configuration reads through to the static store for any field it has not
set itself, so the rewrite re-pointed the RUNNING server's trust anchor at the very CA
that signed the supposedly-unauthorised client, which then authenticated correctly -
24/24 red. The control plane was never open; the test was measuring the wrong thing.

The server now pins its CA chain, certificate and key on its own Configuration
instance, and the differently-signed client is built on a separate instance, so no
global state is touched and the running server's trust anchor cannot move. Both
servers additionally pin the two mechanisms they do not use to false rather than
letting them read through, so an unrelated test that leaves JWT or mTLS enabled cannot
silently chain an extra handler onto them - the same bug class this commit removes.

Adds the missing OIDC negative integration test. The package had mTLS and JWT denial
coverage but nothing for OIDC, and the positive OIDC path proves nothing about
enforcement: a null handler maps to "authenticated" and would pass it. Twenty-five
rejection cases (untrusted signing key, wrong issuer, wrong audience, missing required
scope, expired, no exp, malformed, absent and non-Bearer Authorization, across every
control-plane route) plus one positive control, so the negatives cannot pass vacuously
against a handler that denies everything.

Both suites were verified to discriminate by degrading the production code: forcing
ControlPlaneAuthenticationHandlerFactory.build() to return null (the original
fail-open) turns mTLS 24/24, OIDC 25/26 and JWT 30/32 red, and a permissive handler
does the same. In each case the positive control stays green.

Documents the behaviour itself, which is the substantive change for users: the
control-plane trust anchor is mutable at runtime rather than frozen at startup. That is
what makes hardening a running instance take effect, but it means any configuration
route - system property, Configuration setter, PUT /mockserver/configuration - can
re-point the trust anchor of a live server, and a Configuration left unset follows the
global store. Pin it on the instance the server is started with.

AuthenticationHandler now records that implementations delegate in both directions:
mTLS, JWT and the deny-all handler implement only the boolean method and inherit the
default authenticate(), while the OIDC handler overrides authenticate() and delegates
the boolean back to it. The enforcement point calls authenticate(), so an edit made
only to the boolean method of a handler that overrides authenticate() has no effect.

fix(client-node): generate types from the in-repo spec and gate them against the server schema

mockserver-client-node/scripts/build_server_typescript.sh generated mockServer.d.ts
from a remote SwaggerHub schema pinned to mock-server-openapi/5.15.x — three major
versions behind the server, fetched over the network, and diffed by nothing. Because
no CI step ever regenerated it, the file quietly stopped being generated and became
hand-maintained while the script still claimed to produce it, so running the script
would have silently reverted the Node types to a 5.15-era contract.

Generation now reads the in-repo spec. Investigating this showed the types are not
what is stale: mockServer.d.ts covers all 41 properties of the server's authoritative
expectation.json, while the in-repo OpenAPI spec declares only 29 and is missing seven
expectation actions the server accepts (binaryResponse, dnsResponse, grpcBidiResponse,
grpcStreamResponse, httpForwardValidateAction, httpForwardWithFallback, httpLlmResponse).
Regenerating from the spec today would therefore DROP those actions and break the
type-level fidelity gate with 98 tsc errors. The script refuses to overwrite when
regeneration would lose actions, naming them and pointing at the spec; completing the
spec is left to the unit that owns it.

The new drift gate asserts against expectation.json — the artifact the server actually
validates with — in both directions:

  - every action the server accepts is declared by mockServer.d.ts;
  - nothing is declared that the server would reject. This found a real defect:
    openAPIDefinition was a top-level expectation member, but it is a request-level
    concept and expectation.json sets additionalProperties:false, so an expectation
    using it typechecked green and was then rejected with 400. Removed; the OpenAPI
    request form remains reachable through httpRequest, whose RequestDefinition union
    already includes OpenAPIDefinition;
  - the two committed copies of the spec stay byte-identical, and the spec's own gap
    is pinned as a ratchet that fails when it widens AND when it closes without the
    pin being updated.

A commit touching only the published copy of the spec now also triggers the Node
pipeline, so the byte-identity assertion fires on the change most likely to break it
instead of surfacing later against an unrelated commit.

Also adds an end-to-end acceptance test. The existing action-key test captured requests
with a throwaway listener that replied 201 to anything, so it proved the client emitted
one action but not that a real server accepted the result — and its per-action payloads
were in fact schema-invalid. The new test creates an expectation through the client for
every action the schema declares and asserts a real MockServer accepted and stored it,
and drives the rejection path through .then(onFulfilled, onRejected) rather than await,
so a regression of the single-argument .then() bug that once turned failed verifications
into passes cannot hide behind await's own reject path.

The action/non-action split now lives in test/lib/action_keys.js, required by the three
test files and by the shell guard, replacing four copies kept in sync only by comments.

fix(async): deliver AsyncAPI publishes and subscriptions that silently went nowhere

AMQP publishes were not waited on, so an unroutable message was reported as
delivered. Publisher confirms are now awaited per message, and a nack or
confirm timeout fails the publish instead of passing silently.

A failure on one channel no longer stops the rest of the spec publishing.
Failures are contained per message, accumulated, and reported together, so a
single unroutable channel cannot silence every other channel indefinitely.

MQTT wildcard subscriptions recorded nothing, because recorded messages were
matched against the subscription by string equality rather than by MQTT
topic-filter semantics. Kafka Avro messages written with an unexpected schema
id were decoded against the wrong schema instead of being rejected.

A channel closed by a broker that does not support publisher confirms is now
replaced rather than left dead, and construction fails loudly when it cannot
be replaced. RabbitMQ remains the supported broker: the confirm-less fallback
is covered by a modelled-response unit test, not by a live broker.

fix(http2): deliver SSE, streaming, metrics and MCP responses to HTTP/2 clients

Netty's HTTP/2 codec routes an outbound response onto a stream by reading the
x-http2-stream-id header. When the header is absent it does not fail - it
allocates a fresh server-initiated stream, so the requesting client receives
zero bytes and hangs until its own timeout while the server logs a perfectly
normal successful response.

Why these sites were missed. Only MockServerHttpResponseToFullHttpResponse
knew about the header, and it derives it from HttpResponse.getStreamId(). Every
handler that builds a Netty response by hand therefore bypassed it:

  - HttpSseResponseActionHandler, MetricsHandler, McpStreamableHttpHandler and
    the two WebSocket-upgrade rejections never had the id at all;
  - NettyResponseWriter.writeStreamingResponse is subtler - writeResponse HAD
    already copied the id onto the model response, but the writer copies only
    getHeaderMultimap() onto the Netty head and the id lives in a separate
    field, so it was dropped on the floor;
  - the mapper's own catch-all encoding-failure path built its response
    directly, so an encoding error was invisible to an HTTP/2 client too.

This is the same defect as issue #2419 (server-streaming gRPC delivering zero
messages). That fix's stated remedy - funnel direct writes through one place -
was applied to the gRPC module only, which is why the siblings survived. The
remedy is now applied across every known direct-write site via Http2StreamIds.

GrpcStreamResponseActionHandler also carried a second instance: it stamped
BEFORE applying the expectation's headers, so a user-supplied
x-http2-stream-id overwrote the correct id with a foreign one - a
PROTOCOL_ERROR/GOAWAY that hangs the client just as badly. Stamping now
happens after the header loop, and replaces rather than appends.

Http2StreamIdAuditHandler warns (once per connection) when an HTTP/2 response
head still goes out unstamped, so the next instance is found on the first test
run rather than in production. It deliberately does not repair the head: this
pipeline multiplexes many streams over one connection and streaming responses
are written long after their request was read, so any inferred id would
sometimes belong to another client's stream - leaking one client's data to
another is worse than the hang it would fix.

No test asserted the wire header on any non-gRPC response, and the SSE tests
used HTTP/1.1 raw sockets, which is why this survived. Http2SseStreamingIntegrationTest
now drives a real Netty HTTP/2 multiplex client; degrading the fix makes it
receive nothing and time out, reproducing the reported signature exactly.

fix(http3): stop emitting connection-specific headers HTTP/3 forbids

RFC 9114 section 4.2 bans Connection, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Connection,
Transfer-Encoding and Upgrade on an HTTP/3 message, and permits TE only with
the exact value "trailers". A receiver MUST treat a message carrying one as
malformed, so letting one through does not merely add a useless header - it
can make a conforming client reject the whole response.

toHttp3HeadersFrame filtered only two of the five. The reachable case is
proxy/forward mode: FullHttpResponseToMockServerHttpResponse copies an
upstream response's headers onto the model wholesale, stripping only the
HTTP/2 extension headers, so an HTTP/1.1 origin answering with
"Keep-Alive: timeout=5, max=100" had it relayed verbatim onto an HTTP/3
response. An expectation setting such a header explicitly does the same.

The filter folds header names to lower case, so it is pinned to Locale.ROOT.
Under a Turkish default locale "CONNECTION" folds to "connection" with a
dotless i and the entire filter is silently bypassed. Sibling case-folds in
this package have the same exposure and are left for a follow-up.

Also: streaming responses announced a content-length copied from the model
response, describing a different body than the one actually streamed. It is
now omitted on the streaming path and still sent for non-streaming responses,
asserted both on the bridge and at the writer call site - the call site being
the half that can regress by passing the wrong flag.

test(http): add a per-transport response-encode smoke contract

AbstractTransportDecodeSmokeIntegrationTest has seven methods, all covering
request DECODE. There was no encode counterpart - yet every bug in this family
was a response-ENCODE bug, invisible both to a decode test and to any test
asserting against MockServer's own model objects. That asymmetry is the
structural reason issue #2419 and its siblings shipped.

Each method sends withSecure(true) so the HTTP/2 subclasses upgrade it to
Protocol.HTTP_2 and it runs over real HTTP/2 there, HTTPS elsewhere. Worth
noting: the existing decode methods do NOT set it, so they have only ever run
over HTTP/1.1 even in the HTTP/2 test classes. h2c cannot be reached this way
at all - NettyHttpClient downgrades HTTP_2 to HTTP/1.1 when the request is not
secure - so h2c encode coverage remains a gap.

SSE deliberately has no method here. The shared harness cannot assert an SSE
body: NettyHttpClient installs StreamingAwareHttpObjectAggregator, which
detects text/event-stream and RELAYS rather than aggregates, so makeRequest
returns 200 with a null body on every transport. A method here would have
asserted nothing about SSE anywhere - the vacuous coverage this whole exercise
exists to eliminate. SSE-over-HTTP/2 is covered instead by
Http2SseStreamingIntegrationTest with a real HTTP/2 client.

StreamingBody likewise cannot be expressed: it has no serializer or DTO and is
only ever set by StreamingResponseRelayHandler on the proxy relay path. It
stays covered at unit level.

The WAR transports reject ConnectionOptions outright, so the chunked method is
guarded by supportsChunkedResponses(). Wiring into a base class that ~20
subclasses inherit means the blast radius is every module with a subclass -
mockserver-war, mockserver-junit-rule and mockserver-spring-test-listener - not
just the one module in view.

fix(ui): stop generated code contradicting asymmetric boolean switches

The C# and Rust generators kept their own truthiness guards, so unticking
"close connection" still produced code that closed the connection. The shared
builder and the Java generator were corrected earlier; these two are separate
transducers over the generated JSON and were missed.

fallbackOnTimeout carried the same defect and had never been fixed. Its
handler treats an absent field as true, so turning the switch off omitted the
field and the server fell back anyway.

Loading an expectation into the composer now reads each field with its own
server default rather than assuming absent means off, so opening an existing
SSE or WebSocket expectation and saving it no longer inverts the setting.

Regenerates the python, go, node and ruby golden files, which were left stale
by the earlier partial fix and had been failing since it landed.

test(client-php): exercise every fixture and stop the count assertion drifting

The shared fixture corpus grew to 56 while the PHP count assertion stayed at
44, so the suite failed on every build. Python and Ruby were moved to a lower
bound when the fixtures were added; PHP now matches.

A lower bound alone does not catch a fixture that is present but never run,
so the fixture directory is enumerated independently of the data provider and
the two must agree.

Corrects the class docblock, which read as evidence that the PHP client covers
every field. The zero-gap result follows from replaying the decoded array
unchanged, and says nothing about the typed model, whose coverage is asserted
by the per-class unit tests.

fix(graphql): allow a subscription filter to be set on a running server

The filter could not be set by any route. The expectation schema rejected the
GRAPHQL discriminator that the serializer always writes, and behind that the
body DTO had no creator, so Jackson could not instantiate it from raw JSON
either. Both had to be fixed together; the schema alone only moved the failure
to an opaque parse error.

The server's own serialised output was invalid against its own schema as a
result, so an expectation carrying a filter could be created but not read back.

Covered by tests that drive a real client over graphql-transport-ws against a
running server, asserting a matching subscription receives its payload and a
non-matching one receives an error rather than a message.

fix(grpc): return the real health and reflection answers, and stop locale-folding HTTP/3 headers

BREAKING BEHAVIOUR: a health check for a service that was never registered now
fails the RPC with NOT_FOUND, as the gRPC health-checking protocol requires,
rather than inheriting the overall status and reporting SERVING. The overall
status still answers the empty service name. Register each service explicitly
with PUT /mockserver/grpc/health to restore the previous answer.

Server reflection returned only a file's direct dependencies, so a client
resolving a symbol whose definition sat two imports deep could not link the
descriptor pool. It now returns the transitive closure.

HTTP/3 header names were folded with the default locale, so a JVM running
under a Turkish locale emitted a dotless lowercase i and the header no longer
matched. Six sites now fold with Locale.ROOT.

Connection options are not implemented for HTTP/3. They were silently ignored;
the writer now warns and names them, separating those not yet implemented from
those governing headers RFC 9114 forbids outright.

fix(control-plane): rank the closest expectation by closeness, not registration order

Matching stops at the first field that differs, so every mismatched
expectation recorded exactly one difference. The comparison that picks the
closest match could therefore only ever be true for the first mismatched
expectation, and closestMatch reported whichever expectation happened to be
registered first.

The matched field count came from the same value, so it reported one field
short of the total for every mismatch however badly it missed.

explainUnmatched has the same defect for the same reason: it sorts by the
differing field count, and with every candidate tied the stable sort presents
registration order as a ranking.

The two diagnostic endpoints now ask the matcher for every difference. The
opt-in is per request rather than global, so request matching is unchanged.

test(docker): skip Docker-gated suites instead of erroring when Docker is unusable

The Testcontainers availability probe is documented as returning false when
Docker is unavailable, but converts only IllegalStateException. Starting the
resource reaper and the version check throw other exceptions and errors, which
escape the assumption guard and fail the suite. Testcontainers then caches the
failure and rethrows it, so a single bad probe errors every Docker-gated test
in the JVM.

The probe is now wrapped so any failure becomes a skip, except for errors that
indicate the JVM itself is failing. The guidance for writing a Docker-gated
test names the wrapper rather than the raw probe, since the raw form throws.

The cloud contract suites also could not start their containers: the reaper
defaults to a privileged container, which the build agents reject because they
remap user namespaces. It does not need privileged to reap through the mounted
socket, so it now runs unprivileged rather than being disabled.

A suite that skips every test now fails the build rather than reporting
success, so degrading gracefully cannot be mistaken for passing.

test(container): free the port the helm tests forward to, and record tests that crash

The k3d cluster published host port 1080 to its own load balancer with no
route behind it, so the port forward the helm tests rely on could not bind and
died immediately. Its error was discarded, the readiness poll fell through
without failing, and the tests died later against a socket that accepted the
connection and closed it. The publish had no consumer at all and is removed.

The poll now fails when it runs out of attempts, naming the forward and
printing what it recorded, so the next failure in this path explains itself.

A test that exits without recording a result is now recorded as a failure. The
existing guard keyed on the exit code, so a test exiting zero without
reporting still disappeared from the summary entirely.

Forward cleanup matched on any process whose command line mentioned both
"port-forward" and the port, which selected the invoking shell and forwards
belonging to unrelated runs. It now matches the namespace and both ports.

fix(client-php): carry primary, streamError and the GraphQL subscription filter

The PHP builders dropped fields the other clients gained when the shared
fixtures grew. primary decides which action a re-submitted expectation
executes, so omitting it could silently change behaviour on replay, and
streamError could not be set at all.

The GraphQL subscription filter became settable on a running server in this
release; PHP can now express it.

None of this was visible to the round-trip fidelity test, which replays the
decoded array unchanged and so cannot observe the typed model. The coverage is
in the per-class tests, including cases for primary false and streamError zero,
which a truthiness guard would silently drop.

test(client-node): lint the client and fail when a test suite cannot be built

The lint task pointed at a directory that does not exist, so it checked one
file — its own Gruntfile — and reported success. It now covers the client, the
tests and the examples, which surfaced two undeclared globals, a missing
semicolon, a loose equality and a function used before it was defined.

A suite that throws while being constructed reports no tests, no failures and
exits zero, so both the exit code and the failure count called it green while
nothing ran. Every test file builds its suites this way. The runner now fails
when the exit code is non-zero or any test reports not ok, and pins the
reporter so local and CI runs are read the same way.

fix(ui): let an expectation match HTTP only, and check nested fixture properties

The secure matcher was a two-state switch labelled "HTTPS only", so turning it
off meant "match either" and the field was correctly omitted. An expectation
authored elsewhere with secure false therefore loaded as off and was re-saved
without the field, widening it from HTTP-only to either.

It is now a three-way choice, and the four generators that guarded the value
with a truthiness test rather than a presence test no longer drop it.

Twenty-one fixtures set secure false only because the field was required. They
never intended an HTTP-only constraint, so they now leave it unset rather than
having that constraint written into every generated example.

The fixture coverage gate only compared top-level properties, which is why a
nested field no client could express went unnoticed. It now checks one level
further, and an action present as an empty object no longer opts itself out.

fix(client-php): complete the action builders and read the shared fixtures

The PHP builders could not express delay on errors or forwards, trailers,
generated bodies, status code ranges or recovery, template types on streaming
responses, or the primary selector on an LLM response — the last because the
enumeration that found the earlier gaps only looked at one directory.

Three tests claimed to match a shared fixture and only one read it; the other
two hardcoded the expected array beside a comment naming the file. They now
load the fixture, and refuse to run if the path is wrong or the action is
empty, so a mistyped path cannot pass by comparing nothing to nothing.

The expected values stay literal in the test rather than being read from the
same fixture they check, so the two sides cannot move together.

fix(client-go): let a matcher value start with an exclamation mark or question mark

A header, parameter or cookie value beginning with those markers was sent
bare, and the server reads a leading marker as negation or optionality. So
matching a literal "!foo" silently became "anything that is not foo", which
matches almost everything. The matching request still passed, which is why
this survived: only a request that must NOT match reveals it.

Values that need it are now sent in the object form, decided by re-parsing
rather than by looking for a prefix, so a value that already round-trips is
unchanged on the wire.

Reading an expectation back understands both forms. A field whose values all
survive the plain form is restored as before, so ordinary traffic decodes
exactly as it did. A type mismatch on the path or method is tolerated rather
than abandoning the whole expectation, which would drop the response.

fix(serialization): stop a collection key that starts with a marker inverting when re-read

A header, parameter or cookie name is written as a JSON field name, so a name
that literally begins with an exclamation mark or question mark was written
bare and read back as a negated or optional name. An expectation built with a
literal name therefore changed meaning when it was serialised and read again.

Such a name is now written in the array form, where the name can carry the
object shape that already exists for values. The form is chosen by re-parsing,
so a collection whose names all round-trip is unchanged on the wire, and both
the name and the value can carry it at once.

The cookie deserialiser reads the object form for a name as well; it has its
own serialiser, deserialiser and schema, separate from the multi-value ones.

This covers serialisation only. The inbound request parser still strips the
marker, so a request carrying such a header arrives without it.

test(client-php): set the filter fields the shared fixture now carries

The shared GraphQL subscription fixture gained a type and a variables schema,
and the test that asserts an exact match against it was not updated, so the
PHP build has failed since that fixture changed.

The client can set both; the test simply did not. The assertion stays exact
rather than being loosened, because this is the only client test enforcing
that fixture at this granularity.

test(container): name the service the remote-host test forwards to

The chart appends its own name to the release unless the release already
contains it, so the five tests that take the default release name get a
service called mockserver while this one, which passes its own release name,
gets proxy-target-mockserver. It forwarded to proxy-target, which does not
exist.

The same name is also used as the proxy target, so that address pointed at
nothing either. It was hidden because the forward failed first, and fixing
only the forward would have moved the failure rather than removing it.

Pinning the release name repairs both. Renaming the release to contain the
chart name would have worked by relying on the same coincidence that caused
this, so the name is set explicitly instead.

When a forward fails because the service is missing, the message now says so
and explains the naming rule, rather than suggesting a port conflict.

test(async): run the live-broker suites in CI instead of skipping them all

The MQTT, MQTT5, AMQP, Kafka and Kafka-Avro integration suites were assumed
away on every CI run because the build did not mount the Docker socket, so the
availability probe returned false and all five reported as skipped while the
build passed. A dedicated step now mounts the socket, and the run-recorded
assertion fails the build if a suite skips everything, so the coverage cannot
silently disappear again.

The reaper runs unprivileged, matching the cloud-store step, because the build
agents reject privileged containers.

stop() now waits briefly for an in-flight publish to finish before closing the
publishers, rather than interrupting it, so a scheduled publish is not cut
short mid-cycle.

fix(evals): make AI-component eval gate bind — record baselines + enforce STRICT

The eval gate was vacuous: 5 golden fixtures had no recorded .result
baselines and commit-workflow invoked run-evals.sh without STRICT=1, so an
all-PENDING suite exited 0 "OK". Record the 5 baselines by running each named
agent on its fixture, and require STRICT=1 in the control-change gate so a
missing baseline fails closed instead of passing silently. Recording the
baselines surfaced a defective fixture (review-passes-clean-change added a
factually-incorrect Javadoc claim about match ordering that review-cheap
correctly blocked); reduced it to a bare typo fix so the golden must-PASS case
is genuinely clean.

fix(grpc): log the fail-safe decode and compile failures at WARN so they are visible

When gRPC request decoding, descriptor loading or proto compilation fails, the
fallback path logged the failure with a WARN type but left the entry at the
default INFO level, so it was filtered out whenever the server ran at WARN or
above — silent for exactly the operators most likely to be watching. All three
sites now set the level as well as the type.

Also replaces the event-log coalescing test, which asserted a single dispatch
for a thousand-notification burst against a wall-clock sleep and so raced on a
slow machine. It now drives a manual clock and asserts the actual contract:
the burst is suppressed, one dispatch fires per window, and a later burst
re-arms.

feat(client-php): add the gRPC bidi, forward-validate, forward-fallback and template actions

The PHP client had no builder for grpcBidiResponse, httpForwardValidateAction,
httpForwardWithFallback or the response and forward template actions, so those
expectations could not be constructed from PHP at all. Each is now a typed
builder wired onto the expectation and forward-chain, with the nested bidi
message and rule shapes modelled rather than passed as opaque arrays.

The bidi message carries its own template type, which the existing stream
message builder cannot express, so it is a distinct class. The template action
is referenced by both the response and forward template keys, so it wires
under both.

httpObjectCallback is left unbuilt: it needs a callback WebSocket the REST-only
PHP client does not implement. The template response modifier is left for a
follow-up. Both are noted in source.

build(docker): clear the BuildKit lint warnings across the Dockerfiles

Uppercases the AS keyword in multi-stage FROM lines, replaces the deprecated
MAINTAINER instruction with an OCI authors label, and switches ENV to the
key=value form. Purely syntactic — the produced images are unchanged.

The sync gate matched the port env var by its old space-separated form, which
the key=value change would have broken, so its pattern and messages are updated
to the new form. It still rejects a regression to the old form.

fix(core): record an incoming header, cookie or parameter name literally

A real request has literal names — it is never a matcher — but the request
mappers built header and cookie names through the marker-parsing constructor,
so a request carrying a header named "!foo" was recorded as the negation of
"foo" rather than as the literal name. A literal "!foo" matcher therefore
could not match it, and it was conflated with a plain "foo" header.

The netty and servlet request mappers now build these names as literals, so a
"!foo" header is recorded as "!foo", matched by a literal "!foo" matcher, and
kept distinct from "foo". The shared matcher builder is unchanged, so a matcher
that means "name is NOT foo" still parses the marker as negation.

test(fixtures): use a valid validationMode in the forward-validate fixture

The shared forward-validate fixture set validationMode to LENIENT, which the
server rejects — the enum is STRICT or LOG_ONLY — so an expectation built from
it returned 400. The value is now LOG_ONLY, the mode the "response only"
scenario intends.

The PHP test that matched this fixture built the literal LENIENT string; it now
uses the LOG_ONLY constant. The separate property that the builder passes an
arbitrary mode through untouched moved to its own test with a made-up value, so
it no longer depends on the shared fixture carrying an invalid one.

fix(opencode): wire orphaned rules + add rule-reachability lint

Two rules (aws-ids-file, multi-pass-temperature) had zero inbound references
so were never discoverable — inert. Wire each from a reachable referrer
(AGENTS.md, operating-model.md), and add a rule-reachability check to
validate_opencode_config.sh (BFS from entry docs through rule->rule refs) so
CI fails closed on any future orphaned rule. Reconcile
docs/operations/opencode-configuration.md, which wrongly claimed all rules are
always-loaded, to the actual on-demand reference-based model.

test(container): show what a crashed test was doing, and fix three that crashed

When a test script exits without recording a result, the harness now prints
the last of its output, and the compose helper dumps container status and logs
before tear-down removes them — so a crash explains itself instead of only
reporting that it happened.

Three tests were crashing before they recorded anything. Two read the persisted
expectations file from the host, but the server writes it as a non-host user in
a distroless image with no shell, so the read is now done with docker cp.
The third piped docker logs into head, which took a SIGPIPE under pipefail; it
is now tolerated.

fix(opencode): mechanically enforce operator halt before every consequential tool call

Wire the kill-switch into both harnesses so enforcement no longer relies on
agent compliance. Previously check-halt.sh was only invoked procedurally at the
commit and worktree-merge gates; nothing intercepted individual tool calls.

- Claude Code: a PreToolUse hook (check-halt-hook.sh, wired in settings.json)
  on Bash/Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit/Task/Agent, translating an engaged
  halt (check-halt.sh exit 1) into a blocking exit 2.
- opencode: an operator-halt.ts plugin whose tool.execute.before hook throws on
  bash/write/edit/patch/task when a halt is engaged.

Both call the same source of truth (check-halt.sh) and both fail open so a
broken check can never wedge a session. Read-only tools are not gated. Closes
defect #3 from the AI-config audit.

test(core): cover retrieve export-format dispatch branches

Add HttpState-level tests for the 16 legal (RetrieveType, Format) pairs
that reach real export/collection dispatch branches but previously had no
coverage: REQUESTS, REQUEST_RESPONSES, RECORDED_EXPECTATIONS and
ACTIVE_EXPECTATIONS retrieved as OPENAPI, POSTMAN, BRUNO, HAR (plus
RECORDED_EXPECTATIONS as LOG_ENTRIES).

Each test asserts a format-appropriate marker and that the response is
not the plain-text 'not supported' fallback, so a regression that fell
through to the error branch fails the test rather than passing silently.
BRUNO asserts the application/zip content-type and attachment
content-disposition headers rather than body equality.

fix(client-rust): let a matcher value start with an exclamation mark or question mark

A header, query parameter or cookie value beginning with those markers was
sent bare, and the server reads a leading marker as negation or optionality.
So matching a literal "!foo" silently became "anything that is not foo",
which matches almost everything. The matching request still passed, which is
why this survived: only a request that must NOT match reveals it.

The fix is additive — no existing public field changed type. The plain
headers/queryStringParameters/cookies maps keep their String value types and
their marker-parsing meaning, and new header_matchers /
query_string_parameter_matchers / cookie_matchers fields carry MatcherValue.
A hand-written Serialize/Deserialize on HttpRequest lets a matcher map stand
in for its plain counterpart under the same wire key. A value that needs it
is sent in the object form, decided by re-parsing rather than by looking for
a prefix, so a value that already round-trips is unchanged on the wire.

Reading an expectation back understands both forms. A field whose values all
survive the plain form is restored into the plain map as before; only a field
that needs the object form populates the matcher map. path and method are
tolerated rather than abandoning the whole expectation, which would poison a
retrieved list.

fix(client-dotnet): let a matcher value start with an exclamation mark or question mark

A header, parameter or cookie value beginning with those markers was sent
bare, and the server reads a leading marker as negation or optionality. So
matching a literal "!foo" silently became "anything that is not foo", which
matches almost everything. The matching request still passed, which is why
this survived: only a request that must NOT match reveals it.

Values that need it are now sent in the object form, decided by re-parsing
rather than by looking for a prefix, so a value that already round-trips is
unchanged on the wire. NotLiteral("!foo") stays the shorter "!!foo".

The client gains MatcherValue (Literal/NotLiteral/OptionalLiteral) and the
request builder gains WithHeaderMatcher, WithQueryStringParameterMatcher,
WithCookieMatcher and WithPathParameterMatcher, additive over the existing
plain maps. A JsonConverter<HttpRequest> lets a non-empty matcher map stand
in for the plain one under the same wire key, and reads both wire forms back,
mirroring an all-plain field into the plain map so ordinary traffic decodes
exactly as before. This matches the escape the Java and Go clients already had.

Reading an expectation back understands the object form too, so retrieving an
escaped value survives. An object-form path or method, which this model types
as a plain string, is flattened to its plain string rather than abandoning the
whole expectation, which would drop the response; those two remain recorded as
gaps in the round-trip fidelity ledger.

fix(client): stop hasStopped() reporting a running MockServer as stopped

MockServerClient.hasStopped() probed /status with errors ignored, which
collapsed a connection refusal (genuinely stopped) and a read timeout
(alive but slow to answer) into the same empty result and treated it as
"stopped". A MockServer merely paused by GC or starved of CPU therefore
reported itself stopped while still bound, so callers rebound the port and
got a BindException raised far from the real cause.

Now a refused connection still reports stopped, but a read timeout - and
any other unrecognised failure - reports NOT stopped and logs a warning.
isTimeoutFailure() recognises both shapes a timeout can arrive in: the
client-side future.get() expiring (SocketCommunicationException) and
Netty's ReadTimeoutHandler firing first (a plain RuntimeException wrapping
a Netty TimeoutException, which is not an IOException and so is not
translated to SocketConnectionException).

Both the blocking stop() and the background wait behind stopAsync() now
derive how long they wait for a confirmed stop from stopDrainMillis and
maxSocketTimeoutInMillis instead of a fixed 10 seconds, so raising the
drain timeout no longer makes either give up while the server is still
draining and still holding its port. The background loop is now bounded by
a wall-clock deadline as well as an iteration count, because each probe can
now cost a full socket timeout.

Stop failures in MockServerClient.stop() and LifeCycle.stop(), and giving
up while waiting for a confirmed stop, now log at WARN rather than DEBUG,
so a stop that did not stop is no longer silent until an unrelated
BindException surfaces later.

test(http3): harden QUIC integration tests against flakes under contention

The HTTP/3 (QUIC) tests failed intermittently when the suite ran under load:
a 5-second client idle timeout and 5-second connect/poll waits could not
reliably complete a QUIC handshake and round-trip while the machine was
saturated, and each test's private findAvailableUdpPort() returned port 0
on failure - which means "HTTP/3 disabled", silently turning an
infrastructure hiccup into a test that asserted against a server that never
started.

Raise the client and server idle timeouts to 30s and the connect/poll waits
to 15-20s so a slow handshake no longer trips the timeout, and replace every
per-test findAvailableUdpPort() with a shared TestPortFactory.findFreeUdpPort()
that raises when no port can be found rather than reporting port 0. The
helper deliberately leaves SO_REUSEADDR off, because on BSD-derived systems
two UDP sockets that both set it can bind the same port simultaneously and
silently, which would manufacture the collision the probe exists to avoid.

Test-only; no production behaviour change.

fix(mcp): make MCP transport conformant on failures, sessions and ping

Harden MockServer's own MCP Streamable HTTP endpoint and its conformance
checker against several protocol divergences that a well-behaved client
could not recover from:

- A tool or handler that throws now returns a JSON-RPC -32603 error
  carrying the request id instead of letting the exception escape the
  POST executor with no response, which left the client blocked until
  its own timeout. Conversion happens per request (so one bad batch
  entry no longer discards the others) with a last-resort backstop in
  the transport handler. The exception detail is logged, not returned.
- A JSON-RPC notification's "id": $!{request.jsonRpcRawId} rendered to
  nothing and produced unparseable JSON ("id": followed by the closing
  brace). It now renders the JSON null literal. Partial fix: a matcher
  cannot yet suppress the response entirely, so the response is at least
  well-formed.
- Session HTTP statuses now follow MCP 2025-06-18 basic/transports: an
  unknown or terminated session returns 404 (the signal a client uses to
  start a new session), a missing Mcp-Session-Id returns 400, and a live
  but not-yet-initialized session returns 400 with a message saying so.
  A blank session id counts as missing so HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/3 agree. A
  batch is validated once for the whole POST.
- ping is now answered before notifications/initialized, as the
  lifecycle spec's explicit carve-out requires, while still requiring a
  valid session id (400/404). No other method is exempt.
- run_mcp_contract_test now requires 202-with-no-body for a notification
  instead of tolerating 200/202/204, so the checker no longer certifies
  the exact non-conformant shape MockServer's own mock builders emit. The
  body rule is scoped to 202; a rejection may carry a body.

Also wires McpContractTest against MockServer's own MCP endpoint for the
first time, and documents the mock builders' notifications/initialized
divergence from the server as a known cross-client gap.

feat(core): enforce runtime Configuration + fix redactSecretsInLog leak

Make PUT /mockserver/configuration and Configuration-instance settings
actually take effect for ~30 properties that were previously read from the
static ConfigurationProperties store only, so a value set over the instance
or the REST API is no longer accepted and then silently ignored.

SECURITY: redactSecretsInLog now actually redacts. Enabling it on a
Configuration instance or via PUT /mockserver/configuration previously left
Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, x-api-key and
api-key headers in clear across the event log, dashboard, retrieval/export
surface, persisted recorded-requests archive and the JSON log serializer,
because the redactor was built from the static store only. The redaction
accessors now take the effective Configuration, wired through
MockServerEventLog, RecordedRequestsFileSystemPersistence, DashboardLogEntryDTO
and the log-message serializer. fixtureBodyRedactFields is resolved the same
instance-first way.

Make llmApiKey, prometheusRemoteWriteBasicAuthPassword and
prometheusRemoteWriteBearerToken write-only: settable but masked with
***REDACTED*** on GET, with GET-then-PUT round-trip safety (a masked value is
ignored on write rather than clobbering the real credential).

Fix ringBufferSize doubling on every config round trip: the power-of-two
rounding returned the next power strictly greater than its input, so an exact
power of two grew on each GET/PUT. It is now returned unchanged.

Reconcile capacity-bounded subsystems on update: maxLogEntries,
maxEventLogSizeInBytes, maxExpectations and controlPlaneAuditMaxEntries are
resized in place (a shrink evicts immediately); ringBufferSize and
maxWebSocketExpectations genuinely cannot be resized on a running server, so a
PUT that supplies a differing value logs a WARN and resets the field to the
value in force.

KNOWN GAP: credentials embedded inside llmBackendsConfig and
prometheusRemoteWriteHeaders values are not masked and are disclosed by
GET /mockserver/configuration. This is documented in changelog.md, pinned by a
characterisation test asserting the current unmasked behaviour, and recorded in
docs/plans/later for a per-field/per-header redaction follow-up.

Reachability is guarded in three layers: a bytecode call-site guard, a reflective
risk-property classification, and an end-to-end REST enforcement integration test.

docs(openapi): reconcile control-plane spec with the server and guard against drift

Sixteen implemented control-plane endpoints were described nowhere in the OpenAPI
specification, and eleven Expectation properties (the LLM, gRPC streaming, gRPC bidi,
binary and DNS actions, forward validation and fallback, before/after actions,
multi-step expectations and capture rules) were declared in neither copy of the spec.
Because the Postman and Bruno collections are generated from the spec, every gap
propagated into them and into any client generated from the document.

Document all sixteen endpoints and eleven properties in both copies of the spec
(website source of truth and the embedded copy the server serves), each signature
verified against its handler rather than transcribed, and regenerate the collections.
This is a documentation gap only: the served YAML is never parsed at runtime and
incoming expectations validate against expectation.json, which already declared all
eleven, so these expectations were always accepted on the wire.

Add drift guards so the gap cannot silently reopen:
- OpenApiSpecExpectationSchemaTest drives a spec-versus-DTO comparison from
  ExpectationDTO, so a property the server gains but the spec omits fails the build.
- OpenApiSpecEndpointCoverageTest asserts every dispatched control-plane route is
  documented, with a floor on the route count so a dispatch refactor fails loudly
  rather than extracting zero routes and passing vacuously.
- New end-to-end tests for PUT /crud and PUT /debugMismatch, the two least-defended
  control-plane endpoints, driving a real server over a real socket.

Add a CI step (collections-live-validate.sh, wired into pipeline-infra.yml) that fires
every generated collection example at a live MockServer, so a documented-but-rejected
example body can no longer pass the deterministic collections gate. It starts the
server on the agent and runs the checker over the host network rather than mounting the
Docker socket, which run-in-docker.sh withholds from PR builds. Examples known to be
rejected today are listed as a shrink-only ratchet that fails if an entry starts passing.

docs(website): surface multi-stage experiment features in chaos nav map

The chaos_testing.html "On this page" feature map did not link the
scheduled-experiment sub-capabilities added later (recurring/scheduled
starts, steady-state baseline pre-check, experiment history) — they were
documented in the body but unreachable from the top-of-page nav. Add a
nested sub-list under "Scheduled experiments" linking all three, add the
two missing section anchors (chaos_experiment_scheduling,
chaos_experiment_baseline) so the links resolve, and fix a pre-existing
broken in-page link (#tcp_chaos -> #tcp_layer_chaos). Every feature label
was verified against ChaosExperimentOrchestrator and the /chaosExperiment
endpoints in HttpState.

build(ci): add a measurable-line floor and durable ledger to the diff-coverage gate

The diff-coverage gate was brittle at small denominators: a 6-line diff with a
single uncovered helper failed the 70% threshold. Add a floor of 25 measurable
changed lines below which the ratio is reported but not enforced. Keep the 70%
threshold unchanged.

A floor fixes brittleness, not invisibility: the gate is diff-scoped, so a
sub-floor uncovered line it lets pass is never re-examined and becomes invisible.
Pair the floor with a durable ledger (.buildkite/diff-coverage-ledger.json):

- completeness: below the floor, every measurable-uncovered changed line must be
  covered or recorded in the ledger, so nothing is silently dropped;
- staleness: a ledger entry whose line is now covered fails the build until
  removed, mirroring known-gaps.json's shrink-only ratchet.

Seed the ledger empty: the lines the coverage audit cited (GrpcForwardTranslator
211-217, GrpcProtoDescriptorStore 148) are now covered by GrpcFailSafeLoggingTest.

Add .buildkite/scripts/test/diff-coverage-test.sh, a pure git+python+bash
self-test proving discrimination across all dimensions (large under-covered diff
fails on ratio; sub-floor miss passes with the ratio still printed; unrecorded
sub-floor miss fails on completeness; now-covered ledger entry fails on
staleness; well-covered large diff passes).

docs(plans): record deferred UI competitor-feature ideas

Harvested from the completed ui-detailed-review-2026-07: every actionable
review finding shipped; these are the unscheduled §5 competitor-inspired
feature ideas, recorded as future bets with verified current-state anchors.

feat(core): one-shot / bounded maxHits budget for interactive breakpoints

Add an optional maxHits field to a breakpoint matcher that bounds how many
times it may pause before it auto-deregisters from BreakpointMatcherRegistry.
maxHits=1 is a one-shot breakpoint (pause once, then the next matching request
is no longer intercepted); maxHits=3 fires three times then removes itself.

Only real pauses count against the budget: hits suppressed by a skipCount
window do not consume it, so skipCount and maxHits compose. Each pause
increments a per-matcher pauseCount (a second AtomicLong); when it reaches
maxHits the entry isExhausted() and findMatch/findResponseMatch remove it from
the CopyOnWriteArrayList after returning the winning match. Absent/0/negative
keeps the legacy never-auto-deregister behaviour. Each phase counts as a
separate pause, so a REQUEST+RESPONSE breakpoint with maxHits=1 fires once.

The register endpoint validates maxHits as a positive integer (400 otherwise)
and echoes it; the list endpoint surfaces it. Covers findMatch and
findResponseMatch removal paths (incl. skipCount and response-condition
composition) with unit and endpoint tests.

feat(core): pagination, sorting and filtering on the generic CRUD list endpoint

Add optional query parameters to the CRUD simulation GET-list path, parsed and
applied by a new CrudListQuery helper in the order filter -> sort -> paginate:

- filterField + filterValue: case-insensitive equality on a dot-separated
  attribute path; both must be supplied together (400 otherwise)
- sortBy + sortOrder: sort by a dot-separated path, ascending/asc (default) or
  descending/desc; missing sort values sort last; stable; sortOrder without
  sortBy, or an unknown order, is a 400
- page + size: 0-based page (default 0), page size (default all, size<=0 means
  no limit); a non-integer page/size or negative page is a 400

Pagination uses long math throughout so a large page/size cannot overflow int
and fault the subList. When any list parameter is active the response adds
X-Total-Count (total after filtering), X-Page and X-Page-Size headers; a plain
list request with no parameters returns the exact legacy array with no extra
headers. This is the generic CRUD store's own query surface, independent of the
SCIM list callback's sorting/filtering.

feat(core): enforce the rateLimit clause on SSE, gRPC-stream and WebSocket actions

The declarative, protocol-agnostic rateLimit expectation clause was applied
only to buffered RESPONSE/FORWARD actions, so a matched SSE_RESPONSE,
GRPC_STREAM_RESPONSE or WEBSOCKET_RESPONSE was never throttled (a v1
deferral). Wire the same rateLimitResponseOrNull(rateLimit, expectationId)
check into the top of each of those three stream cases in
HttpActionHandler.processAction: an over-limit request receives the
deterministic 429 (Retry-After + X-RateLimit-* headers) via the existing
7-arg writeResponseActionResponse path instead of opening the stream; within
the limit the stream proceeds unchanged. The check runs exactly once per
matched request (the 429/501 writes thread rateLimit=null, so no second
acquire) and reuses the existing RateLimitRegistry — no second implementation.
LLM_RESPONSE keeps its own token-based TPM/TPD limiter and is unaffected.

docs(core): record recoverAfter as RESPONSE-only and defer it on FORWARD

Investigated whether the recoverAfter retry/backoff primitive applies to
FORWARD actions (the feature-value plan flagged its forward coverage as
PARTIAL/unverified). Finding: recoverAfter is a field on HttpResponse and
selectRecoveryResponse is interposed only in the case RESPONSE arm (early and
main dispatch); RESPONSE_TEMPLATE, RESPONSE_CLASS_CALLBACK and the whole
FORWARD family carry no HttpResponse and never consult it, so the clause is
not expressible there at all.

Extending it to forwards is an M-L cross-cutting change (field + DTO +
serializer + schema plumbing across the forward action models, plus a
forward-shaped recovery selection threaded into six dispatch sites) that
overlaps the existing forward-path HttpChaosProfile fault surface — not an S
tail item, and half-doing one forward action would ship an inconsistent
surface. Recorded precisely in docs/plans/later/recover-after-on-forward.md
and added a scope note to the RecoverAfter section of request-processing.md
rather than implementing.

fix(core): percent-decode WAR servlet request paths in the getRequestURI fallback

Under the WAR / servlet (Tomcat) deployment a request for a percent-encoded
path such as /ab%40c.de was not decoded back to /ab@c.de in one servlet-mapping
case: a ROOT-context deployment where the container reports a null path-info even
for a /* mapping. HttpServletRequestToMockServerHttpRequestDecoder.setPath() then
fell back to the raw, still-percent-encoded getRequestURI() and used it undecoded,
so the request failed to match an expectation registered for the decoded path and
returned 404 instead of the mocked response (red mockserver-java pipeline).

The fallback now percent-decodes the raw request URI (preserving a literal +,
which in a path is a plus and not a space), making it consistent with the
getPathInfo() branch, which the container already decodes.

fix(fixtures): restore the dotnet known-gaps entries dropped in a merge

The .NET negation-escape merge resolution rewrote known-gaps.json from the
rust-merged base plus two hunks, which discarded the dotnet commit's own
changes to the "dotnet" ledger: it should have dropped the now-stale
<unrepresentable-expectation>:matcher_request_literal_not sentinel and added
httpRequest.path, httpRequest.method and httpRequest.headers.X-Negated.* (the
gaps the .NET client now legitimately has after gaining the object-form
escape). Without them the dotnet fidelity test saw unexcused diffs and a stale
ratchet entry. Restores the intended ledger; dotnet RoundTripFidelityTests
58/58 green.

test(config-guard): allow-list the client-side stopDrainMillis reads

The configuration call-site guard flagged two static-store reads of
stopDrainMillis in MockServerClient#stop and its stop(boolean) thread
lambda (lambda$stop$3), introduced by the hasStopped fix.

These are legitimate instance-unreachable client-side reads, not

test(docker): stop graceful-shutdown harness crashing before it records a result

The docker_compose_graceful_shutdown container test failed in CI with
"exited 1 without recording a result" even though MockServer served the
graceful response and persisted the file correctly. It is a harness bug:
under set -euo pipefail a command aborted before logTestResult ran.

Root cause: the persisted-file mtime was read with BSD-syntax
stat -f "%m" tried first. On the Linux CI agent stat -f means
--file-system and does not fail cleanly - it prints a filesystem-info
blob for the file and treats "%m" as a bogus operand, so PRE/POST_STOP_MTIME
captured that non-numeric blob. The [[ -lt ]] arithmetic then evaluated
"File" as a variable and aborted under set -u ("File: unbound variable").

Fixes:
- read mtime GNU-first (stat -c "%Y" || stat -f "%m" || true) so Linux CI
  gets a clean integer and macOS keeps working via the BSD fallback
- require purely-numeric mtimes (=~ ^[0-9]+$) before the -lt arithmetic so
  a non-numeric read is recorded as a genuine FAIL instead of aborting
- guard the remaining unguarded command substitutions used during the
  shutdown window (CONTAINER_ID, docker stop, the two RESPONSE_BODY reads)
  so a transient hiccup sets TEST_EXIT_CODE=1 and falls through to
  logTestResult rather than aborting the script
- apply the same RESPONSE_BODY guard to the sibling
  docker_compose_with_persisted_expectations test

ci(buildkite): auto-retry Spot-reclaimed steps across all pipelines

Recurring `exit -1` / "agent lost" flakes (rust #331/#333/#339, dotnet,
php, ruby and others) are Spot-reclamation evictions of the agent
mid-step, not real test failures. The default queue is partly Spot, so
any step can be reclaimed. pipeline-java.yml and pipeline-editors.yml
already carried the mitigation on their long-running steps; this
propagates the same block to every command-bearing step in the remaining
pipelines and to the always-on step emitted by generate-pipeline.sh.

The retry fires only on -1 (agent lost) and 255 (agent forced shutdown),
never on exit 1, so a genuine test failure is never masked. Release
pipelines are deliberately excluded: those steps run on the dedicated
`release` queue and publish to non-idempotent registries, where retrying
a half-completed publish is unsafe. Pre-existing retry blocks (including
the partial -1-only triggers in generate-pipeline.sh) are left untouched.

fix(config): redact credentials embedded inside structured configuration values

Credential masking on the configuration control plane was keyed on the whole
property name, so a secret carried *inside* a structured value was returned in
clear. `prometheusRemoteWriteHeaders` typically holds an `Authorization` or
`Api-Key` header, and `llmBackendsConfig` holds an `apiKey` per backend when it
is given an inline JSON document rather than its usual file path. On a control
plane left unauthenticated (the default) any reader could retrieve them once set.

Redaction is now per-header and per-JSON-field, expressed as one rule shared by
every disclosing surface rather than a per-endpoint check:

- GET /mockserver/configuration (ConfigurationDTO)
- GET /mockserver/config, --print-config (effectiveConfiguration)
- the startup property-file log dump

`ConfigurationProperties` gains `redactSensitiveValue`, `restoreRedactedValue`
and `containsRedactionMask` next to `isSensitivePropertyName`, so the nested
name rule is the same rule, not a second one. Write-back ignores a masked field
and keeps the held value, so a GET-then-PUT round trip cannot destroy a working
credential; a masked field with nothing behind it is dropped rather than
written, so the mask can never become a credential. Mixed masked/edited input
applies the edits and restores only the masked fields, matching JSON array
elements by name so reordering cannot transplant one backend's key onto
another. Unparseable input fails closed and is logged rather than silently
discarded.

The credential-shape tables are declared before PROPERTIES because
readPropertyFile() runs during static initialisation; the #2338 regression
guard is extended to load one property of each shape so that ordering is
pinned rather than assumed.

Remaining limitation, documented in the changelog and the class javadoc:
redaction is keyed on the header/field name, so a credential carried inside an
otherwise ordinary value (classically a URL with an inline user:pass@) is still
returned in clear.

feat(ui): shared filter DSL with per-call-site operator vocabulary

The dashboard search operators (`status:`, `method:`, `path:`) were
hard-coded into searchMatcher.ts as a KNOWN_FIELDS set, a fieldValue
switch and a matchesOperator that special-cased `path` for globbing.
Extract a field registry into lib/filterDSL.ts where each field declares
its own resolver plus whether it supports numeric comparison or glob
matching, so adding an operator no longer means editing three switch
arms. The three existing operators keep their exact previous behaviour;
searchMatcher.ts becomes a re-export shim so every existing consumer
compiles unchanged.

Register two further fields for the traffic views to consume: `host:`
(glob, from the request Host header, resolved identically to the value
the Traffic host column already derives via summarizeTraffic) and
`operation:` (glob, from a request body operationName).

Give call sites a way to declare which operators they support, so the
DSL cannot advertise an operator that silently does nothing in a given
context. Log rows have no httpRequest/httpResponse to compare against,
so LogPanel declares an empty subset: its placeholder offers only
/regex/, and typing `status:>=400 error` now marks the field invalid
and explains that no field operators apply. Without that, widening the
vocabulary would have regressed the Log panel from "operator ignored,
free text still matches" to a silent empty result.

Both the panel's advertised subset and matchesLogSearch derive from the
same LOG_FILTER_OPTIONS constant, and the rejection is keyed off each
operator's `unsupported` flag rather than a bare operator count, so
adding a log-capable field later cannot make the two disagree.

The body decode behind `operation:` is memoised on the httpRequest
object reference, which the store preserves across WebSocket pushes for
unchanged rows, keeping it off the per-keystroke hot path. Built-in
fields are re-registrable and resetFilterFields() restores them, so a
feature module can swap in a richer resolver and tests can undo it.

feat(ui): named network-condition presets for TCP chaos

Reproducing "this service on a slow link" meant hand-entering latency
and bandwidth numbers and knowing which units the TCP chaos form wanted.
Add seven named presets to the TCP register form: dial-up, Slow 3G and
Fast 3G in throughput and latency variants, satellite, and a fragmented
link. Throughput and latency figures are anchored to Chrome DevTools'
throttling profiles and cited in the JSDoc, with the caveat that Chrome
models latency as a per-request RTT while MockServer charges it per
inbound read, so the numbers are anchors rather than an equivalence.

Each preset sets exactly one fault. TcpChaosHandler.channelRead is
first-match-wins with an early return per branch (down > reset_peer >
limit_data > slicer > bandwidth > latency), so a preset carrying both a
latency and a bandwidth value would display one number the engine never
applies -- for a 50 KB/s ceiling that is any read of 50 bytes or more,
i.e. every real request. The fault is modelled as a discriminated union
so the literal form of a two-fault preset is a compile error, and a
test sweeps every preset asserting exactly one populated field, citing
the handler's order so a future move to composing faults breaks it
deliberately.

Bandwidth is integer-divided in the handler, so reads below
ceil(bytesPerSec/1000) round to a zero delay and pass untouched. Show
that threshold in every throughput summary rather than let a preset
appear inert on small requests.

Presets fill latency, bandwidth and fragmentation only. The TCP engine
has no probability-gated fault, so there is no honest approximation of
packet loss or jitter at this layer; the caption points at HTTP service
chaos drop-connection probability for loss instead of inventing a field
the server would ignore. It also records that TCP faults shape inbound
request bytes only, not the response, since the handler overrides
channelRead and close but not write.
