feat(ui): inline Try It request/response widget in the composer

Checking whether a draft expectation actually catches the request you
had in mind meant leaving the dashboard for curl or an HTTP client. Add
a Try It button beside Test Matcher that opens an inline panel: it
derives an editable request from the draft matcher, fires it at
MockServer, and renders status, headers, body and round-trip time.

A matcher is a pattern, not a request, so deriving one is only safe for
exact non-negated values. Regex, glob, schema, JSON-path, XPath and
negated forms are left blank and listed as underivable rather than sent
verbatim. That includes two syntaxes that look literal but are not:
RegexStringMatcher takes its numeric-comparison and accept-negotiation
branches before the string-equality fallback, so a header matcher of
"> 60" fired as the text "> 60" can never match. The numeric pattern
mirrors NumericComparisonMatcher.OPERATOR_PATTERN exactly, including
its optional whitespace, so ">60" is refused while "> abc" -- which
Java does match, by string equality -- is kept. Send stays disabled
until the path is filled, and the request on the wire is always read
from the form, never from the matcher.

Cookie and Host are forbidden request-header names: fetch accepts them
on a standalone Headers object and then strips them silently when the
Request is constructed. Pre-filling a Cookie header would therefore
show the user a header that never travelled and a false not-matched
with no recovery, so the whole Fetch forbidden list is filtered out of
the derived set and named as unexercisable from a browser instead.

The dashboard is served by the same Netty listener that serves mock
traffic, so the default target is same-origin and needs no CORS. Other
bound ports are offered as one-click targets with an up-front CORS
warning, and because fetch reports a CORS block and a dead port
identically, the failure message branches on origin rather than
guessing.

feat(ui): host focus list in the traffic inspector

A proxy-mode session can capture traffic from dozens of upstream hosts,
and the traffic list offered no way to narrow to one or to see the shape
of what was captured. Add a collapsible host list at the top of the
master list: each distinct host with its request count, busiest first,
clicking to pin `host:<value>` into the search and clicking again to
unpin.

Pinning is expressed purely as a search term rather than as new store
state. `host:` is already an operator on the shared filter DSL and
`trafficSearch` is already persisted, so a pin narrows an existing
search instead of replacing it, stays editable in the box, composes
with the other operators, and survives a view switch and a reload with
no extra state to keep in sync.

Counts are derived from the unfiltered summaries deliberately: deriving
them from the filtered rows would collapse the list to the host just
pinned, leaving no way back to the others.

The list renders only when captured traffic spans more than one
distinct host, so a mock-only session -- where every request targets
localhost -- does not get a control that can only ever show one entry.

Hosts are read from the row summary, the same value the row displays
and the same first-case-insensitive-Host-header value the `host:`
operator resolves, so the counts and the rows a pin selects agree.
Values outside the RFC 3986 host character set are omitted rather than
offered as a broken pin: a Host header containing a space would
tokenise into `host:foo` plus stray free text and select nothing, and
one containing `*` would pin a glob matching every row while the list
claimed one.

feat(ui): GraphQL operation awareness in traffic and log rows

Every GraphQL request is a POST to the same path, so the Traffic and Log
views showed a wall of identical `POST /graphql` rows with the only
distinguishing signal -- the operation name and type -- buried in the
body. Parse it out and surface it as a chip on the row, and back the
shared `operation:` filter operator with the same parser so
`operation:Get*` narrows to one operation.

The name is taken from the operationName member when the payload
carries one, and otherwise scanned out of the query document, which is
where it usually lives. That second case is why the built-in resolver
registered with the filter DSL was not enough on its own.

Detection is deliberately strict, because the plan's named risk was
false positives on ordinary JSON that happens to carry a `query` key:
the content type must mention json or graphql when present, the body
must decode to an object with a string `query` (or be raw non-JSON
text), the candidate document must look like GraphQL and must not
itself parse as JSON, and an operation definition must actually be
found. An Elasticsearch or Mongo query body does not qualify.

Parsing is bounded so a hostile or accidental body cannot hang the
tab: bodies over 256 KB are not analysed, at most 8 KB of document is
scanned, at most 16 operations are collected, and binary bodies are
never decoded -- which is also the graceful degradation for the
compressed and streamed bodies this cannot see. Results are memoised on
the request object reference the store preserves across WebSocket
pushes, keeping the parse off the per-keystroke path and giving the
memoised traffic row a stable prop.

Registration of the parser-backed resolver happens in the app entry
rather than as a side effect of importing a component, so an unrelated
change to how the log panel is loaded cannot silently downgrade the
operator back to the built-in resolver on other search surfaces.

feat(ui): multiple workspaces in one dashboard tab

Investigating two things at once meant losing your filters on every
switch, because the window shared one view and one set of search terms.
A workspace now bundles the view and the five panel searches, so a
filtered Traffic investigation and a Log Messages search can sit in
separate tabs and neither loses state.

The active workspace's state IS the existing top-level store state, and
`workspaces` holds a snapshot per workspace refreshed only when the
active one changes. Nesting the live state under `workspaces[active]`
would have touched every panel selector and every setter; keeping the
top-level fields means `setView` still writes only `view`, so the
failure mode the plan named -- a view switch silently resetting filter
state -- is structurally impossible rather than merely tested against.
With one workspace no snapshot is ever read or written, so that case is
byte-for-byte the previous behaviour.

`mockserver-view` and `mockserver-search` keep their keys and formats
and stay authoritative for the active workspace; the new
`mockserver-workspaces` key holds the list and is not written until a
second workspace exists. An upgrading user lands in one workspace
carrying exactly their persisted view and searches. Malformed blobs
degrade field by field -- duplicate ids, unknown views, non-string
searches and wrong shapes all fall back rather than poisoning startup.

Only the active workspace is connected. The four data arrays are one
global slice fed through module-level reconcile caches, so two sockets
pushing full-state snapshots would each erase the other's data every
tick; there is still exactly one useWebSocket call site, so closing a
workspace cannot orphan a socket it never had.

The switcher is its own row below the app bar and does not exist until
a second workspace does, leaving one bare icon button in the app bar's
fixed utility cluster. The earlier pinned/recent-view tabs were
reverted in d55d7077d for crowding the flexible nav region with
labelled tabs; this keeps out of that region entirely and scrolls on
overflow rather than wrapping.

Per-workspace connection params are deliberately NOT included.
useConnectionParams derives purely from the URL and several components
call it directly, so a partial override would send deleteExpectation,
clearLoggedRequest, replayRequests and setServerMode to the wrong
MockServer instance. Landing half of it is worse than none, so the
plan's multiple-instances use case remains open; parallel
investigations, its other stated use case, is served in full.

feat(ui): shared scope syntax on breakpoint and verification forms

The status:/method:/path: operators were wired only to the Traffic
inspector and the dashboard mini-panels; breakpoints, verification and
chaos each had bespoke filter widgets with no shared vocabulary. Add a
quick-scope box backed by the shared filter DSL to the breakpoint and
verification forms, so a term learned in the Traffic search fills the
matcher fields.

The box FILLS the form rather than replacing it. A wholesale swap would
have traded the header, query-parameter and cookie multi-value matchers
and raw-regex paths for a strictly weaker glob -- a worse filter that
merely looked more uniform. Every existing control is untouched, and a
term carrying an operator the form cannot express applies nothing at
all rather than its valid half.

path: is a glob, but MockServer matches a path as an anchored regex, so
passing /api/* through untranslated compiles to "/api then zero-or-more
slashes" -- which does not match /api/orders, silently selecting the
wrong traffic. globToRegexSource compiles it to /api/.* and escapes
every other metacharacter, mirroring filterDSL's own glob compiler so
the box and the matcher agree. A test asserts the untranslated form
would have been wrong, so the translation cannot silently become a
no-op.

Breakpoints and verification advertise method/path/host only:
registerBreakpointMatcher takes a bare httpRequest with no response and
no body matcher, so status: and operation: have no destination.

Chaos is deliberately NOT swapped. ServiceChaosRegistry.get is an exact
ConcurrentHashMap lookup after normalizeHost, with no pattern matching
in either registry or at either call site, while the DSL's host: field
is a glob advertising host:*.example.com in its placeholder. Offering
it there would store a wildcard as a literal key that can never fire --
exactly the "operator that silently does nothing" this unit exists to
prevent. Instead the plain Host field now refuses wildcards, a pasted
host: operator, a URL scheme and a path, on all four entry points that
write a host key: the HTTP and TCP register forms, Quick Chaos, and
each chaos-experiment stage. The experiment stage is the one that
matters most -- a dead wildcard there yields a completed experiment
reporting a clean resilience verdict, corroborated by an auto-halt
monitor that sees a non-empty registry, having injected nothing.

fix(config): stop a masked configuration round trip destroying credentials

GET /mockserver/configuration masks credentials embedded inside
structured values, and a PUT restores the real secret from the value in
force. Several inputs broke that reconciliation, each of them either
disclosing a secret or silently destroying a working one while the
control plane still answered 200 OK.

A value carrying a second JSON document was returned in clear. The
parser stopped at the first document and reported no credential found,
so a value such as {"a":1}{"name":"o","apiKey":"..."} was disclosed
whole -- over the configuration endpoints, --print-config, and the
startup property-file log. Parsing is now whole-value-or-nothing, so
such a value is unparseable and masked in full.

A masked header carrying a comma tail wrote the mask itself as the
outbound credential, losing the real one. A masked header whose name the
operator re-cased found nothing under that exact key and was dropped
entirely. A masked backend key whose entry had been renamed was removed
from the document. All three now either resolve to the real value or
refuse the whole value and log why, leaving what is in force untouched.

Header names now resolve case-insensitively, but only when unambiguous:
a list holding two names differing only in case is two distinct headers
that are both sent, so the mask cannot be resolved and is not guessed.

Credential detection also missed several real header spellings --
X-Signature, X-Hub-Signature-256, Authentication, X-JWT, X-Auth and
others. Terms that match no configuration property name join the shared
sensitive-name list; jwt and auth are confined to header and JSON field
names, because masking them as property names would hide the
authentication configuration an operator reads precisely when debugging
authentication.

docs(opencode): state reviewer independence and the git deny-list at their true strength

context, a distinct adversarial prompt, restricted tools — and demotes

ignore a custom sampling temperature.

review-final is not sandboxed. write and edit are denied, but bash is granted in
both harnesses and permission.bash denies only destructive git and rm -rf

is instruction-level, which is why the agent prompt spells it out. The docs said
the reviewer "physically cannot" modify what it reviews. They now say the
enforcement is partial and where the gap is.

The banned-git-command table has the same shape: three of its eleven entries
(push --force, reset --hard, clean -fd) are in the deny-list and hard-blocked;
the other eight are instruction-only. The text claimed all were enforced at both
levels.

Also fixes the pitfalls entry that prescribed tools: { write: false } as a
sufficient read-only boundary, which is the overclaim corrected above.

fix(config): stop the cluster peer token being read back over the control plane

GET /mockserver/configuration returned clusterFanInPeerAuthToken in
clear. It is the credential a node presents on cross-node verify and
retrieve queries, sent verbatim as the control-plane Authorization
header, so a principal able only to READ the configuration could lift a
token granting MUTATE access to every peer in the cluster. The sibling
GET /mockserver/config already masked it, which is the divergence the
shared redaction rule exists to prevent.

Make it write-only, the pattern the other credentials in this DTO
already use: absent from the GET body, still settable by PUT, and a
round trip therefore leaves the held token untouched.

The reason it was missed is worth fixing more than the leak itself. The
test enumerated a hand-maintained list of write-only credentials, so a
new credential property was unprotected by default and nothing failed.
Replace that with a reflective guard: every serialized property whose
name the shared sensitive-name predicate recognises must be absent or
masked, and must also be covered by the round-trip guard. A future
credential now has to be deliberately exempted rather than silently
forgotten, and an exemption must carry a written justification.

One property is exempted: dashboardAnalyticsKey. The browser dashboard
reads it back to initialise analytics, and an ingest-only project key is
designed for that exposure, so masking it would break the feature while
protecting nothing. A positive test now fails if someone masks it,
turning a silent feature-kill into a build failure. The diagnostic
surfaces -- GET /mockserver/config and the startup log dump -- still
mask it.

fix(editors): regenerate the expectation schemas the editors validate against

The committed editor schemas rejected expectations MockServer itself

foo" -- by letting the server emit the structured form for a key the
plain form would misread. It updated the server schemas and the
serializers but did not re-run the editor generator, so the editors
kept validating header, query-parameter and cookie names and values as
plain strings.

The generator's contract is that the editors validate against the same
schema as the server, never stricter nor laxer. They were stricter:
three of the four server-authored fixtures the server's own validator
accepts were rejected in-editor, flagging valid files as errors.

Regenerate both. The change is a widening -- plain strings validate

validates identically either way.

Note the JetBrains resource has no build path that runs the generator;
it refreshes only as a side effect of packaging the VS Code extension,
which is why it drifted.

fix(grpc): honour wire base64 for -bin metadata and stop derived header spoofing

gRPC carries metadata keys ending `-bin` as base64 on the wire. MockServer
neither encodes nor decodes them, which is correct: the value in an expectation
is the wire form. That contract was undocumented, so users had to guess, and one
consequence of it was wrong.

grpc-java encodes with BASE64_ENCODING_OMIT_PADDING, so the wire value is
unpadded (`AQIDBA`). A user writing the natural padded form (`AQIDBA==`) in an
expectation silently failed to match. `-bin` header values are now compared
ignoring base64 padding, at the comparison site so a regex matcher key still
selects a literal `-bin` request key. Only structurally valid padded base64 is
stripped: a value whose length is not a multiple of 4 is left exactly as
written, so `A+=` stays a regex and is not rewritten into one that matches more
than it did. The unmatched-request diagnostic reports the values as the user
wrote them and notes that padding was ignored.

HTTP/2 bidi streams synthesised the request from the path alone, so inbound
metadata was not mapped and an expectation could not match on it — over HTTP/3
the same expectation did match. Non-pseudo headers are now mapped, using the
received-message convention so a value beginning `!` stays literal;
Http3RequestBridge is corrected to the same convention.

Client-supplied `x-grpc-*` headers were appended alongside the values MockServer
derives from the path, so a request could carry a forged `x-grpc-service` into
matching and an expectation qualified by that name could match a stream
belonging to a different service. The derived names now have one definition and
are stripped before being set, on every transport: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 unary and
streaming, HTTP/2 bidi, HTTP/3 unary and streaming, and HTTP/3 bidi. The h1/h2
conversion is structured so every exit strips, rather than relying on an
invariant asserted elsewhere. Empty-bodied gRPC requests over HTTP/1.1 and
HTTP/2 now receive the derived headers, matching HTTP/3.

Binary metadata semantics, including the unpadded form grpc-java emits and the
pre-existing case-insensitivity of header comparison, are documented for users.

Add an integration test that opens a real TLS connection presenting a chosen,
non-default SNIHostName and asserts the served peer certificate's Subject

host on the same running server to prove per-host certificate regeneration.

asserting the hostname was added to the SAN configuration set; no handshake test

fix(build): stop resolving MockServer's own snapshots from Sonatype

A build could fail with a 403 in a module that had nothing to do with
the change being tested. The maven-invoker child builds declared
central-portal-snapshots with snapshots enabled, so Maven periodically
re-resolved our own 7.4.1-SNAPSHOT artifacts over the network; when the
corporate proxy held a freshly published jar for sandbox scanning, the
reactor failed after the tests under test had already passed. Only the
jar 403s -- the pom and checksums return 200 -- which is why it looked
random rather than like a broken repository.

The same declaration also made the build resolve a remote snapshot in
preference to the copy the reactor had just installed, whenever the
local install was the older of the two. That is routine on a developer
machine that has not rebuilt, and it means the integration tests can
verify a previously published artifact instead of the working tree.
CI is not expected to have hit either mode -- it builds with install
before integration-test and deploys after the build behind a wait, so
its own install always wins -- but the declaration reached every Maven
process, including child builds, as a latent hazard.

Nothing needed it: the only SNAPSHOT coordinates in the reactor are our
own and the invoker projects' own.

The maven-plugin declared the repository in its pom rather than only in
its build, so it was copied into the pom published to Maven Central --
consumers of a released plugin inherited a third-party repository their
Maven queries for release artifacts too. Published poms are immutable,
so this stops the injection from the next release onwards.

Publishing is untouched: distributionManagement and the credentials
remain the only places the URL appears.

Also fix the tomcat scratch directories, whose ignore patterns and
clean filesets still used pre-monorepo paths and so matched nothing.

test(telemetry): drive forward-path GenAI span emission through a running server

Add an end-to-end behavioural test that boots a real forwarding MockServer
proxying a chat-completions POST to an upstream MockServer stubbed as an OpenAI
endpoint, and reads the emitted span back out of an in-process
InMemorySpanExporter wired into the process-wide tracer. The span asserted here
can only exist if the running server executed the production
HttpActionHandler.emitForwardGenAiSpan (provider sniffing, response parsing and
span recording) on the forward path.

Previously the forward path's GenAI span emission was guarded only by
ForwardPathGenAiSpansTest in mockserver-core, which hand-mirrored the production

through it and asserts on the client-received bytes:

- a schema-invalid POST /pets is rejected with 400 and never reaches the

test(h2c): prove respond/forward/callback/error over cleartext HTTP/2 with a real client

Adds H2cMockingMatrixIntegrationTest, which drives a real prior-knowledge

asserts on the bytes the client receives on its own stream for each core

Closes test-coverage audit gap #3: the full action matrix previously ran only

test(breakpoints): drive the interactive breakpoint round trip over a live transport

Adds an integration test that starts a running MockServer, opens the real
breakpoint callback WebSocket via MockServerClient.addBreakpoint, and drives a
real JDK HTTP client through the full pause -> dispatch -> resolve loop:

- a RESPONSE-phase breakpoint whose client handler rewrites the matched mock
  response has the originating caller receive the modified status and body
- a REQUEST-phase breakpoint whose client handler returns a response ABORTs
  before the mock is generated, so the caller receives the abort response

Assertions are made only on what the originating HTTP client reads back from the
running server, proving the pause/resume/modify happened server-side rather than
below the wire. Previously breakpoints were exercised only by client unit tests
(mocked HTTP client) and registry/handler tests over EmbeddedChannel; no test
connected the real callback WebSocket client to a running server and drove a
live request through a pause-resolve cycle.

test(http3): drive the mocking-action matrix over QUIC with a real client

Add Http3MockingMatrixIntegrationTest, which stands up an HTTP/3-enabled

- respond delivers its status and body
- class callback delivers its produced (echoed) body
- forward relays the upstream body back
- forwardOverride rewrites the request and relays the overridden body back
- error resets the QUIC request stream (RFC 9114 RESET_STREAM) with no response

Previously the HTTP/3 tests covered trace-context, mTLS capture, gRPC,

fix(persistence): bound the cloud blob-store restore and make it verifiable

Restoring cloud-persisted expectations ran a synchronous blob-store read
from the HttpState constructor, which happens before any port is bound,
with no timeout on the call and no timeout on the client. A blob-store
endpoint that accepts a connection and never answers -- a typo, a VPC
egress rule, a DNS blackhole -- held startup for the SDK's full retry
budget: measured at 121 seconds before the server bound, against 10
after this change. Readiness probes, Testcontainers wait strategies and
CI harnesses all time out well inside that window.

The restore now runs on a daemon thread with a deadline, controlled by
the new blobStoreRestoreTimeoutSeconds (default 10, 0 to skip). On
expiry a warning names the deadline and the property, and startup
proceeds. Nothing is deserialized or applied unless the read returns in
time, so a late reply cannot revive expectations behind the running
server; if it eventually fails it logs its own cause at debug, which is
usually the real diagnosis.

The test covering the original fix never ran. It was named with an IT
suffix, which matches neither the surefire nor the failsafe include
pattern, so it compiled and was never executed -- the fix shipped with
no executing coverage at all. Rename it, and add the core unit tests
that were missing: the restore itself, the filesystem skip, a blank
payload, a malformed payload, and a missing key.

Restored expectations could then be deleted by the initializer. Both
tagged their entries with the persisted file's absolute path, and the
initializer runs second and removes every entry carrying its own tag
that is absent from the file it read -- so pointing initializationJsonPath
at the persisted path silently discarded everything just restored.
Prefix the restore's tag so the two can never collide, and warn when the
two paths resolve to the same place.

A missing key logged nothing at any level, which made the most common
misconfiguration invisible: the key embeds the absolutely-resolved
persisted path, so an instance started from a different working
directory looks for a different object. It now says so, with the key.

docs(testing): a -Dtest run of a quarantined class is not evidence

mockserver-core splits its tests across two surefire executions: a
parallel one that excludes 123 classes which mutate JVM-global state,
and a sequential one that runs exactly those. Passing -Dtest defeats
the split. AbstractSurefireMojo.getExcludeList returns an empty list
whenever a specific test is named, and getIncludeList replaces the
configured includes with it, so every execution's filters are discarded
and the named class runs in both -- in one reused fork, the quarantined
phase first.

That makes targeted verification untrustworthy in both directions. A
quarantined class can fail in the parallel phase for contention the
real build never has; and because the correct-phase run comes second
and passes, the log tail reads green. One such invocation reported
BUILD SUCCESS over four real failures.

Record the mechanism, how to tell whether a class is quarantined, and
the command that runs it once in the phase it belongs to. Configuring
the split through includesFile or excludesFile does not help -- both
sit behind the same branch.

fix(config): refuse a whole-value credential that merely contains the mask

The three whole-value credentials -- llmApiKey,
prometheusRemoteWriteBearerToken and prometheusRemoteWriteBasicAuthPassword
-- compared an incoming value to the redaction mask with equals. A value
that merely carried the mask therefore passed the guard and was written
verbatim: PUT of "sk-***REDACTED***" destroyed the held key and made the
literal mask the outbound credential, while the control plane answered
200 OK. The value-embedded credentials were fixed for this in an earlier
change; this closes the same defect one field over.

Both write paths now treat containment, not equality, as the signal.
applyTo goes through the shared restore, which leaves the held credential
untouched and logs which property was refused and how to recover.
buildObject leaves the field unset so a property file or environment
variable can still resolve it, rather than pinning an empty value that
would shadow them.

An untouched round trip is now silent. It was warning once per credential
for the flow the documentation explicitly blesses -- take a GET, change
something unrelated, PUT it back -- which trains an operator to ignore the
warning that matters. The header-list path has been silent here since it
was written.

The consumer documentation stated the refusal rule over all five masked
properties, but two of those are structured values where leaving a mask
in place is the supported edit and the secret is restored into it. An
operator following that text would have concluded they must paste the
real credential back into the request body to change anything around it.
The whole-value and embedded rules are now stated separately, with the
embedded one saying plainly never to do that.

docs(chaos): cross-link recoverAfter and chaos count-window for retry testing

The site described two ways to test a client's retry/backoff logic against a
transiently-failing dependency without connecting them: recoverAfter on a
response action, and the chaos succeedFirst/failRequestCount count window on a
forward action. A user reading either page had no route to the other, and no
guidance on which fits their case.

recoverAfter is the response-path answer; the chaos count window is the
forward/proxy-path answer. Each page now points to the other and says which
applies, so a user testing a forwarded dependency is sent to chaos and a user
mocking a response directly is sent to the simpler recoverAfter clause.

fix(test): accept a refused mTLS handshake surfacing as SocketException

The runtime-mTLS enforcement test asserted the certificateless handshake is
refused, but only accepted SSLException. On CI the server closes the socket
before the client finishes writing its handshake records, so the refusal
surfaces as SocketException (Broken pipe / Connection reset) instead of a fatal
TLS alert. Accept both: only a COMPLETED handshake means enforcement failed.

fix(ci): avoid ls|grep in ui-e2e.sh jar lookup to satisfy shellcheck SC2010

The infra pipeline's validate-scripts step runs shellcheck -S warning over all
CI scripts; the ui-e2e.sh runnable-jar lookup used `ls -t ... | grep` which
trips SC2010. Replace with find -printf | sort -rn (newest matching jar,
excluding -sources/-javadoc/original- variants) — same result, shellcheck-clean.

test(dashboard): pin the WebSocket frame to a drift-proof cross-boundary contract

Close the gap where the dashboard's WebSocket consumption was tested with
test-authored payloads (useWebSocket.test.ts) rather than server-derived frames,
so the server DashboardWebSocketHandler and the UI store/panels could silently
drift apart.

A single checked-in contract file (dashboardFrameContract.json) lists, per panel
(log messages, active expectations, received and proxied requests), the fields
the UI reads and their JSON types. The Java side drives the REAL handler across
all four panels, captures the emitted frame and asserts every required field is
present with the right type and that the server-assigned key correlations hold.
The UI side feeds the same file's representative frame through the real store
applyMessage and asserts the resulting items expose those same fields. Renaming a
field name in the one file reddens both tests; a server-side rename reddens Java.

Unlike the reverted byte-equal captured golden (green locally, drifted in CI),
the check is a per-field SUBSET assertion — immune to non-deterministic emission
ordering, to timestamp/UUID/port/hostname values and to environment-dependent
extra fields. A companion assertion captures the frame twice and proves a
value-blind, order-independent structural fingerprint is identical across both,
catching the ordering non-determinism that only surfaced in CI last time.

test(openapi): prove forward-validate LOG_ONLY forwards unmodified and logs only

HttpForwardValidateAction LOG_ONLY mode (validate + log, forward unchanged)
was only asserted via a getter; the behavioural passthrough was untested while
the STRICT reject branches were covered. Add two handler tests that drive
handle(...) with validationMode LOG_ONLY: a schema-violating request is still
forwarded upstream and the upstream 200 flows back unchanged (not 400), and a
schema-violating upstream response is returned unmodified (not 502).

test(http2): guard the stream-id audit safety-net with a unit test

Http2StreamIdAuditHandler is wired into the HTTP/2 server pipeline in
PortUnificationHandler but had no test anywhere. It is the only thing that
turns a response head written without an x-http2-stream-id header - which the
HTTP/2 codec silently mis-routes onto a new server-initiated stream, so the
client receives nothing and hangs - into a loud WARN. An unguarded safety-net
can regress to silence undetected, which is exactly how issue #2419 and its
SSE/streaming/metrics/MCP siblings shipped.

Add Http2StreamIdAuditHandlerTest driving the handler on an EmbeddedChannel
with a capturing logger, asserting the observable behaviour: an unstamped head
warns exactly once, a stamped head is silent, and a second unstamped head on
the same connection warns-once-per-connection (matching the handler's dedup).

test(velocity): cover disallowClassLoading toggled on a live engine

The existing coverage flipped velocityDisallowClassLoading and then built a
fresh VelocityTemplateEngine, so the runtime rebuild-on-live-engine path in
currentEngineHolder() -- which rebuilds the underlying VelocityEngine with the
SecureUberspector when the configured flag differs from the flag the current
engine was built with -- was never exercised. A regression that made the
setter / system-property / PUT /mockserver/configuration toggle inert on an
already-constructed (cached) engine would have reddened nothing.

Add a test that builds ONE engine with class loading allowed, renders a
class-loading template and asserts it genuinely EXECUTES the class-loading line
(reaching Runtime.exec), then flips velocityDisallowClassLoading(true) on the
SAME configuration and re-renders through the SAME engine, asserting the
class-loading line is now BLOCKED (inert, empty body, no exception).

Positive control: disabling the currentEngineHolder() rebuild makes the
post-toggle render still execute Runtime.exec and throw, reddening the block
assertion; restoring it passes.

test(metrics): drive GET /mockserver/metrics enabled path to 200 + Prometheus body

The only enabled-path coverage was a mock-ctx unit test asserting content-type
was non-null; it never proved GET /mockserver/metrics returns 200 with a real
exposition body. Add two HttpRequestHandlerTest cases that route the request
through the real HttpRequestHandler and MetricsHandler with metrics enabled and
the mock_server_requests_received counter incremented: assert 200 (mapped through
the same wire encoder the server uses, since the handler writes a status-less
response the encoder resolves to 200 OK) and that the body carries the
mock_server_requests_received_total series. A second case negotiates the
OpenMetrics exposition format via the Accept header. Complements the existing
disabled -> 404 negative so the enabled path is provably the difference.

test(persistence): cover reflective cloud-blob-store auto-discovery in StateBackendFactory

The reflective blobStoreType=s3 discovery path -- discoverBlobStoreBackend
plus the BLOB_STORE_REGISTRARS map (Class.forName of the registrar ->

StateBackendFactoryTest only instanceof-checked the filesystem/memory
blob stores, so a broken registrar-class name or map wiring redded nothing.

Add S3BlobStoreDiscoveryTest in mockserver-blob-s3 (which has the S3 module
on its classpath): it configures blobStoreType=s3 and calls
StateBackendFactory.create(...) with NO manual register(), asserting the
backend's blobs() is an S3BlobStore -- provable only if discovery loaded the

Add two core-only assertions to StateBackendFactoryTest: blobStoreType=s3
with the module absent fails hard with the documented IllegalStateException
('add the mockserver-blob-s3 dependency'), and an unrecognised type is

test(war): cover cookie surrounding-quote stripping in servlet decoder

Feed a jakarta Cookie whose value carries RFC 6265 surrounding double

HttpRequest cookie value has the quotes stripped, plus an unquoted value
that must pass through unchanged. Pins stripSurroundingQuotes(), which
every prior fixture left unexercised by only using plain ASCII values a

test(dashboard): cover default MIME-type fallback for unmapped asset extension

Every existing DashboardHandlerTest serves a mapped extension (.js, .svg), so
MIME_MAP.getOrDefault(extension, DEFAULT_MIME_TYPE) never exercised its fallback
arm — the branch that returns a non-null application/octet-stream for an unmapped

test(tls): cover IPv6 Subject-Alternative-Name branch in BCKeyAndCertificateFactory

The SAN-IP handling has IPv6/netmask branches (IPAddress.isValidIPv6 /
isValidIPv6WithNetmask) but the only IP-SAN tests used IPv4 literals, so those

Add shouldIncludeIPv6AddressesInSAN, which configures IPv6 SAN IPs (::1 and

test(mock): assert exhausted Times is passively removed from active expectations

Adds shouldRemoveExhaustedTimesFromActiveExpectations next to the existing

test(memory): cover outputMemoryUsageCsv memory-usage CSV export

MemoryMonitoring writes a CSV header from buildStatistics() keys on

test(ratelimit): prove TOKEN_BUCKET burst-then-429 through the handler path

test(wasm): pin custom-rule host-isolation — a module importing a WASI host function is refused

WASM rule modules run under chicory with NO host imports wired: WasmRuntime
instantiates every module with a bare Instance.builder(module).build(), never
withImportValues(...), so a module cannot reach the filesystem or any host/WASI
capability. Nothing asserted this, so a regression that began wiring host imports
would have gone undetected.

Add WasmRuntimeHostIsolationTest, which hand-assembles a minimal-but-valid module
whose import section declares wasi_snapshot_preview1.fd_write and whose exported
match actually calls it, then asserts:
- chicory refuses to instantiate it (UnlinkableException), mirroring the runtime's
  own bare build call;
- WasmRuntime.callMatch therefore fails closed to false through the public API;
- positive control: supplying a stub fd_write host import (the wiring MockServer

The refusal assertion was verified to go RED when the host import is wired into the

test(trafficValidate): cover a request-side OpenAPI violation end-to-end

Both existing TrafficValidateIntegrationTest cases triggered only
response-schema errors, leaving the request-validation half of the

test(drift): cover the responseTimeThresholdMs performance-flag gate

DriftAnalyzer.checkPerformanceDrift raises a PERFORMANCE drift record only
when an expectation's observed p95 latency exceeds the instance-set
responseTimeThresholdMs, but no test drove responses straddling that
threshold, leaving the flag->behaviour mapping unverified.

Add DriftPerformanceThresholdTest, which feeds the real PercentileTracker
latencies under and over the threshold and asserts on the production
DriftStore outcome: the over-threshold case flags exactly one PERFORMANCE
record (expectedValue=<=threshold, actual p95), the under-threshold and
disabled (0) cases flag nothing, a slow-tail distribution whose p95 crosses

flag is raised and its severity meets the notifier threshold.

The class mutates the process-wide PercentileTracker and DriftAlertNotifier

from parallel, included in sequential) per the ParallelStaticStateGuard.

providers (OpenAI, OpenAI-Responses, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure-OpenAI,
Ollama) encode the canonical text and tool-call completions and assert the

test(telemetry): cover GenAI span emission on the LLM serve path

The serve-path GenAI span that HttpLlmResponseActionHandler emits via
GenAiSpans.recordCompletion(...) when serving a locally-mocked
httpLlmResponse completion had no end-to-end test — only the
forward/proxy path was guarded (ForwardPathGenAiSpanEmissionTest).

ServePathGenAiSpanEmissionTest installs an InMemorySpanExporter through
the GenAiSpanExporter.startWithProcessor(...) seam, drives a real
MockServer serving an OpenAI-shaped completion, and asserts exactly one
GenAI span carrying gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.system, and input/output
usage-token attributes is produced by the production serve path, read
back from the exporter rather than reconstructed.

Positive control: commenting out the recordCompletion call on the serve
path drives the test to 0 spans (RED); restoring it returns GREEN.

test(parser-limits): prove maxHeaderSize truncates over-limit headers over a real socket

The three HTTP parser limits (maxInitialLineLength, maxHeaderSize,
maxChunkSize) are wired into the Netty HttpServerCodec in the HTTP/1.1
request pipeline (PortUnificationHandler.switchToHttp) but had no
behavioural coverage, so a regression that ignored the configured value
and fell back to Netty's 8192-byte default -- or dropped the wiring --
would have gone unnoticed.

HttpParserLimitsIntegrationTest starts a server with maxHeaderSize=1024
and drives raw HTTP/1.1 requests over a plain Socket against a
header-conditional expectation. The observable effect of the limit is
header truncation: Netty's decoder stops at the byte that crosses the
limit and drops every header after it (MockServer logs the decode
failure but serves the request from what it parsed). A control request
whose marker header is within the limit matches and returns 200; an
otherwise-identical request with a ~2KB filler header ahead of the
marker pushes the marker past the boundary, it is dropped, the request
no longer matches and MockServer returns 404. The filler size sits
strictly between the configured limit and the 8192 default, so the test
is a genuine positive control: reverting the wiring to the default lets
the marker survive and the over-limit request returns 200 -- confirmed
red.

test(llm): drive OpenAI Responses previous_response_id chaining + GET retrieval over the wire

The Responses API server-side state (automatic storing of an issued response,
previous_response_id reconstruction of a prior turn, and GET /v1/responses/{id}
retrieval) was covered only at the handler+store level (OpenAiResponsesStateTest),
never over a real socket. Add OpenAiResponsesStateEndToEndTest: it boots a real
MockServer, POSTs a first /v1/responses turn with default store:true and captures
the issued response id, POSTs a second turn carrying only new input plus
previous_response_id, and asserts over the wire that the chained turn matches
(via a whenTurnIndex(1) predicate that only matches once the prior assistant turn
has been reconstructed) and that GET /v1/responses/{id} returns the stored body.

fix(test): run HttpActionHandlerDriftDetectionTest in the sequential Surefire phase

It mutates the process-wide DriftStore singleton (DriftStore.getInstance().clear())
but was not registered in mockserver-core's parallel-exclude / sequential-include
lists, so GlobalStateMutationGuardTest failed the build. Register it in both lists
symmetrically, matching the sibling drift tests.

fix(client-node): stop the jar downloader deleting other versions and leaking on failure

The mockserver-node suite flaked because downloadJar deleted every jar
whose name did not match the version being fetched, so a test requesting
6.0.0 removed the 7.4.0 jar out from under a sibling test process
launching 7.4.0 -- surfacing as "Unable to access jarfile" and
ECONNREFUSED. It no longer deletes anything: the finished download is
renamed over the old jar in one step, and only a SNAPSHOT of the same
version is re-fetched.

The download path is hardened along the way. The temp file is created
with an exclusive open (O_CREAT|O_EXCL) under an unpredictable name, so
a pre-existing file or a planted symlink is refused rather than written
through; the descriptor is handed straight to the write stream, so the
"created it" flag is set in the same tick and a failure before the
stream opens cannot orphan a partial. A completed download is validated
(non-trivial size, ZIP magic) before it is renamed into place, so a
captive-portal HTML page can never be cached as the jar. A connection
that establishes and then goes idle is abandoned after a configurable
timeout instead of hanging, and every failure path now tears down the
request and response so a failed download cannot keep transferring.

Jar resolution no longer globs '**' and takes the first hit -- it checks
three known directories and throws a named error if none holds the jar,
rather than passing undefined to spawn. glob moves to devDependencies.

Also fix a mockserver-client-node test that asserted nothing: its helper
rejected any status >= 400, so the assertion after a self-forwarding
callback (which 404s) was unreachable. It now forwards to a real
upstream and asserts the relayed response, proving the callback path.

All of the above is covered by a new test/downloadJar_test.js, each case
checked by reverting the fix and confirming the named test goes red.

fix(grpc-web): re-frame matched responses over the wire + add socket IT

Every prior gRPC-Web test drove the handler via EmbeddedChannel and set
x-grpc-web-content-type directly on the response, so the real mock-matching
path was never exercised. There the gRPC-Web marker lives on the request only
and was lost, so a matched expectation returned application/grpc with
grpc-status in HTTP trailers no browser gRPC-Web client can read.

Retain the original request content-type in the per-stream GrpcPendingRequests
record alongside service/method, so GrpcToHttpResponseHandler re-frames the
matched response as gRPC-Web (message frame + 0x80 trailer frame carrying
grpc-status in the body, base64 for -text).

Add GrpcWebOverTheWireIntegrationTest: posts real application/grpc-web and
application/grpc-web-text framed requests to a running server over a raw
socket and asserts on the exact bytes a browser client receives.

test(asyncapi): drive control-plane load/status/verify endpoints over the wire

The AsyncAPI control-plane HTTP endpoints (PUT/GET /mockserver/asyncapi and
PUT /mockserver/asyncapi/verify) were only exercised at the orchestrator/
control-plane level, leaving the Netty -> HttpState -> AsyncApiControlPlaneRegistry
-> AsyncApiControlPlaneImpl routing and response wiring untested end to end.

Add AsyncApiControlPlaneIntegrationTest, which boots a real MockServer and
drives all three endpoints over a raw socket with no live broker: it asserts
the broker-less load response (201, loaded, channel count, zero publishers/
subscribers), the status response (200, channels, counts, and the empty case),
and the reachable broker-less verify verdict (406 with the failure detail),
plus the blank-body 400. The passing (202) verify verdict requires recorded
messages from a live broker and stays with the live-broker suite.

test(h2): prove StreamingBody response reaches a real HTTP/2 inbound client as incremental DATA frames

Closes the coverage gap flagged in Http2SseStreamingIntegrationTest: the
StreamingBody sibling of #2419 exercises NettyResponseWriter.writeStreamingResponse
(which re-stamps the request's HTTP/2 stream id onto the streaming head and flushes
each chunk as it arrives) but was untested against a real HTTP/2 inbound client.
The existing streaming-relay ITs drive an HTTP/1.1 inbound socket; H2cMockingMatrix
drives h2c but only non-streaming actions.

Http2StreamingBodyIntegrationTest drives a real prior-knowledge h2c multiplex client
through a streamingResponsesEnabled forward MockServer to an SSE upstream and asserts
on the frames received on the client's own request stream: both events arrive (stream-id
stamp), and the early event's DATA frame arrives promptly as one of at least two
separate in-order DATA frames rather than buffered into one. Verified the assertion
goes red when the write path is degraded to buffer chunks until stream completion.
test(proxy-protocol): prove PROXY-header destination drives transparent-proxy forwarding over a real socket

test(drift): prove live forward -> analyse -> DriftStore -> GET /mockserver/drift assembly

The DriftAnalyzer, DriftStore, and the driftDetectionEnabled gate in
HttpActionHandler were each unit-tested, but no test drove the assembled
drift pipeline through to the GET /mockserver/drift retrieval endpoint the
dashboard consumes. Add DriftEndToEndAssemblyTest: it forwards a request
through the real HttpActionHandler whose upstream (500) differs from a
co-registered response stub (200), runs drift analysis synchronously, then
serves GET /mockserver/drift through a real HttpState and asserts the JSON
contains the recorded STATUS drift (unfiltered and via the expectationId
filter). A companion case proves a non-drifting forward leaves the endpoint
empty. Registered in the sequential Surefire phase (mutates the singleton
DriftStore + PercentileTracker).

test(llm): serve a refusal preset with quota + rate-limit headers over the wire

The LLM refusal presets, provider-specific rate-limit headers, and stateful
request-count quota were only asserted at the body-builder / handler-unit level;
no test drove them through a running server. Add an over-the-wire integration
test that serves an httpLlmResponse configured with an Anthropic refusal preset
and a 2-request quota, and asserts on the raw socket response that the first two
requests return a 200 refusal envelope with anthropic-ratelimit-* headers and
the third flips to a 429 rate_limit_error envelope with Retry-After.

fix(config): guard every omitted write-only credential against a pasted mask

GET /mockserver/configuration omits a credential that is @JsonIgnore-d,
but --print-config, GET /mockserver/config and the dashboard's Server
Info tab all render it as ***REDACTED***. An operator who copied one of
those masks back into a PUT body had it stored verbatim as the
credential -- the working secret destroyed, the mask sent as outbound
auth, and the control plane answering 200 OK with nothing logged.

Route all fifteen credential-shaped DTO properties through the same mask
guard on both write paths: applyTo restores the held credential and logs
the refusal, buildObject leaves the field unset so a property file or
environment variable still resolves. A reflective test enumerates every
credential-shaped property with no exclusions, so a new one is covered
the day it is added, and asserts through effectiveConfiguration() that
the diagnostic surfaces really do mask each one.

The silent short-circuit added for the whole-value credentials keyed on
isSensitivePropertyName, which every omitted credential also satisfies,
so a bare mask pasted onto one of them was refused silently. Narrow it
to the three whole-value credentials that GET actually masks, so an
omitted credential's bare mask is refused and logged -- the very signal
this change exists to restore -- while the blessed untouched round trip
of a whole-value credential stays silent.

fix(core): serve a FILE response body verbatim when no template engine is set

A static response whose body is type FILE with a filePath but no
templateType returned the file path string instead of the file
contents: the FileBody passed through untouched and, on the wire, its
value is the path. Only setting a templateType (MUSTACHE/VELOCITY)
caused the file to be read at all -- so the UI's "None (serve file
verbatim)" option did the opposite of what it says.

HttpResponseActionHandler now reads any FILE body that is not going to
be template-rendered -- no templateType, or an unsupported one such as
JavaScript, which previously fell through a branch whose comment claimed
it served raw contents but returned the path -- and serves the file
verbatim. A text content type yields the decoded string; a binary
content type, or none, yields raw bytes via a new
FileReader.readBytesFromClassPathOrPath, so an image or archive is not
charset-corrupted. A missing file throws, exactly as the templated path
does.

The one test that covered this case asserted the body stayed a FileBody
-- it encoded the bug as correct. It is replaced with assertions on the
served contents, including a binary fixture whose exact bytes (invalid
as UTF-8) must survive.

This covers the static response action -- the reported case. A FILE body
returned from a callback, a response template, or a forward override
reaches the wire without passing through this handler and keeps the old
behaviour; closing that needs a FileBody branch in the shared
BodyDecoderEncoder and is left to its own change.

test(kafka): prove SASL credentials reach and are enforced by a real broker

Kafka SASL/SSL security was only asserted at the property-map level
(KafkaMessagePublisherSecurityTest) and every live-broker Kafka
integration test used a plaintext bootstrap, so nothing proved the
configured credentials actually authenticate against a broker.

KafkaSecurityLiveBrokerIntegrationTest starts a Testcontainers Kafka
whose external listener is SASL_PLAINTEXT/PLAIN with a broker-side JAAS
config that knows a single credential, then drives the
KafkaMessagePublisher with a KafkaSecurity: a correctly-credentialed
publisher publishes and the message is read back by a matching
credentialed consumer, while a wrong-password publisher is rejected
with an authentication exception (enforcement, not just that plaintext
works). Docker-gated via DockerAvailability so it skips off-Docker.

test(mqtt): prove MqttSecurity credentials enforce against a secured live broker

Add MqttTlsLiveBrokerIntegrationTest driving MockServer's MQTT publisher
against a Testcontainers Mosquitto broker configured with a password_file
and allow_anonymous false. Proves correct credentials authenticate and
deliver to an authed subscriber, while a wrong password and an anonymous
connection are both rejected at CONNECT. Docker-gated via the shared
DockerAvailability probe so it skips cleanly off-Docker.

Previously MqttSecurity was only asserted at the options-carrier unit level
and the sole live Mosquitto IT ran an allow_anonymous plaintext broker, so
nothing proved credentials are applied and enforced on the wire.

test(asyncapi): prove control-plane load() connects to a live Kafka broker and publishes on load

The AsyncAPI control-plane load() broker-connecting path
(createBrokerConnections / publishOnLoad) was untested against a real
broker: AsyncApiControlPlaneImplTest loads without a reachable broker
(asserting publishers=0/subscribers=0) and AsyncApiControlPlaneIntegrationTest
covers only the broker-less HTTP endpoints.

Add a Docker-gated AsyncApiControlPlaneLiveBrokerIntegrationTest
(Testcontainers Kafka) that drives load() with a real brokerConfig,
publishOnLoad:true and consume:true, then proves the control-plane
genuinely connected and published by consuming the on-load message with
a plain third-party Kafka consumer and asserting status() reports
publishers>0, a subscriber, and the recorded round-tripped message.

Positive control: skipping createBrokerConnections in load() turns the
publishers>0 / consumed-message assertions RED; restoring turns them GREEN.

test(go): prove forward and error response actions over the wire

The Go client's response-action coverage was builder/JSON only: no test
registered a forward or error action and drove a request proving the server
actually performs it. Add integration tests that do.

TestIntegration_ForwardActionReachesUpstream registers a match-once,
higher-priority httpForward that forwards to the server's own loopback, so a
second lower-priority respond expectation on the same path becomes the upstream
once the forward is consumed. This needs no externally-reachable upstream and
runs identically in the CI sibling-container harness and against a locally
port-mapped server. The caller only sees the distinctive upstream body if the
forward was genuinely performed and looped back.

TestIntegration_ErrorActionDropsConnection registers an httpError
dropConnection and asserts the matched request fails at the transport level
with no HTTP response, while a control respond endpoint on the same server
still answers cleanly -- so the transport error can only come from the error
action, not an unhealthy server.

test(rust): prove server enforces NottableString negation and performs forward/error actions over the wire

Close two MEDIUM Rust-client coverage gaps (#43, #46). The integration
suite only asserted control-plane serialization and registered a forward
expectation it never drove, so nothing proved a running MockServer acted
on either negation matchers or response actions.

Add three data-plane wire tests (dependency-free raw-socket HTTP client):
- test_negation_matcher_enforced_over_wire: bare !foo, MatcherValue::not_literal,
  and escaped literal !foo; asserts 200 for non-foo, 404 for foo, and that an
  escaped !foo matches literally rather than as a negation.
- test_forward_action_actually_forwards: registers a higher-priority run-once
  FORWARD that loops back to the server's own port, plus a lower-priority
  fall-through RESPOND; the caller sees the distinctive fall-through body only
  if the forward genuinely executed. Topology-independent (no external upstream),
  so it passes whether the test runs on the host or in a sibling container.
- test_error_action_actually_returns_raw_bytes: registers an ERROR action and
  asserts the server writes the configured raw bytes back (418/TEAPOT).

Verified all three RED under degradation (plain foo; dead loopback forward port
-> 502; non-418 error bytes) and GREEN restored, against MockServer 7.4.1-SNAPSHOT.

test(dotnet): prove header negation and forward/error actions over the wire

The .NET integration suite asserted expectation creation but never proved the
server honours what the client sends. Two coverage gaps: no test that a literal
!foo header matcher (NottableString negation) is transmitted and enforced over
the wire, and no test that a registered forward/error action is actually
performed rather than merely created.

Add WireBehaviorTests, driving real requests through a running MockServer via
the existing MOCKSERVER_URL harness:
- a 'not foo' header matcher (MatcherValue.NotLiteral) matches a non-foo request
  (200) and rejects a foo request (404), proving the '!' negation crosses the
  wire and is enforced;
- the escaped literal MatcherValue.Literal("!foo") matches only a header whose
  value really is !foo;
- a forward action is genuinely forwarded — the path is received twice (original
  plus the re-entered forward), which a server that ignored the forward could not
  produce;
- an error action actually drops the connection (a transport failure, not an
  HTTP status).

Each assertion was confirmed to redden when the corresponding client behaviour
is degraded.

and replays it unchanged -- so it records zero gaps for every fixture BY
CONSTRUCTION and can never detect a field the typed builders (HttpResponse,

build(vscode): compile under TypeScript 7 by declaring the node types

TypeScript 7 no longer auto-includes every installed @types/* package

capturing ClientInterceptor on the success path and StatusRuntimeException

fix(persistence): compose a valid cloud blob key from the file name and prefix

Cloud expectation persistence derived the blob key from the ABSOLUTE local
persistedExpectationsPath and concatenated blobStoreKeyPrefix onto it with
plain string addition. With the documented prefix shape
(blobStoreKeyPrefix="mockserver/") that composed
"mockserver//var/folders/.../persistedExpectations.json" — a doubled separator
that MinIO rejects with HTTP 400, "Object name contains unsupported
characters" — so under that one prefix shape nothing was persisted and nothing
could be restored. Under every other prefix shape the write SUCCEEDED and
restore worked, because a leading '/' is a legal byte in an S3 object name and
the read composed exactly the same name back; the cost there was that the
object was named after the writing container's local filesystem layout, so an
instance that resolved persistedExpectationsPath to a different absolute path
looked under a different name and silently restored nothing.

The key is now derived by the shared org.mockserver.state.BlobKeys helper in
mockserver-core: the FILE NAME alone for every store other than
FilesystemBlobStore, with prefix and key joined by exactly one separator,
leading separators dropped and repeated separators collapsed. Every store that
applies blobStoreKeyPrefix routes put/get/list/delete through it.
FilesystemBlobStore is unaffected — it interprets the key as a file path, so it
keeps the absolute path.

This is BREAKING for existing data. The old key always embedded the absolute
path and the new key never does, so the object name changes for every
non-filesystem persistence user, under every prefix shape and on every platform
— there is no configuration in which the old name is preserved. On the first
start after upgrading the restore misses (logged at INFO with the name it
looked for), the instance starts with no restored expectations, and the next
expectation change writes a fresh object under the new name, leaving the old
one behind. State can be carried across the upgrade by renaming the object
once, for example "aws s3 mv s3://<bucket>/<prefix>/<old absolute path>
s3://<bucket>/<prefix>/<file name>". Separately, a blobStoreKeyPrefix without a
trailing separator is now folder-style for ANY blob key, not only the
persistence document: "mockserver" + "x.json" was "mockserverx.json" and is now
"mockserver/x.json". The changelog bullet and persisting_expectations.html
carry the user-facing upgrade note.

Proven by a Docker-gated MinIO round trip with a trailing-slash prefix (the
exact configuration that returned HTTP 400), a MinIO put/get/list/delete round
trip across all four prefix shapes, and Docker-free unit coverage of the key
composition and of the key the persistence layer derives.

test(verify): prove the response-side eviction false-green guard over HTTP

MockServerEventLog implements the eviction guard twice: once in verifyRequest
and once, over a separate count of recorded request-response pairs, in
verifyResponse. Only the request arm had an *IntegrationTest; the response arm
was covered solely by an engine-level test against an in-process event log.

Add a Netty integration test that boots a real server with maxLogEntries=2 and
failVerificationOnEvictedLog=true, registers an expectation so GET
/was-responded is recorded as a real EXPECTATION_RESPONSE pair, floods the
bounded log with unmatched traffic until that pair is evicted, then asserts
verify(request, response, never()) through the Java client throws an
AssertionError stating the Response could not be verified because entries were
discarded after reaching maxLogEntries.

never() is the only verification shape that reaches the guard: it sits on the
PASS branch behind an upper bound (getAtMost() != -1), so atLeast(1)/once()
would fail earlier with an ordinary "Response not found". The response arm also
only sees EXPECTATION_RESPONSE/FORWARDED_REQUEST entries, so the evicted entry
must come from a matched expectation and the filler traffic can be plain 404s.

Confirmed via a positive control: replacing the verifyResponse guard call with
null makes the verification pass silently and turns the test red.

fix(config): stop the enforcement-evidence guard silently skipping cross-module pointers

ConfigurationEnforcementClassificationTest records, per risky configuration
property, the Class#method test that proves an instance-set value changes
observable behaviour. It validated those pointers by loading the class, but it
runs in mockserver-core, so any pointer naming a test in a sibling module was
silently skipped on ClassNotFoundException. That exempted precisely the most
valuable evidence — the end-to-end Layer C pointers — so renaming, moving or
deleting a referenced test left a dangling pointer and the guard still passed
green, for maxRequestBodySize, wasmEnabled, redactSecretsInLog, clusterEnabled,
dnsEnabled, grpcBidiStreamingEnabled, http3ConnectUdpEnabled and
transparentProxyEnabled.

An unloadable class is now resolved by locating its .java source under any
module's src/test/java and asserting the file declares both the class and the
referenced method. Source is always in the working tree, so this works in a
full reactor build and when only some modules are built, and resolution is
targeted per fully-qualified name rather than a repository walk. The guard
fails closed: a pointer resolvable by neither route is a failure naming the
dangling pointer, never a silent skip.

Anti-vacuity assertions mirror the sibling ConfigurationCallSiteGuardTest: the
set of pointers resolved by source scan must equal the declared CROSS_MODULE_
EVIDENCE ratchet exactly (fewer means the scan stopped seeing sibling modules,
more means a new cross-module pointer was not declared), mockserver-netty and
mockserver-state-infinispan must both have contributed evidence, and classpath
resolution must still cover the bulk of the pointers.

Verified by degrade-and-confirm-red: renaming the referenced mockserver-netty
method makes the guard fail naming the dangling pointer, while the previous
version passed green with the identical defect in place; pointing an entry at a
class that exists nowhere also fails closed.

fix(grpc): emit user-authored trailing metadata over HTTP/3

Every trailer an expectation authored - response().withTrailer(...) and the gRPC
chaos profile's customTrailers - reached an HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 client but never
reached an HTTP/3 client at all, in every branch of the HTTP/3 gRPC response path
(with a body and body-less, with and without proto descriptors). The same
expectation produced different trailing metadata depending only on the transport,
with no error or warning to indicate the loss.

Http3GrpcResponseWriter builds its HTTP/3 frames by hand rather than through
MockServerHttpResponseToFullHttpResponse.mapResponseWithTrailers, and
GrpcHttp3Adapter.buildTrailingHeadersFrame / buildTrailersOnlyFrame populated only
grpc-status and grpc-message - the response's own trailers were never read. They
are now emitted on the terminal frame: the trailing HEADERS frame when the response
has a body, folded into the Trailers-Only frame when it does not, which is the shape
gRPC defines for that form (HTTP-Status Content-Type Trailers, where Trailers
includes custom metadata). The framing is unchanged: still exactly one terminal
frame written with SHUTDOWN_OUTPUT, so an added trailer cannot strand grpc-status in
a non-end-of-stream frame the way it did on HTTP/2 before e1dc3207c.

A user trailer cannot override or spoof the transport's status: the new shared
GrpcResponseStatusResolver.passThroughTrailers (the trailer twin of
passThroughHeaders) excludes grpc-status / grpc-message / grpc-status-name,
mirroring the HTTP/2 path's remainingTrailers, and also the connection-specific
fields, content-length/content-type and pseudo-header names RFC 9114 forbids in a
trailer section. Field names are lower-cased with Locale.ROOT and CR/LF stripped
from values, because DefaultHttp3Headers throws on an upper-case field name - an
authored withTrailer("X-Request-Cost", ...) would otherwise have taken the whole
response down rather than dropping one field.

Two new tests in Http3GrpcIntegrationTest drive a live in-JVM Netty QUIC client and
read the metadata off the HEADERS frames it actually received, asserting which side
each value arrived on (a trailer must not be folded into the initial headers, a
response header must not be repeated as a trailer) and asserting the HEADERS-frame
count so the metadata cannot arrive at the cost of correct framing. Six further
tests in GrpcHttp3AdapterTest cover the frame builders directly, including the
anti-spoofing exclusion and the name/value normalisation.

Positive control: neutering the trailer pass-through in production turns all seven
new trailer assertions red with the trailer absent (5 adapter-level, 2 wire-level);
restoring it turns them green, with the 25 pre-existing GrpcHttp3AdapterTest tests
and 4 pre-existing Http3GrpcIntegrationTest tests passing throughout.

test(cluster): peek the clustered blob store under the file-name key

ClusteredExpectationPersistenceReloadTest read the blob store back under the
absolute persistedExpectationsPath, which was the production key until the cloud
blob-key fix (f5f28e87b) made ExpectationFileSystemPersistence key every
non-FilesystemBlobStore by the file name alone. The two changes were reviewed and
merged in separate worktrees, so neither review saw the other: the test's key
assertion went stale the moment both were on master and the precondition poll timed
out waiting for a blob that was really stored under the bare file name. Derive the
peek key via BlobKeys.forPersistedFile, exactly as production does. The reload
itself was never broken - write and read both use the file-name key - only the
test's out-of-band peek looked at the wrong key.

fix(core): materialise a FILE response body (and match a FILE request body) on every path (#2450)

A response whose body is a FileBody (a filePath, optionally with a
Velocity/Mustache templateType) was only read on the static RESPONSE
action. The same FileBody returned from an object callback, class
callback, response template, or forward responseOverride reached the
wire unread, emitting the file path string instead of the file contents.

Materialisation now lives in a single shared FileBodyMaterialiser
invoked from the two response-write funnels in HttpActionHandler
(writeResponseActionResponse, covering the static, object-callback,
class-callback, response-template and SSE paths, and
writeForwardActionResponse, covering the forward responseOverride), so
all five producers - and the shared WAR/servlet path - serve the file
contents. Templated FILE bodies are rendered against the request on
these paths too; a text content type yields the decoded string and a
binary or absent content type yields the raw bytes intact so
images/PDFs/archives are not charset-corrupted. A missing/unreadable
file throws a typed FileBodyException that the funnels (and the static
path via handleAnyException) turn into a clean, logged 500 whose body
does not leak the path.

BodyMatcherBuilder gains a FILE case: a FILE request body was silently
ignored (no case left the matcher null, matching any body); it now
matches the request body against the exact file contents (an
ExactStringMatcher for a text content type, a BinaryMatcher otherwise).

HttpResponseActionHandler is refactored to delegate to the shared
FileBodyMaterialiser, removing its duplicated inline logic.

(and the co-upgraded balanced-match 4.0.4) require Node 20+, bump the
module's engines from >=18.0.0 to "20 || >=22" to match the real floor
(Node 18 is EOL).

fix(ci): give the cloud/broker/proxy docker steps 7g so mvnw does not OOM

Each of these steps ran ./mvnw inside a --memory=4g container. mockserver/.mvn/jvm.config
pins the Maven JVM to -Xms2048m -Xmx6144m and mvnw prepends jvm.config to MAVEN_OPTS, so
the -am dependency build was allowed a 6g heap inside a 4g cgroup; with -T 1C building the
reactor concurrently in that one JVM, live heap climbed toward the ceiling and the kernel
intermittently killed it (exit 137) during the FIRST command, before any contract test ran.

fix(testcontainers-node): target the brace-expansion override so archiver.glob works

The blanket "brace-expansion": "^5.0.8" override closed CVE-2026-14257
(GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg) but broke every brace glob. 5.x changed the
CommonJS export from a callable function to an object
({ expand, EXPANSION_MAX, EXPANSION_MAX_LENGTH }), while the minimatch
copies actually installed -- 3.1.5, 5.1.9 and 9.0.9 -- all call it as
expand(pattern). Any pattern containing "{" threw

  TypeError: expand is not a function

which crashes archiver.glob(), the path testcontainers uses to copy
files into a container. minimatch short-circuits patterns with no "{",
so plain globs kept working, npm audit stayed clean and the unit suite
stayed green -- the breakage was silent.

Target the override instead: readdir-glob and archiver-utils' glob take
minimatch@^10.2.5, which itself depends on brace-expansion@^5.0.5 and is
written against the new API. Both runtime copies land on the patched
5.0.8 paired with a minimatch that can call it. jest keeps its own
minimatch@3.1.5 + brace-expansion@1.1.16 pairing untouched.

Verified: npm ci, tsc build, 16/16 unit, 5/5 Docker integration, and
npm audit --omit=dev reporting 0 vulnerabilities (8 high before).

Add a dependency-integrity unit test that drives a brace pattern through
both runtime minimatch copies and a real archiver.glob() tar, and
asserts expansion stays bounded. It fails with "expand is not a
function" against the blanket override, so this cannot regress silently.

docs(changelog): scope the brace-expansion blast radius accurately

testcontainers copies files with archiver.directory()/.append(), which
pass no brace pattern and keep working under the blanket override --
verified against master's own tree. What the override breaks is brace
globbing (archiver.glob() and direct minimatch use) in this module's
runtime tree, not the container file-copy path. Correct the changelog,
which implied the copy path itself crashed.

fix(core): stop a responseOverride body inheriting the upstream Content-Length

A forward responseOverride replaces the body but HttpResponse.update()
left the UPSTREAM response's Content-Length header in place, so the
header then described bytes that were no longer being sent. The client
read only as many bytes as the body that had been replaced -- or hung
waiting for bytes that never arrived.

The stale header is now dropped when the override supplies a body, so
the encoder recomputes it from what is actually written. A Content-Length
declared by the override itself is kept, as a deliberate choice, and
connectionOptions.contentLengthHeaderOverride is applied downstream and
is unaffected. A header-only override, which leaves the body alone,
keeps the upstream length because it is still correct.

This is also the remaining reason a FILE response body returned from a
responseOverride still reached the client wrong after #2450. The shared
FileBodyMaterialiser reads the file correctly on that path, and the
correct contents were then cut short by the stale length: a 34-byte file
behind an upstream Content-Length: 13 arrived as 13 bytes. Every layer
above the encoder holds a correct response, which is why only a real
client reading a real socket sees it.

The new Netty integration test therefore drives all four FILE-body
producers end to end -- class callback for text and for binary, response
template, and forward responseOverride. Three of them pass without this
change and are kept as regression cover for FileBodyMaterialiser; the
responseOverride case is the one that fails without it.

fix(editors): build LLM expectations in the shape the server actually accepts

The JetBrains LLM tool window's "Load into Server" was answered with
400 incorrect expectation json format because LlmExpectationBuilder
emitted a document whose shape never existed server-side: a flat
completion string, a top-level finishReason, stream, and usage, and a
provider of OPEN_AI (issue #2455).

The completion text, streaming flag, stop reason, and token usage all
belong INSIDE the completion object -- text, streaming, stopReason,
usage.inputTokens, usage.outputTokens -- and httpLlmResponse sets
additionalProperties: false, so emitting them alongside it is rejected
outright. Providers are the Provider enum names (OPENAI, AZURE_OPENAI),
not the invented OPEN_AI / AZURE_OPEN_AI / VERTEX_AI spellings.

Nothing caught this because the builder's tests asserted its output
matched the same invented shape the builder produced -- self-derived, so
they would have passed however wrong the document was. The plugin has
always BUNDLED the correct schema, the one MockServer validates against;
it simply never checked its own output against it. It does now, and a
negative case pins the checker itself by requiring the exact payload from
the bug report to still be rejected. The completion catalogue shared with
the VS Code extension carried the same fiction (messages, stream,
toolCalls, finishReason, a top-level usage) and is corrected the same
way, with the nested completion fields offered when the cursor is inside
completion; the VS Code suite gains equivalent schema assertions.

Fixing the provider list exposed a second gap: the httpLlmResponse
provider enum listed 9 of the 14 Provider constants, so MISTRAL, XAI,
DEEPSEEK, GROQ, and OPENROUTER were rejected with the same 400 despite
each having a fully registered response codec. All five are added to the
core schema, to both generated editor schemas, and to both copies of the
OpenAPI specification, and the provider list in the LLM response mocking
documentation and in the Rust client's field docs is brought up to date
with them. A new parity test asserts the enum and Provider agree in both
directions, and that every provider the schema admits has a codec to
serve it -- the missing link that let them drift.

fix(core): stop a forward responseOverride truncating to the upstream Content-Length (#2450)

When a forwarded request's response is overridden with a new body,
HttpResponse.update() replaced the body but kept the Content-Length
inherited from the upstream response. The response encoder computes
Content-Length from the actual body only when the model carries no
Content-Length header, so the stale upstream value was emitted verbatim
and an override body longer than the upstream body was truncated on the
wire (a shorter one over-ran). Every layer above the encoder held the
full, correct response, so only a real client saw the truncation.

update() now drops the inherited Content-Length whenever the override
supplies a new body (or a generateFromSchema body, whose length is
unknowable at merge time), unless the override itself sets an explicit
Content-Length - which the encoder still honours verbatim. update() is
called only from the two forward paths
(HttpOverrideForwardedRequestActionHandler and
HttpForwardTemplateActionHandler), so this only ever discards a stale
upstream length, never a user-authored one.

This closes the forward-responseOverride residual left by the FILE-body
fix (6fe8b9aa3).

test(breakpoints): prove mock-stream frames park and honour MODIFY/DROP on the write path

Closes audit gap #61. Stream-frame breakpoints for mock-generated streams
were only covered at the registry level (MockStreamBreakpointTest,
StreamFrameBreakpointRegistryTest), which exercise
StreamFrameBreakpointRegistry.pauseFrame with no Netty channel and so cannot
show a frame is actually withheld from — or written to — the wire.
