(NettyResponseWriter.writeStreamingResponse) over an EmbeddedChannel with a
RESPONSE_STREAM breakpoint matcher registered and a callback-WS client, then
assert against channel outbound that:
- each frame is PARKED (not flushed) until a decision arrives over the WS;
- CONTINUE flushes the original frame bytes;
- MODIFY flushes the replacement bytes;
- DROP suppresses the frame (nothing flushed).

The decision is delivered exactly as in production: the server serialises a
PausedStreamFrameDTO to the client channel and the test replies with a
StreamFrameDecisionDTO via WebSocketClientRegistry.receivedTextWebSocketFrame.

test(proxy): prove streaming forward publishes FORWARDED_REQUEST before the client sees stream end

The streaming forward path (HttpActionHandler.writeStreamingForwardActionResponse)
writes the response head and body chunks to the client first, then publishes the
FORWARDED_REQUEST log entry from the stream-completion listener. The existing
ordering test HttpActionHandlerForwardLogOrderingTest scopes itself to the
direct-write and non-streaming forward paths, leaving the streaming path uncovered.

Add an integration test that forwards to an SSE upstream, reads the stream to
completion on the client side, then does a retry-free retrieve/verify (no
pollUntilTrue, no eventual-verify overload) and asserts the forwarded exchange is
already visible. This guards the happens-before guarantee that
StreamingBody.complete() fires the log-publishing listener synchronously before the
deferred socket-close reaches the client.

test(http): enforce maxInitialLineLength parser limit over the wire

Extend HttpParserLimitsIntegrationTest, which previously proved only
maxHeaderSize enforcement, with a raw-socket case for maxInitialLineLength:
an over-limit request line (method+URI+version) is rejected by Netty's
decoder so the configured path is never parsed and the request 404s, plus
a control under the limit that matches. The filler sits strictly between
the configured 250-byte cap and Netty's 4096-byte default, making it a
genuine positive control.

Documents why maxChunkSize is not covered: Netty applies it only as
Math.min to bound per-HttpContent emit size, splitting (never rejecting)
oversized chunks, which HttpObjectAggregator reassembles - so there is no
client-observable effect to assert.

test(container): fail closed when a manifest-declared test case produces no result

The container integration-test harness only failed closed on result presence
for an INVOKED test: a test case silently deleted from run_all_tests() was
never called, recorded nothing, and the suite stayed green having run one test
fewer — an undetected coverage loss with no manifest / expected-count guard.

Add container_integration_tests/expected_tests.manifest as the single source of
truth for the test cases the harness must run, and assert_manifest_complete()
which enforces it bidirectionally in the summary phase:

test(clients): assert Rust and .NET decode server-echoed NottableString negation/escape

The Rust and .NET wire tests proved the server ENFORCES a NottableString
negation/escape the client sends, but neither asserted the client correctly
DECODES that negation/escape when an expectation is read back from a live
server. Fold a retrieve-decode assertion beside each existing negation wire
test: register both a not_literal("foo") negation and an escaped literal
"!foo", call retrieve active expectations, and assert the decoded matcher
round-trips with its negation/escape intact.

A negation echoes back as the plain string "!foo" and decodes via the
NottableString plain-string reader into the plain headers map; an escaped
literal echoes back as the object form {"not":false,"value":"!foo"} and
decodes into the header-matchers map. Both homes are checked so the '!' is
proven to survive server echo -> client decode as either a negation or literal
data. Degrade-and-confirm-red verified locally in both clients: dropping the
negation-flag strip in the decoder turns the new assertion red.

fix(test-node): wait for TLS readiness before the launcher's HTTPS assertions

The two mockserver-node launcher tests that exercise jvmOptions do so over
HTTPS against a server started with
dynamicallyCreateCertificateAuthorityCertificate=true, and issued that HTTPS
request as soon as start_mockserver resolved.

start_mockserver only proves the HTTP control plane is answering - it polls
"PUT /mockserver/retrieve" over plain HTTP. With a dynamically created
certificate authority the server still has to generate a CA key pair and a leaf
certificate before it can serve TLS on that same (port-unified) port, so a
handshake arriving in that window was closed mid-negotiation and surfaced as
ECONNRESET "Client network socket disconnected before secure TLS connection was
established".

That race was the sole cause of the mockserver-node pipeline's intermittent red:
every failure across the preceding 40 master builds (5 of 40, ~12%) was one of
these two tests, always with this error, never the HTTP-only test beside them.

Both tests now wait for a real TLS handshake to complete before asserting, which
gates them on the condition they actually depend on instead of retrying the
assertions. waitForTlsReady is verified to reject rather than resolve both when
nothing is listening and when a listener accepts the TCP connection then
destroys it mid-handshake - the exact failure signature it absorbs.

ci(node): install Node from the official tarball instead of the NodeSource apt repo

deb.nodesource.com began answering 403 to every request - the repository index
and the GPG key alike - so this step died at

  curl: (22) The requested URL returned error: 403
  gpg: no valid OpenPGP data found

and took the node launcher integration tests, and so master, red with it. The
first casualty was mockserver-node build 817; builds up to 813 had passed, so
the outage began this evening.

Node now comes from the official nodejs.org binary tarball, verified against the
published SHASUMS256.txt and unpacked into /usr/local. That removes the
third-party apt repository and its signing key entirely - one fewer external
service able to take the pipeline down - and pins a full version rather than a
major so the toolchain is reproducible.

The checksum step fails closed both ways: a corrupted tarball fails
"sha256sum -c", and a tarball missing from SHASUMS256.txt fails the grep rather
than leaving an empty file for sha256sum to trivially accept.

Verified by running the real step, .buildkite/scripts/steps/node-launcher-test.sh,
end to end in the CI image: 73 tests, 0 failures. The install path was also run
under linux/amd64 to match the CI agents.

fix(test-node): probe TLS readiness without disabling certificate validation

CodeQL flagged the readiness probe as js/disabling-certificate-validation
(high): it passed rejectUnauthorized: false so that MockServer's freshly
generated, self-signed certificate would not fail the handshake.

Turning validation off was never what the probe needed. The question it asks is
"has the server got as far as serving TLS", not "do we trust its certificate" -
and a certificate the client cannot verify answers that just as well, because the
server had to produce one. So validation is left on and a verification failure

fix(security)!: block Java class access from response templates by default

Resolves GHSA-7pwj-xvc2-hfpc: a caller who can reach the management API
registers an expectation whose response template reaches java.lang.Runtime
and executes OS commands in the MockServer process.

Three separate routes are closed, all safe by default:

- velocityDisallowClassLoading now defaults to true, installing Velocity's
  SecureUberspector. This is the more exposed half and the half the report
  did not cover: Velocity ships in the DEFAULT distribution, whereas the
  GraalJS engine is an optional dependency present only in the -graaljs
  image variant.
- JavaScript templates resolve no Java class unless one is granted via
  javascriptAllowedClasses. Previously an empty allow-list AND an empty
  deny-list - the out-of-the-box state - meant unrestricted Java.type(...).
- The GraalJS guest context denies the members of java.lang.Class and
  java.lang.ClassLoader. Gating Java.type(...) alone was NOT sufficient:
  real host objects are bound into the context, so a template could walk
  faker.getClass().getClassLoader().loadClass('java.lang.Runtime') and
  reach Runtime without the class filter ever being consulted.

Both flips are reversible with one property and remove no functionality;
templates that do not touch Java classes are unaffected. A refused class is
logged once at WARN naming the class and the property to set, bounded and
de-duplicated so a hostile template cannot flood the log. A deny-list-only
posture now warns too, since it is weaker than the default it replaces.

javascriptAllowedClasses is now settable through the Spring test listener,
which it was not before - a nice-to-have while the default was unrestricted,
and the only way to grant a class now that it is not.

Proven end-to-end by a Netty integration test that registers the reported
payload through the real management API and asserts the OS command creates
no marker file, with a negative control on a deliberately unsandboxed server
that DOES create it, so a regression cannot pass as an inert payload.

Lands DEF-2 and DEF-3 of docs/plans/later/security-defaults.md ahead of the
other default flips there; JavaScript went further than that plan proposed
(deny everything rather than a built-in "safe types" allow-list) because
deny-by-default is the only form that stays safe as the JDK grows new
reachable classes.

BREAKING CHANGE: response templates can no longer reach Java classes unless
explicitly granted via mockserver.javascriptAllowedClasses (use * for any
class) or mockserver.velocityDisallowClassLoading=false.

fix(test-ui): survive jsdom's unresolvable-calc length regression

jsdom 30.0.0 added pixel conversion of length values to getComputedStyle().
Its resolver reduces calc() through cssValues.resolveCalc and then destructures
FONT_SIZE_REGEXP.exec(resolvedSize) with no null check. A calc() mixing a
percentage with a length cannot be reduced without layout, which jsdom has no
notion of, so resolveCalc returns the value unchanged, the regex does not match,
and destructuring null throws "object null is not iterable".

MUI's Dialog sizes itself with calc(100% - 64px) and @testing-library calls
getComputedStyle() on every accessibility/role query, so this takes out any test
that renders a Dialog - 169 across 12 files - despite none of them asserting
anything font-related.

Guard the resolver so an unresolvable length yields NaN. jsdom's own caller
already treats a non-numeric result as "leave the value alone", so this restores
the pre-30 behaviour exactly rather than inventing one. The wrapper only changes
anything when the original throws, so it neutralises itself once jsdom ships a
fix, and it re-raises any TypeError that is not this one.

Reached by path import rather than node:module so the file stays free of node
typings, which the UI tsconfig does not carry.

Verified against both jsdom 29.1.1 and 30.0.0: 3044 tests, 192 files, green on
each, with lint and the strict build clean.

fix(config): report a property file that cannot be read instead of ignoring it

When a property file an operator had explicitly configured could not be read,
MockServer applied none of its properties and logged nothing about it at any
level. The only symptom was every property in the file appearing to sit at its
default, which surfaces far downstream as unexplained behaviour.

In #2358 a mounted mockserver.properties was present - confirmed with
docker container cp - but unreadable by the process. initializationJsonPath was
therefore never set, so no expectations loaded, no "loading JSON initialization
file:" line appeared, and no error was logged either, leaving nothing to point
at the cause.

The message already existed but was unreachable: gated at DEBUG and emitted
during static initialisation, before any log level has been applied, so neither
-Dmockserver.logLevel=DEBUG nor a -logLevel argument could surface it.

Log it at WARN, naming the path and the underlying reason verbatim.
FileNotFoundException covers "not there" and "not allowed to read it" alike, and
that distinction is usually the whole answer - "Permission denied" here, which
points straight at SELinux labelling or a rootless/user-namespace UID mismatch.

Only for a file the operator actually chose. A default that is simply absent
stays quiet, and so does the Docker image's built-in
-Dmockserver.propertyFile=/config/mockserver.properties: the entrypoint always
passes it, so it expresses no intent, and treating it as intent would warn on
every container started without a mounted config - training users to ignore the
warning this adds. Inside the image only MOCKSERVER_PROPERTY_FILE can express
that intent, matching how propertyFile() already resolves it.

That decision is the regression-prone part, so it is exposed as a pure
package-private overload and tested across every combination without touching
system properties or environment variables, which would be global state and
unsafe under parallel execution.

Verified in a real JVM across all four paths - explicit+missing warns, Docker
default stays silent, nothing configured stays silent, env override warns - and
against the actual #2358 shape: a present-but-unreadable file now reports
"(Permission denied)", and the same file readable loads normally with no warning.

fix(test-node): give TLS readiness a budget that survives a loaded agent

The readiness gate added for the launcher HTTPS tests used a 30s budget. That
went green five builds running and then expired on master build 6343 with
"MockServer did not serve TLS on port 1082 within 30000ms" - the same flake as
before, wearing a clearer error message rather than actually gone.

The gate itself is right: it turned a confusing mid-assertion ECONNRESET into an
explicit statement about readiness, which is how the cause was identifiable at
all. Only the limit was wrong, and it was a guess rather than a measured bound.

Raise it to 120s. Waiting costs nothing when the server is healthy - a ready
server completes the handshake on the first attempt in milliseconds - so this
number only decides how much CI contention is tolerated before a slow start is
misreported as a fault. Being generous is free; being tight is a flake.

Two ruled out before settling on contention, so this is not another guess:

  * Not the property file change on the same commit - the launcher never sets
    -Dmockserver.propertyFile, so that path is unchanged for these tests.
  * Not stale dynamically generated CA files surviving in the gitignored
    mockserver-node/tmp across builds on a reused agent checkout. Plausible,
    since the directory persists and the CA is only generated when absent, but
    planting a truncated CA key showed the server regenerates and serves TLS.

Retrying the job on the same commit passed, which is what a contention-bound
slow start looks like and not what a deterministic fault looks like.

Also report a readiness that takes over 5s even when it passes, and include the
attempt count and elapsed time on failure - "one attempt that hung" and
"hundreds that were refused" are different faults. A green run that took 40s is
the warning that the next one will not make it, and previously that was
invisible.

docs(security): stop naming a release the template sandbox may not ship in

The template sandbox change documented itself as landing in 7.4.1, matching the
current 7.4.1-SNAPSHOT. Its changelog entry is prefixed BREAKING, which by the

as both 7.4.1 and, implicitly, 8.0.0, and at least one of those is wrong.

Which one is a release-preparation decision, not something these comments should

Drop the number and describe the behaviour relative to earlier versions instead.

fix(oidc): revoke every spelling of a token, not just the string presented

Revocation keyed on the exact string submitted to /revoke, so a revoked JWT kept
working under a different spelling (GHSA-x2rq-8p73-q36w).

Nimbus decodes Base64URL leniently, skipping characters outside the alphabet,
and verifies the signature from the decoded bytes. Appending "=", "\n", "!" or
"*" to the signature segment therefore yields a string that is not equal to the
revoked one yet still verifies as the same signed token. isRevoked missed it,
verifyAccessToken accepted it, and /userinfo served claims for a token the
caller had already revoked - "my application rejects a revoked token" passing
while proving nothing, which is the exact failure mode this store exists to
close.

Confirmed against Nimbus directly before fixing: all five spellings above
produce a different string that still verifies.

Key revocation on the token with every character outside the Base64URL alphabet
removed, the dot separators aside, so every spelling Nimbus accepts as a given
token maps to one key. Opaque tokens are matched exactly elsewhere, so this only
widens what counts as revoked; two opaque tokens differing solely by ignored
characters would share a key and be revoked together, which is fail-closed and
consistent with revocation already being global rather than per-provider.

Covered in both directions - revoking a token rejects its alternate spellings,
and revoking an alternate spelling rejects the canonical token - because a
one-directional fix just moves the bypass. Each asserts the spelling is accepted
BEFORE revocation, so the test cannot pass merely because the token was invalid.
Reverting the fix fails exactly these two and nothing else.

The affected code has never been released: /revoke doing anything at all is
itself unreleased, so no published version is exposed and the existing entry is
strengthened rather than a fix being claimed for users who were never at risk.

fix(release): truncate GitHub release notes instead of failing the step

GitHub rejects a release body over 125,000 characters with HTTP 422
"Validation Failed / body is too long". The step passed the whole changelog
section through unconditionally, so a release that accumulated a lot of
changelog simply failed.

7.5.0 accumulated 245,801 characters over 25 days - nearly double the limit -
and release build #69 died here AFTER Maven Central, Docker, npm, PyPI and
RubyGems had already published. That is the worst place to stop: the release is
public and irreversible by that point, but has no GitHub Release, and the step
cannot be made to pass by retrying it.

Truncate rather than fail. The release body is a convenience copy and
changelog.md is the source of truth, so a body that ends with a pointer to the
full entry loses nothing. Cut on a line boundary so the markdown does not end
mid-table or mid-fence, and leave headroom under the limit for the pointer.

Also preview only the first 40 lines. Echoing the whole body made the job log
almost entirely release notes - 2,653 lines for 7.5.0 - burying the one line
that said what actually went wrong.

Verified against the real 7.5.0 entry: 245,801 -> 120,262 characters, under the
limit and ending cleanly. A normal-sized release is untouched: 7.3.0 is 42,765
characters and does not enter the truncation branch.

The 7.5.0 release itself was completed by creating the release with these exact
truncated notes, after which the failed step retried green through its existing
already-exists idempotency path.

fix(release): verify the Docker tag against the registry, not Docker Hub metadata

The release verify step gated on
hub.docker.com/v2/repositories/mockserver/mockserver/tags/<version>/, which lags
a freshly pushed tag by minutes. Release build #69 failed this HARD check for
7.5.0 and failed the whole release, while the image was already pullable:

  hub API   7.5.0 -> 404      registry 7.5.0 -> EXISTS
  hub API   7.4.0 -> 200      registry 7.4.0 -> EXISTS
  hub API   latest -> 200     registry latest -> EXISTS

So the check works for tags that have settled and reports a false negative for
exactly the tag a release cares about - the one just pushed. Gating on an
eventually-consistent metadata surface fails releases that are fine and, worse,
teaches everyone to wave this step through.

Ask registry-1.docker.io instead. That is what docker pull talks to, so a 200
means the image is genuinely available to users rather than merely indexed.
Needs an anonymous pull token first, the same shape as the GHCR check directly
below it.

Verified both directions, so this is not just a check made permissive:
7.5.0 -> 200, 7.4.0 -> 200, a deliberately bogus tag -> 404.

fix(vscode): match @types/vscode to the engine, and package in CI

Release build #69 failed publishing the VS Code extension:

  ERROR @types/vscode ^1.125.0 greater than engines.vscode ^1.80.0.
        Either upgrade engines.vscode or use an older @types/vscode version

A Dependabot bump moved @types/vscode to ^1.125.0 while engines.vscode stayed at
^1.80.0. vsce refuses to package that combination: an extension must be typed
against the OLDEST VS Code API it claims to support, or it can compile against
APIs that do not exist on the versions it declares support for.

Pin to ~1.80.0 rather than ^1.80.0. The caret range is not a fix - ^1.80.0 still
resolves to 1.125.0, so the declared range would satisfy vsce's check while the
INSTALLED types stayed newer than the engine, which is the actual hazard. The
tilde installs 1.80.x.

The gap that let it reach a release matters more than the bump. CI ran
npm ci && npm run compile && npm test, and this is a vsce rule, not a tsc rule -
so compile was green the whole time and the FIRST time anything packaged the
extension was mid-release, after Maven Central, Docker, npm, PyPI and RubyGems
had already published. Add vsce package to the CI step so it fails on the PR
that introduces it. Packaging to /tmp keeps the .vsix out of the bind-mounted
workspace the agent cannot clean under userns-remap.

Verified both directions: with ^1.125.0 compile still PASSES and vsce package
fails with exactly the release error; with ~1.80.0 compile, 173 tests, and
vsce package all pass.

fix(release): publish the VS Code extension from the released code

vscode.sh was the only publishing component that did not sync to origin/master
before building - 16 others do. It published whatever was on the commit the
build was created from, with the release version sed'd into package.json, so it
could ship code that differs from what was actually released: anything added by
the release's own Prepare or Update Version References commits was missing.

It also made the step unretryable. A fix landed on master could never be picked
up by a retry, which is exactly where build #69 ended up when the
@types/vscode-vs-engines.vscode mismatch failed the publish - the one artefact
that could not be recovered by fixing forward.

Sync before the version sed so the sed applies to the released tree.

build(deps): stop Dependabot re-raising @types/vscode past engines.vscode

@types/vscode's MINOR version is the VS Code API level, so it is not a routine
minor bump - vsce refuses to package an extension whose @types/vscode exceeds

21d7ae412 swept it 1.80.0 -> 1.125.0 inside the npm-minor-and-patch group.

jsdom 30.0.1 guards the destructure that 30.0.0 left unchecked:

  const matchLength = LENGTH_REGEXP.exec(resolvedSize);

so getComputedStyle no longer throws "object null is not iterable" on a calc()
it cannot reduce - MUI's Dialog calc(100% - 64px) being the one that took out

docs(release): Homebrew is automated, not a manual follow-up step

The release-management skill and its mirrored command both told the operator
Homebrew was "always manual", with a brew bump-formula-pr command to run after
every release. That is wrong, and it contradicted this repo's own authoritative
doc: release-process.md 9 is titled "fully automated, no action required" and
states plainly that no human action is needed.

Both formulae publish on their own:

  * Homebrew/homebrew-core (mockserver, JAR-based) is bumped by BrewTestBot from
    the *-brew-tar.tar artifact on Maven Central, typically within hours.
  * mock-server/homebrew-tap (self-contained bundle) is pushed by the pipeline's
    own homebrew step - which ran and passed in release build #71.

brew bump-formula-pr remains documented, but as the fallback for a broken bot
rather than the normal path.

This mattered in practice: the skill is what the release preparation report is
generated from, so every release told the operator to perform a manual step that
does not exist - and it did exactly that for 7.5.0.

Also fix a stale cross-reference while here: 9 pointed at "12 below" for the tap
formula, but 12 is "Announce (optional)". The tap is covered by 11
(Package-manager channels).

scripts/validate_opencode_config.sh passes.

fix(core): make JSON body matching independent of the json-unit provider

MockServer parses the expectation and request bodies with Jackson and hands
json-unit the resulting nodes, so a repeated body is not re-parsed on every
match. That made matching depend on which JSON provider json-unit resolves to:
it selects a NodeFactory by asking each in turn whether it claims the value and
falls back to the last one registered, and only its Jackson provider claims a
Jackson node.

Where another provider won - org.json, for instance, whether because Jackson was
not visible to json-unit or because json-unit.libraries pinned it - that factory
rejected the node with "Unsupported type class
com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.node.ObjectNode", so every JSON match threw and
no JSON body ever matched. Probe once whether json-unit accepts Jackson nodes
and, where it does not, give it the raw JSON text, which every provider parses.

The failure was also undiagnosable: the match difference said only "exception
while perform json match failed" and the exception itself was recorded solely at
TRACE, so at the default log level a malformed body, a missing class and a
runtime error all looked identical. Report the cause in the difference, as the
XML schema, JSON path and JSON-RPC matchers already do.

Also exclude the lazily populated caches from equals/hashCode, matching the
sibling matchers, so whether a matcher has matched yet does not change what it
is equal to.

Fixes #2496

test(core): cover the raw JSON text fallback in the JSON body matcher

Adversarial review found that the fix itself - falling back to giving json-unit
the raw JSON text where it will not accept pre-parsed Jackson nodes - had no
automated coverage; the tests added with it exercised only the reported cause
and the equality change.

Production picks between the two inputs once per JVM from a system property that
json-unit reads at class load, which a test cannot vary without forking, so make
the choice an explicit argument to a package-private matches(). Cover the
fallback directly: the bodies from #2496, ONLY_MATCHING_FIELDS, nested objects
and arrays, genuinely different documents, a body that is not JSON, and STRICT;
and assert both inputs reach the same verdict across a table of cases, so the
fallback cannot drift from the node path. Both tests fail if the fallback is
broken.

Also soften the changelog claim that every provider can parse the raw text - a
version-incompatible provider jar can still fail, it just cannot be worse than
every match throwing.

declares spring.version / spring-web.version as 7.0.8 - but spring-webflux is not
declared, so in the examples module Spring Boot's own dependency management won
and resolved it to 7.0.7, inside the affected range.

${spring-web.version} for exactly this Boot-versus-build conflict; spring-webflux
was missed. Add it alongside them, which takes every Spring artifact in the
reactor to 7.0.8.

resolved 7.0.8, and spring-webflux only ever reached the examples module, which
is in the reactor to stay compiled and is not part of any published artifact.

fix(tls): make the dynamic certificate cache expiry-aware, bounded and race-free

The dynamic TLS certificate cache could serve stale, torn or over-broad
material. `certificateNotYetCreated()` was only a null check, so nothing ever
inspected `notAfter` on the cached leaf, the memoised CA or the cached
SslContext - a long-running server served an expired certificate for the
lifetime of the JVM with no self-healing.

Cache reuse is now driven by a content signature over the SAN set, CA identity,
key/cert paths, mTLS inputs and protocols, replacing a single consumable
boolean that could hand back a certificate missing a just-added SAN when two
SNI hosts were provisioned concurrently. Client SSL contexts and the memoised
CA self-invalidate when their inputs are rotated at runtime; previously
`rebuildTLSContext(true)` was called from no production code at all, so a
rotated forward-proxy key or trust-manager type was silently ignored.

Only the leaf drives renewal. A dynamically-generated CA nearing its own expiry
is warned about once rather than demanding a leaf regeneration that the CA
guard can never satisfy, which would otherwise re-mint the leaf on every
handshake indefinitely.

The dynamically-grown SAN list is bounded by a new `maxSubjectAlternativeNames`
property (default 100). Every distinct SNI hostname previously appended to an
unbounded set and re-minted the whole leaf, so any client could force unbounded
memory and CPU use and eventually a certificate too large to fit a handshake.
Eviction is FIFO over dynamically-discovered entries only - configured and
default SANs such as localhost are never evicted - and hostnames are normalised
and validated before being added.

Generation now publishes the new key and certificate atomically, so a
mid-flight failure keeps the previous working pair instead of leaving a new key
paired with the old certificate, which failed every subsequent handshake
permanently. Provisioning runs off the Netty event loop with per-host
coalescing rather than performing RSA keygen inside a global lock on an event
loop thread.

Private key material (leaf key, CA key and the JKS key store) is written
owner-readable-only and atomically, public certificates 0644. A corrupt or
unreadable CA PEM now fails loudly instead of being silently treated as absent
and overwritten, which invalidated every pinned client trust store, and CA
generation takes a cross-process lock so two instances sharing a certificate
directory cannot both generate.

BouncyCastle registration is deferred off the `PEMToFile` class-load path,
restoring the lazy-BouncyCastle startup optimisation that a static initialiser
had been defeating.

Certificate validity periods and certificate extensions are deliberately
unchanged; those follow separately.

test(tls): renew the test certificate fixtures so no leaf outlives its issuer

The two mutual-TLS authentication CAs were 151 days from expiry and the three
Netty TLS integration CAs 550 days. Both sets have been re-issued with a
10-year validity, and every leaf they sign re-issued with a shorter 5-year
validity.

The structural bug this fixes is that leaves were outliving their issuers
everywhere - the mTLS leaves ran to 2036 under a CA expiring in January 2027,
so the documented renewal model (long-lived CA, short-lived leaf, regenerate
the leaf) produced no benefit at all.

The existing CA and leaf private keys are preserved and only the certificates
re-minted, so key encodings, Subject and Authority Key Identifiers and existing
signatures are unchanged. That also keeps the intentionally-expired negative
fixture chaining correctly to its renewed CA while remaining expired, and
avoids the PKCS#1-to-PKCS#8 conversion that `openssl req -keyout` performs by
default - which had already silently destroyed the PKCS#1 encoding-variant
coverage for the Netty leaf keys in a previous renewal.

Note these CAs are used as PKIX trust anchors, and neither RFC 5280 section 6.1
nor the JDK's PKIXCertPathValidator date-check the anchor, so the affected
tests would most likely have continued to pass past the expiry date, going
silently stale rather than failing cleanly.

Renewing the mTLS leaf changed its SHA-256 fingerprint, which
ClientCertificateMatcherTest pinned as a literal in two places. Both are
corrected, and a guard test now recomputes the fixture's fingerprint and fails
with the replacement value if it ever drifts again, so a future renewal reports
an instruction rather than an unexplained match failure. The colon-separated
upper-case case derives its value from the same constant instead of repeating
it, since the formatting is what that test exists to verify.

Also removes the unused PKCS1CertificateAuthorityPrivateKey.pem resource from
the published jar. It was the explicit PKCS#1 half of an encoding pair added in
2020 for the JDK key and certificate builder, whose removal in 2022 left it
with no references anywhere for around four years. It was byte-identical to
CertificateAuthorityPrivateKey.pem, which is retained because it backs a
published raw-URL link in the HTTPS documentation.

fix(clustered): warn on and document per-node CA divergence, add shared-CA chart support

In a clustered deployment every MockServer pod mints its own certificate
authority, so a client that imported one pod's mockserver-ca.pem gets a TLS
trust failure the moment the load balancer routes it to a different pod. The
symptom is intermittent, which makes it read like a flaky network rather than a
configuration fault.

This was undocumented anywhere - it was not in the clustered-state limitations
table, the TLS documentation, or the chart README - while the example config
ships dynamicallyCreateCertificateAuthorityCertificate=true and the chart
documents replicaCount: 3 for clustered mode.

StateBackendFactory.create now logs a warning when clustering is enabled
together with dynamic CA generation. That is the cluster configuration layer,
which is where the two settings first meet; the TLS layer cannot see the
cluster topology.

The supported fix - one shared CA supplied to every replica - was previously
awkward enough to be a trap. The chart had no extraEnv, so the documented
MOCKSERVER_* route was unreachable; the only documented way to ship TLS
material was app.config.extraFiles, which puts a CA private key in a ConfigMap;
and dynamic generation had nowhere writable to go anyway, with the default
directory of "." against a cwd of / running as uid 65534 and /config mounted
read-only.

The chart now has a dedicated Secret template for TLS material, the volume and
mount wiring, a writable emptyDir for the dynamic certificate directory,
extraEnv support, a checksum annotation so a rotated Secret restarts pods, and
a required guard so a misconfigured create:false fails the render instead of
deploying broken. All of it is opt-in and the default render is unchanged.

The environment variable names are taken from the ConfigurationProperties
constants rather than derived from the property names, because several
MockServer TLS variables are not the upper-snake form of their property and a
guessed name is a silent no-op.

Also fixes a latent dead condition in the Deployment template, which tested
app.mountConfigMap - a value that was never declared.

fix(deps): resolve the outstanding npm security advisories in shipped packages

Bumps dompurify 3.4.12 to 3.4.13 in the bundled dashboard, brace-expansion
5.0.8 to 5.0.9 (ReDoS) in mockserver-testcontainers/node, and js-yaml 4.3.0 to
4.3.1 in mockserver-client-node, mockserver-node and
mockserver-testcontainers/node.

These are the advisories that survived triage of the 28 open Dependabot alerts.
Twenty-one were not applicable and have been dismissed: twenty Spring
advisories bounded at "<= 5.3.39" with no patched version, against a tree
running Spring 7.0.8, and one netty advisory whose first patched version is
exactly the version already resolved.

The brace-expansion fix deliberately bumps only the parent rather than adding
an override. A previous blanket override to 5.0.8 broke archiver's glob
handling, because the 5.x CJS export is an object rather than a function; the
nested minimatch 3.x copy stays on 1.1.18 and archiver's glob path was
exercised directly to confirm it still produces a valid archive.

Also records the certificate-hardening work in the changelog.

fix(tls): short-lived leaf certificates with the extensions modern clients require

Closes #2531.

Dynamically-generated leaf certificates were valid for ten years and carried no
extendedKeyUsage, so Apple platforms reject them. Both are fixed here.

Leaf validity is now split from CA validity. The CA keeps its long life; the
leaf defaults to 397 days, overridable via a new
`sslCertificateLeafValidityInDays` property for anyone who needs the previous
behaviour. The window is anchored to the existing five-day back-dated notBefore
so clock-skew tolerance is preserved.

The operative standard is not the one the issue cites. Apple's 398-day App
Transport Security limit explicitly exempts certificates issued from user-added
or administrator-added roots, which is exactly MockServer's case. The rule that
does apply is the 825-day cap on TLS server certificates from the iOS 13 and
macOS 10.15 requirements, which has no such carve-out and which a 3650-day leaf
exceeded. 397 days sits inside both that cap and the CA/Browser Forum's
tightening trend.

Validity alone would not have been enough. Apple also requires the leaf to
carry an id-kp-serverAuth extendedKeyUsage, and MockServer's leaf had no EKU at
all, so iOS would most likely still have failed after a validity-only fix. The
leaf now carries serverAuth and clientAuth EKU, a critical keyUsage of
digitalSignature and keyEncipherment, and an authorityKeyIdentifier matching
the issuing CA's subjectKeyIdentifier so chain building works in stacks that
match the two.

The root CA's own extendedKeyUsage is removed. EKU on a trust anchor is not
idiomatic, and `anyExtendedKeyUsage` alongside two specific EKUs is
self-contradictory. Removing it can only relax validation, and only newly
minted dynamic CAs are affected - the bundled default CA is a static resource
and an existing on-disk dynamic CA is never regenerated.

The override is clamped to 30 days at the low end and the CA's own validity at
the high end. Below 30, the five-day back-date meant a leaf could be minted
already expired (failing generation outright), and around six days a fresh leaf
was already past the renewal threshold and regenerated on every handshake.

Serial numbers are now forced positive. `new BigInteger(64, random)` could
produce zero, which RFC 5280 forbids.

The HTTP/3 self-signed fallback gains a back-dated notBefore, SAN entries, EKU
and keyUsage, but deliberately keeps a long validity: it is simultaneously
trust anchor and server certificate with no renewal loop behind it, so a short
life would simply expire the endpoint.

Also adds `maxSubjectAlternativeNames` and `sslCertificateLeafValidityInDays`
to the ConfigurationDTO mirror, so neither is silently lost when configuration
is transferred between instances or set over the control plane, and classifies
`maxSubjectAlternativeNames` as enforcement-verified. Documents both properties
for users, including the eviction behaviour that affects anyone proxying more
than a hundred distinct hostnames.

The existing ten-year assertion is deliberately split rather than deleted: the
CA still pins a long window and the leaf pins the short one, so the guard
against silent validity drift survives in both directions.

test(control-plane): stop parameterisations racing on the global static store

ControlPlaneAuthenticationRouteDenialTest flaked nondeterministically, failing
two or three of its "via system property" parameterisations on some runs and
none on others. A test that guards control-plane authentication and passes by
luck is worse than no test, because it is trusted - and it had already produced
one false red that cost a full investigation.

The cause is not an ordering leak. The @Before/@After resets were already
present for every route, so ordering was never the problem. It is a concurrency
data race: the class mutates the process-global ConfigurationProperties static
store, and JUnit4 @Parameterized runs up to four parameterisations at once, so
one parameterisation's enable or reset lands in the middle of another's
assertion.

The pom already accounts for this - the class is excluded from the parallel
phase and pinned to the sequential one. But `-Dtest=` overrides surefire's
excludes, so any filtered run forces the class back into the parallel phase and
reintroduces the race. That is why it looked like a flake on master while CI
stayed green.

Each parameterisation's setup, assertions and teardown are now serialised on a
class-wide lock, so behaviour is identical whether the class runs in the
sequential phase or is forced into the parallel one by a test filter. The lock
is uncontended in the normal sequential run.

No @FixMethodOrder: ordering is irrelevant to a data race, and pinning it would
misdirect the next reader.

Verified by ten consecutive green filtered runs, a clean full module run, and a
vacuity check - breaking the production enforcement path turns 27 assertions
red across the two affected methods, so the fix did not silence them.

fix(tls): verify upstream hostnames, modernise protocol defaults, warn on the shared CA

BREAKING: the default `tlsProtocols` becomes `TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3` and
`tlsAllowInsecureProtocols` becomes `false`. TLSv1 and TLSv1.1 are deprecated
by RFC 8996 and eligible for BEAST and POODLE, and TLSv1.3 was previously never
negotiated because it was absent from the default list. A client that speaks
only TLSv1 or TLSv1.1 will stop connecting; restoring the old behaviour needs
BOTH `tlsProtocols=TLSv1,TLSv1.1,TLSv1.2` and `tlsAllowInsecureProtocols=true`,
because the flag only filters the list and can never add a protocol to it.

Hostname verification on the forward path is now controllable and correct on
every route. Netty 4.2 already enables HTTPS endpoint identification by default
for clients created with a host and port, so the common forward path was
verifying hostnames - this is not a previously-open hole. The real gaps were
the relay handlers, which used the no-host handler overload and so had
verification enabled with no peer identity to check against, making it a no-op,
and the absence of any way to switch verification off for the legitimate
testing case of a deliberate hostname mismatch.

`forwardProxyTLSHostnameVerificationEnabled` (default true) now applies for the
`JVM` and `CUSTOM` trust-manager types, forcing the algorithm on or explicitly
clearing it when disabled. `ANY` is untouched: trust-all remains the documented
default for a mock proxy. The flag is part of the client context signature, so
changing it at runtime invalidates the cache rather than being silently
ignored.

The reverse-proxy relay now verifies against the CONNECT target host and port
rather than the connected socket address. The socket address was the wrong
identity: for a forward CONNECT proxy it resolves to 0.0.0.0, which can never
match an upstream certificate, and for a reverse proxy it matched only
coincidentally.

MockServer ships a certificate authority whose private key is published in this
repository, and nothing told an operator when it was in use. A single startup
warning now names the condition and both remedies. It is emitted once per JVM
and only for server contexts.

A user-supplied fixed certificate is now re-checked for expiry and rotation on
the cached fast path, throttled to at most once a minute and using only a stat
call. Previously a long-running server would serve an expired fixed certificate
indefinitely, since only self-generated material self-renewed. A replaced file
triggers a rebuild; an unchanged expired one warns rather than failing silently.

Lowering TLS posture over `PUT /mockserver/configuration` - downgrading the
trust manager to `ANY`, disabling mutual authentication or hostname
verification, or repointing certificate paths - now emits an audit warning. It
warns rather than blocks, since the control plane is unauthenticated by default
and refusing the change would itself be a breaking change.

No cipher change was needed: `configureALPN` is applied unconditionally, so
HTTP/1.1-only servers already receive the strong cipher list and the new
protocol defaults leave no weak combination reachable.

build(deps): bump netty with its coupled tcnative pin, and log4j-api and jsoup

Unblocks Dependabot PRs #2523 and #2532, which both failed CI for the same
single cause.

netty 4.2.17.Final realigns its BOM's tcnative to 2.0.81.Final, so the
native-classifier jars resolve transitively at 2.0.81 while
`netty-tcnative-boringssl-static.version` was pinned at 2.0.78.Final. The
maven-enforcer DependencyConvergence rule then failed in mockserver-core before
compilation, and everything else red on those PRs was a cascade of it - the
CodeQL Java analysis fails because its autobuild runs Maven, and each
per-language client pipeline fails waiting on a Java artifact that never built.

The two versions have to move together: bumping the tcnative pin alone, with
netty still at 4.2.16, would produce the same convergence failure inverted.
Dependabot cannot do this itself because dependabot.yml ignores
netty-tcnative-boringssl-static outright, so it raises the netty half and is
forbidden from moving the other - which is why every netty bump re-breaks
convergence until someone intervenes. The pom comment now spells that coupling
out.

The NETTY_TCNATIVE build arguments in the six Dockerfiles move in step, as the
pom comment requires.

Also pins log4j-api to 2.25.5, closing GHSA-qv9r-c865-cp47. It was resolving to
2.25.4 at compile scope via spring-boot-starter-logging and shipping inside a
shaded artifact. Only log4j-api is managed - log4j-core is not on the tree, and
log4j-to-slf4j stays at 2.25.4, which is patch-compatible.

Pins jsoup to 1.23.1, closing GHSA-pmhh-3w7g-xqp8. It already resolved there
transitively at test scope, so this is a guard against a future transitive
downgrade rather than a live fix.

Verified by the enforcer rule that was failing (DependencyConvergence passes,
with every tcnative coordinate and classifier converged on 2.0.81.Final), the
full mockserver-core suite, and the netty TLS integration suites over real
handshakes on the new netty and tcnative pair.

The other 22 bumps in PR #2532 are deliberately left out. Once this lands that
PR's netty entry becomes a no-op and Dependabot will re-raise the remainder
against a green base, where they can be reviewed on their own merits.

ci: guard against certificate expiry and unblock the Dependabot updater

Two controls that were missing or broken, plus the skills that describe them.

Certificate expiry had no automation at all. It has been discovered by the
build going red four times in five years, most recently with two CAs 151 days
from expiry that no existing check would have flagged. A new guard sweeps every
committed certificate PEM, hard-fails under 30 days and warns between 30 and
180, and checks every certificate in a chain file rather than only the first.

The guard is fail-closed by design: it fails on an unparseable PEM, fails if
its allow-list names a file that no longer exists, fails when no PEMs are found
at all, and asserts that the one intentionally-expired negative fixture is
still expired - so the allow-list can never quietly mask a real regression. It
also enforces two structural invariants nothing previously checked: every leaf
must expire on or before its sibling CA, and the shipped default-CA files must
stay in lockstep, with the PKCS#1 and PKCS#8 keys being the same key, that key
matching the CA certificate, and the two committed copies of the CA certificate
byte-identical. The first of those caught a real pre-existing violation on its
first run - all three Netty leaves were outliving their CAs.

It runs in the Java pipeline and, because that pipeline is path-gated while
expiry is time-based, also weekly via GitHub Actions. A certificate can
otherwise cross the 30-day cliff with no commit and the guard would never fire.
GitHub Actions is the right home: it already runs this repository's scheduled
hygiene jobs, the check needs only git and openssl, and a hosted runner cannot
be starved the way the scale-to-zero Buildkite queue can.

Separately, the Dependabot updater had been failing daily and raising no PRs at
all - which is why the alert backlog looked quiet. Three ecosystems were dead.
GitHub enabled a maven-wrapper-updater experiment that cannot parse the legacy
Takari wrapper format, so the reactor failed with "No pom.xml!"; both wrappers
are migrated to the Apache only-script wrapper 3.3.4, keeping Maven at the
3.9.16 CI already uses. One npm directory failing an override resolution was
aborting the grouped job for all five, so mockserver-vscode is split into its
own block and pins js-yaml. And /.opencode had only an orphan lockfile with no
tracked manifest, so it could never resolve; it is removed from the directories
list and the lockfile untracked.

The renew-test-certs skill is corrected. It omitted both mutual-TLS directories
entirely - including the two nearest-expiry CAs, so running it returned a clean
bill of health while the real problem went unexamined - inverted the CA and
leaf longevity model, and had a working-directory bug that made three of its
recipe blocks fail as written.

Adds a github-pipeline-audit skill covering the surfaces this work had to
discover by hand, chiefly that a calm pull-request list can mean the updater
itself is broken.

build(tls): derive the tcnative native version instead of hand-syncing it

netty-tcnative has broken the build twice (PR #2332, and PRs #2523/#2532).
mockserver/pom.xml imported netty-bom and then separately overrode
netty-tcnative-boringssl-static with an explicit version, so the base artifact
followed the override while the five per-platform classifier natives followed
the BOM. Every netty bump made them diverge and the enforcer's
DependencyConvergence rule failed. The override is removed; netty-bom now
governs base and classifiers together, so they cannot diverge.

The native library was a second, worse duplication. The shaded jar strips
META-INF/native (for JNI relocation correctness, issue #1778), so the six
Dockerfiles downloaded the platform classifier jar separately at a hardcoded
NETTY_TCNATIVE build argument and copied the .so into /usr/lib. The tcnative
classes and the native library were therefore two literals kept equal by hand,
and a mismatch is an UnsatisfiedLinkError or a TLS failure inside the image
that no Maven test would ever catch.

Both jars the Dockerfiles consume are now stamped at build time with
META-INF/mockserver-tcnative.version, written from the same Maven resolution
that produced the tcnative classes, and every Dockerfile derives the download
version by reading that stamp back out of the jar it already has. No literal
remains for anyone to keep in sync. A missing or empty stamp fails the build
rather than falling back to a default, so a pre-stamp published jar errors
clearly instead of producing a mismatched image.

Both jars matter and an earlier revision stamped only one. The maven-shade
mockserver-netty-no-dependencies jar backs source=copy builds; the
maven-assembly mockserver-netty jar-with-dependencies is what the default
source=download path fetches from Maven Central. Stamping only the former left
the public path deterministically broken, which review caught and no test would
have - nothing in CI builds that path.

Verified by building both paths for real: the image builds, the arch-correct
.so lands in /usr/lib, its version equals the stamp, and the container serves
TLS with the native provider actually selected (OpenSsl.isAvailable=true,
defaultServerProvider=OPENSSL) rather than silently falling back to JDK TLS.
Enforcer convergence passes with every tcnative coordinate and classifier on a
single version, and the full mockserver-core suite is green.

Also documents MOCKSERVER_LOCAL_CA_BUNDLE and docker/ensure-ca-bundle.sh, which
make these image builds runnable behind a corporate TLS-inspecting proxy. That
mechanism already existed but was undocumented, which is why the Docker
verification gap went unclosed for so long - and corrects the stale claim that
GitHub Actions builds the Docker images. It does not; Buildkite does.

docs(docker): explain why the tcnative .so is copied to /usr/lib

The `COPY ... META-INF/native/libnetty_tcnative_linux_*.so /usr/lib/` line
looked vestigial: the assembly jar the download path fetches already bundles
those natives, so Netty loads them from the jar and never touches /usr/lib.

It is not vestigial. It is a native-TLS fallback for read-only-rootfs
deployments, introduced by e4dd3a61b ("ensured that tcnative boringssl can be
used inside docker container with readonly file system"). Under
`docker run --read-only` the jar extraction to java.io.tmpdir fails, and
System.loadLibrary finding the pre-placed .so is the only thing keeping
BoringSSL native TLS alive. Without it those deployments silently fall back to
the JDK provider - TLS still works, so nothing looks wrong.

It only looked redundant because a later ARM64 change (cff4bbe3d) moved the
target from a specific glibc path to plain /usr/lib, and because the download
path switched to the assembly jar. Verified empirically: with a writable /tmp
the native loads from the jar even with /usr/lib off java.library.path; under
--read-only it loads from /usr/lib, and removing it makes
OpenSsl.isAvailable false.

The copy is inert for the shaded no-dependencies jar, which relocates tcnative
to shaded_package.io.netty.* - the stock .so exports Java_io_netty_ symbols and
cannot bind the relocated classes.

Each of the six Dockerfiles now says this above the line, so the next person
does not have to rediscover it.

ci: build and verify the Docker images on docker/** changes

Nothing built these images when only docker/ changed. The single image build
lived in a master-only step inside pipeline-java, which triggers on
mockserver/, mockserver-ui/ and test-fixtures/ - so a Dockerfile-only edit ran
a static lint and nothing else. The default source=download path was built by
nothing at all, and docs/testing.md said so outright.

That is how the tcnative stamp landed in only one of the two jars the
Dockerfiles consume, deterministically breaking the public download path for
every release. Review caught it; no gate could have.

docker/** now routes to mockserver-container-tests, which owns a real image
build. Two guards run there and locally from the same scripts, so the two
cannot drift:

verify-tcnative-stamp.sh checks both stamped jars - the assembly jar the
download path consumes and the shaded jar the copy path uses - asserting the
stamp is present, well formed, consistent between them, and equal to the
Maven-resolved tcnative version. It is the cheapest thing that catches the
defect that actually occurred, and needs no image build.

docker-build-verify.sh builds the image and asserts what a green build does
not: the arch-correct .so is in /usr/lib, the native provider genuinely loads
rather than silently falling back to JDK TLS, and the container serves a real
TLS handshake.

It also probes under `docker run --read-only`. That is the only check that
protects the /usr/lib copy's reason to exist. The ordinary probe is satisfied
by the native bundled in the assembly jar, so it stays green even when the
/usr/lib copy is dead - demonstrated by running a deliberately broken image
both ways: red under --read-only, green with a writable /tmp.

Locally the derive check runs by default in the pre-commit path and the full
build is opt-in, because a gate slow enough to skip is worse than an honest
one.

source=download is still not built in CI - a pre-stamp release fails the derive
by design, so it would need a locally served jar. It is covered by the derive
check on the exact jar it consumes and by a copy-mode build using that same
jar. docs/testing.md states that gap rather than implying coverage.

Also drops the now-moot dependabot ignore for
io.netty:netty-tcnative-boringssl-static. The artifact carries no version in
any manifest now that netty-bom governs it, so there is nothing to bump and no
pin to reintroduce.

test(config): clear the property cache, not just the system property

Fixes a red master. SslCertificateLeafValidityInDaysTest.shouldResolveSystemPropertyOverride
failed on CI with "Expected: is <825> but: was <397>".

ConfigurationProperties getters are cache-first: readPropertyHierarchically
stores every resolved value in a static cache, including built-in defaults. The
test mutated state with raw System.setProperty and tore down with raw
System.clearProperty, neither of which touches that cache. Its sibling tests
read the getter with nothing set, caching 397 for the lifetime of the fork, so
the later override was silently ignored.

That makes the test pass only when it happens to be the first read of the key
in its fork. It passed locally on a luckier ordering and failed deterministically
on CI's. The caching is intentional and correct - a real -D at JVM startup is
read before any default is cached, and the control plane and programmatic
setters go through the cache-coherent helpers - so the defect is entirely in the
test.

Both affected tests now follow the convention already established by
PrometheusRemoteWriteProtocolVersionConfigurationTest: evict the cache entry
around the raw mutation, rather than widening the visibility of production code.

MaxLlmConversationBodySizeTest carried the identical latent fault and is fixed
here too. It was green only because this JVM happened to run its default-value
test first; forcing NAME_ASCENDING ordering reproduced the failure
(expected 1048576 but was 16384). The other ten tests that touch mockserver.*
system properties were checked and are safe - they either drive state through
the fluent setter or already evict the cache.

Verified by running each class alone five times across both Surefire phases and
by the full unfiltered mockserver-core suite (2459 tests, 0 failures - the same
count CI reported failing). Breaking the getter turns both override tests red,
so the fix has not made them vacuous.

Documents the hazard in the configuration reference, since a single green run
cannot reveal an ordering-dependent fault like this.

ci: unblock master by removing the docker build-verify step, and fix why it failed

The `:docker: build & verify image` step added in b63d0b4da has never passed in
CI. It fails master's container-tests pipeline and blocks every docker/**
change, including six open distroless digest bumps that are otherwise innocent.

Removing it returns docker/** CI coverage to where it was before b63d0b4da - a
static lint - while both guards keep running in the developer pre-commit path,
so the tcnative stamp defect they exist to catch is still caught before a push.
The step can be re-landed once it has been proven green on a real agent.

The failure message was misleading. It reported "no host JDK and no usable
mockserver/mockserver:maven image", which is false: that tag pulls anonymously,
and pipeline-java runs the whole reactor inside it on the same queue every
commit.

The real cause is a bash unmatched-glob bug in docker-build-verify.sh.
first_real_jar enabled nullglob inside itself, but its caller's jar glob is
expanded by the parent shell, with nullglob still off, before the function
runs. Under bash an unmatched glob stays literal, so the function received the
pattern itself, failed to match its -sources/-javadoc/original- exclusions, and
reported a jar that did not exist. The build was therefore skipped, nothing
warmed ~/.m2 - this pipeline has no cache-restore - no jars were produced, and
the inner stamp gate then failed while guessing at the cause. The same bug also
disabled the post-build guard, so a build producing nothing would have passed.

nullglob now applies at script scope, which fixes both the detection and the
guard. Reproduced and verified under bash for three cases: no jars present
(build now runs), jars present (build correctly skipped), and a build producing
nothing (guard now fires and exits non-zero, where before it returned success).

verify-tcnative-stamp.sh no longer blames a missing maven image for every
Maven failure. It distinguishes no-Java-and-no-Docker from Maven-ran-and-failed
(reporting the real exit code and stderr) from Maven-ran-but-parsed-nothing. A
guard that misdiagnoses its own failure costs nearly as much as one that does
not run - this message sent a full investigation down the wrong path.

Its header also claimed it was wired into the Java pipeline. It is not, and
never has been; the header now says where it actually runs.

ci: submit the Maven dependency graph again

Dependabot alerts are computed from the submitted dependency graph, not from
the manifests. GitHub's managed Maven auto-submission discovers only a root
pom.xml, and 386750356 moved the Java project into mockserver/ - so submission
stopped seventeen minutes after that commit and has not run since 5 May.

The graph has been frozen ever since. The submitted SBOM still reports
spring-core 5.3.39, log4j-api 2.17.2 and jsoup 1.21.1, describing a codebase
that no longer exists.

Two consequences, both observed. Phantom alerts: twenty Spring advisories
bounded at "<= 5.3.39" were open against a tree running Spring 7.0.8, and had
to be dismissed as inaccurate. Undetected fixes: log4j-api is pinned to 2.25.5
and jsoup to 1.23.1 on master, yet both alerts remain open because the graph
does not know. The serious case is the one not yet seen - a genuinely new Maven
CVE would not surface at all, because nothing has been measuring since May.

Note Dependabot's security update PRs read manifests directly and kept working
throughout. It is the alerting graph that went stale, which is why the repo
looked quiet rather than broken.

Submission is now explicit, with two jobs and distinct correlators so neither
snapshot clobbers the other: the main reactor at mockserver/ (which includes
examples/java as a module) and mockserver-maven-plugin, which is a separate
build whose dependencies resolve only after a targeted install of its
unreleased sibling modules. Those are exactly the two Maven directories
dependabot.yml is configured for. It runs on pushes to master that touch a pom,
plus workflow_dispatch.

The GitHub-managed submission is left alone: it is already inert without a root
pom.xml, so it cannot compete. It would only need disabling if a root pom were
ever reintroduced.

Verified locally that the resolved tree this submits contains log4j-api 2.25.5
and jsoup 1.23.1, so both open alerts should clear once it runs. That clearing
is the proof, and cannot be observed until it runs on master.

The documentation asserted the opposite and is corrected. security.md claimed
GitHub automatically indexes all manifests; ci-cd.md recorded that an earlier
submission workflow was removed because the built-in graph gave equivalent
coverage - the belief that caused this outage.

fix(ci): pass an absolute directory to the Maven dependency submission action

The first run failed with
"Unable to locate executable file: .../mockserver-monorepo/mockserver/mockserver/mvnw"
- note the doubled path segment.

The action's `directory` input defaults to ${{ github.workspace }}, so it
expects an absolute path. Given a relative one it joins the workspace prefix a
second time when locating the Maven wrapper, and the resulting path does not
exist.

Both jobs now pass ${{ github.workspace }}/... explicitly, matching the shape of
the input's own default.

build(scripts): add github-stars.sh for exact star counts

The GitHub UI rounds star counts over 1,000 ("4.9k"), so reading the precise
figure meant hand-rolling a gh/curl call each time. This adds a small utility
that prints the exact count, defaulting to the monorepo.

Supports several repos at once, --number for scripting, and --all/--owner to
enumerate every non-fork repo an owner owns with a total. Prefers the local gh
