fix(tls): serialise dynamic certificate authority generation within the JVM

A MockServer started from the CLI, the standalone jar or Docker could
permanently fail every TLS handshake for the life of the process. It presented
as a roughly ten percent flake in the Node launcher tests; it is a shipped
concurrency bug.

Two paths generate the dynamic certificate authority concurrently at startup,
each holding its own factory instance because the factory method returns a new
one per call: LifeCycle.logProxySetup writing the CA to disk on the startup
thread, and the first HTTPS handshake building a leaf on the SNI executor. Main
defaults proxySetupLogging to true, which is why embedded ClientAndServer never
saw this.

Generation was guarded by a cross-process file lock only. A second
FileChannel.lock on the same file within one JVM throws
OverlappingFileLockException, which was caught and swallowed as "proceeding
without cross-process serialisation" - so the second thread ran with no
serialisation at all. The two CA accessors were unsynchronised lazy memoisers,
so two generations interleaved their PEM writes and the leaf was signed with
one generation's private key while being verified against the other's public
key:

  SignatureException: certificate does not verify with supplied key

The mismatched pair was then memoised, so every later handshake threw and the
connection was closed with no certificate. Not a slow start - permanently
broken TLS.

Generation now also takes a JVM-wide monitor keyed by the certificate
directory, so two factory instances pointed at one directory serialise even
when the file lock degrades to a no-op, and the file lock is retained for the
multi-process case. The key is the canonical path: keying on the merely
absolute path meant two spellings of one directory produced two monitors over a
single lock file, which reopened the race - twelve of sixty iterations failed
that way in testing.

The CA key and certificate are published as a matched pair under that monitor,
both volatile, with the fast path requiring both non-null so no reader can
observe half of an update. This is scoped to the dynamic case: a user-supplied
verify-only authority legitimately has a certificate and no usable private key,
and an unconditional paired load would break writeCertificateAuthorityToDisk
and certificateChain for it.

The Node launcher was discarding the evidence that would have identified this
quickly - it routed MockServer's output to 'ignore' unless verbose, so the
SEVERE line naming the exception was thrown away. Output is now captured to a
bounded ring buffer and the tail is surfaced, with process liveness and exit
status, when a readiness check fails.

waitForTlsReady also had a fallback claiming a peer certificate on a
verification error proves TLS was served. That branch is dead on Node 20 and
22, so readiness only ever succeeded via secureConnect - which fired only
because an unrelated test sets NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED process-wide. It
now sets rejectUnauthorized on its own connection and no longer depends on
another test's side effect.

Verified end to end rather than by unit test alone: the released jar fails 4 of
50 launcher runs, the rebuilt jar passes 50 of 50. Defeating the monitor
reproduces the SignatureException in 7 of 60 iterations, and the full
mockserver-core suite is green.

test(mqtt): prove TLS-listener handshake enforcement with a secured Mosquitto

Restores c8584bf05, which was reverted 80 minutes later by a89772480 and then
stranded as an untracked file in an abandoned worktree.

Nothing was wrong with what the test asserted. Buildkite mockserver-java#1796
shows the revert cause: the server certificate's SAN was hard-coded to
localhost and 127.0.0.1, but CI runs this step inside a container against a
mounted Docker socket, so Testcontainers resolves the broker to the bridge
gateway address instead. Paho enables HTTPS endpoint identification by default,
so the handshake failed on identity rather than trust, with "No subject
alternative names matching IP address 172.16.0.1 found".

The connect host is now resolved before the container starts, so it can be
baked into the SAN, and the test asserts afterwards that the container's
reported host still matches - a future Testcontainers change then fails with a
readable message rather than an opaque handshake error.

This is the only wire-level coverage of the MQTT sslProperties path. The
similarly-named MqttTlsLiveBrokerIntegrationTest is misnamed: it connects over
tcp:// on 1883 with a password file and never performs a handshake, so it
covers credentials over plaintext. MqttSecurityOptionsTest only asserts the
options object was populated.

Verified to discriminate rather than merely pass: commenting out
setSSLProperties in MqttSecurityOptions turns the positive case red with a PKIX
path failure. Note the negative case alone is not a wiring discriminator, since
a client with no SSL properties also fails PKIX - the positive case carries the
load.

Runs green on the Docker host, green with the host forced to a non-loopback
address (reproducing the CI topology that caused the revert), and green across
the full 32-test async live-broker suite.

docs(plans): record the twelve open test-coverage gaps and delete the stale audit

The 2026-07-21 coverage audit produced a 93-entry JSON that has sat untracked
ever since, duplicated across the main checkout and an abandoned worktree. All
93 entries were re-verified against master: 81 are closed, each with a named
test class or commit.

That makes the original file worse than absent - its status field is now wrong
for 81 of 93 rows, so anyone reading it would be misled about what is covered.
It is replaced by this list of what actually remains, ranked by real risk of an
undetected defect rather than by the original severity labels.

Two of those labels are worth ignoring deliberately. The mutation smoke-gate was
rated HIGH as an audit-integrity control, but its value has largely been paid
down by degrade-and-confirm-red being performed by hand in recent work, so
building it now is a large investment against a much-reduced risk. Conversely
the node and python testcontainers gap was rated MEDIUM, yet it means two
published client libraries have CI jobs that pass having started no container
at all.

Committed rather than kept local: the Kubernetes and CI-plumbing items need to
survive across sessions and machines, which is precisely what a gitignored
*.local.md prevents.

Also records what the audit cannot tell us. Its four TLS entries are all closed,
but by the July coverage wave rather than by the later certificate programme -
which added leaf validity windows, EKU and keyUsage and AKI, expiry-driven cache
renewal, SAN bounding, upstream hostname verification and the dynamic-CA race
fix. None of that surface has ever been audited, because this audit predates all
of it.

test(blob): prove GCS and Azure configuration actually reaches the client

S3 already had S3BlobStoreRegistrarConfigWiringTest (36258e097). GCS and Azure
did not, and their contract tests hand-build the client - new GcsBlobStore(storage,
...) and new AzureBlobStore(containerClient, ...) - so the registrar that turns
configuration into a working client was never exercised. A wrong bucket,
container, endpoint or credential would ship silently: the contract tests would
still pass, because they bypass exactly the code that was broken.

Both new tests drive the registrar from configuration only, as production does,
and assert against the same emulator the contract tests use - fake-gcs-server
for GCS, Azurite for Azure.

They verify the settings that can actually be got wrong rather than that a
client is non-null: endpoint override, credentials, project id, and container or
bucket name. The round-trip assertions use an independent admin client to
confirm the object landed in the configured bucket at the configured key prefix,
so a mis-wired bucket cannot pass merely because the store reads back what it
wrote.

Each is proven to discriminate. Making the GCS registrar ignore the configured
bucket fails the round-trip with "Storage Not Found"; dropping its setHost call
retargets real storage.googleapis.com and fails the endpoint assertion; making
the Azure registrar ignore the configured container fails on the container name
and 404s the round-trip.

Both suites run with Docker genuinely executing - 26 tests for GCS and 32 for
Azure, none skipped. Azurite is pinned to 3.36.0 with --skipApiVersionCheck,
matching the contract test, because the current SDK negotiates a Storage REST
API version the emulator rejects.

Note the S3 test is not itself emulator-backed: S3Client.builder() performs no
I/O, so its configuration is introspectable offline. These two cannot rely on
that, so they combine the same style of introspection with a live round-trip.

ci(ui): compile the code the composer hands users, in every language

The dashboard composer emits client code in seven languages, verified only by
string assertions. Broken generated code reaches users directly and nothing
would catch it. Java was gated by javac and C# by an equivalence test; Python,
Ruby, Go and Rust had no gate at all.

All four now compile or parse real composer output in CI. The samples come from
the 26 shared parity combos the byte-identity tests already use, driven through
the actual emitters - not hand-written snippets, which would prove only that
someone can write valid code in that language.

Python and Ruby get a parse check. Both clients are dynamically typed with no
shipped type stubs, so that is the strongest credible static gate: it fails on
any emitter bug producing malformed source. Go and Rust compile the generated
code against the real in-repo clients, so they additionally catch client API
drift - a renamed client method fails the build, which is the direct analog of
the Java gate.

Every gate is proven to bite. Breaking each emitter turns its step red - python
and ruby and go exit 1, rust exits 101 - and all four return green once
restored, in both native and Docker execution modes.

The Node arm needed no work: typecheck-node-codegen.mjs is not orphaned as
previously recorded. It is imported by node.test.ts and runs under npm test in
CI, type-proving every emitted literal against the client Expectation type with
a committed negative control. Verified rather than assumed - 29 tests pass.

One limitation worth stating. These live in pipeline-ui, which fires on UI
changes, so they fully cover emitter drift. The Go and Rust arms also catch
client API drift, but only when a UI change happens at the same time; a pure
client rename with no UI change will not trigger them. The Java gate avoids
this by living in pipeline-java, which fires on both paths - there is no single
pipeline firing on both mockserver-ui and a client directory. Adding the Go and
Rust arms to their own client pipelines would close that, and is deliberately
left out of scope here.

ci(testcontainers): actually start a container in the node and python jobs

Two published client libraries had CI jobs that passed having started nothing.
Node ran only unit tests. Python was the starker case: the step already mounted
the Docker socket and then ran pytest -m "not docker", deselecting every
container test. The socket was mounted and deliberately unused.

Both now run their container tests against a real MockServer and grep for a
status marker the test emits only after a successful HTTP round-trip, so a run
that starts no container fails the step rather than reporting green. That
mirrors the approach already used for go, dotnet and rust.

The guard earned itself immediately. Wiring the tests up surfaced four defects
that would each have left the jobs unable to start a container, and each was
caught by the guard failing closed rather than by anything passing:

Node probed for Docker with execSync("docker info"), but the node:20 CI image
has no docker binary, so all five tests skipped and the job went green with no
container. testcontainers-node talks to the mounted socket directly and needs
no CLI, so the probe is now a socket check.

testcontainers-python resolves a mapped port to localhost, because docker-py
rewrites a bind-mounted unix socket to an http+docker://localhost base URL,
which stops its inside-container gateway fallback from ever firing. From a
sibling container that address is unreachable. TC_HOST is now exported
explicitly; node, go and dotnet resolve this themselves, python does not.

testcontainers-python's Ryuk reaper is unreachable across the bridge in a
socket-mounted setup, so it is disabled; the tests clean up through their own
context manager on an ephemeral agent. Node never used Ryuk, which is why it
appeared to work.

And the step scripts captured output with out="$(cmd)" under set -e, which
aborted before printing anything or running the marker guard, swallowing a real
failure entirely.

Both step labels change from "unit tests" to "unit + container tests", because
a label that says unit on a container-starting step is the same reads-as-green
problem in miniature.

Verified by running both for real: node 16 unit plus 5 integration, python 26
tests, each emitting its marker with a 200 response from a started container.
Then verified the guard bites by filtering the container test out - the
remaining tests still pass green, and both steps exit 1 because no container
ran.

One environment caveat: on Docker Desktop for Mac the 172.17.0.1 gateway does
not reach published ports, while host.docker.internal does, so the python step
prefers the latter and falls back to the route gateway on plain Linux CI.

ci: run the WAR Tomcat integration test instead of skipping it

container_integration_tests/docker_compose_war_tomcat has been skipping since
it was written, with "WAR artifact not present (built locally only); CI wiring
is a follow-up". The test works; it simply never ran.

That matters more than a generic skip. WAR deployment is a demonstrated weak
spot - the ROOT-context percent-decode regression 66b5d51d2 shipped and broke
builds, and this is the suite that would have caught it.

The WAR was already built by the reactor in the Java pipeline's maven step; it
was just never published, and Buildkite steps share no filesystem. So the
pipeline now uploads it as an artifact and the container-tests step downloads
it into the path the test already globs.

The skip is gone. A missing WAR now fails the case loudly rather than reporting
green, both in the test itself and via a presence check in the CI step.

Verified by running it: Tomcat 10.1 auto-deploys the WAR at ROOT, the
expectation is seeded, and the request is served. Verified fail-closed by
moving the WAR aside - the case exits non-zero and is recorded as a failure,
with the skip log empty.

Two things worth knowing. The case runs only in the Java pipeline's master-only
container-tests step, so it fires on mockserver/, mockserver-ui/ and
test-fixtures/ changes - the mockserver-container-tests pipeline lints this
script but does not execute it, which is pre-existing and unchanged. And it
stays invisible on pull requests for the same pre-existing reason; making it
run there would require that pipeline to build the WAR itself.

expected_tests.manifest already declared the case as blocking, so it was
already required to produce a result - previously a skip satisfied that, and
now only a genuine pass or fail does.

test(cassettes): prove an auto-registered cassette is retrievable, and settle the policy

The recorded gap said neither loading nor recording auto-registers a cassette,
leaving it an open product decision. That premise was stale. Commit 76ae2f232
already made the decision, implemented it in both MCP tool handlers, and
documented it - docs/code/llm-mocking.md states plainly that the fixture is
auto-registered so the cassette appears under GET /mockserver/cassettes without
a separate PUT.

The real residual was narrower and genuinely untested: nothing proved an
auto-registered cassette is retrievable *through* the endpoint. The netty
endpoint test only exercised PUT-registered entries, and the handler tests only
inspected the in-process registry object. The seam between them was unproven.

A new core test drives the real GET handler against a registry populated the way
the load and record handlers populate it, pinning the documented body shape and
answering the question the gap raised: record-then-load on one path yields one
upserted entry, not two. It also covers the bare /cassettes alias and clearing
on reset.

CassetteRegistry now carries the policy as javadoc, naming the three entry
points and stating why registration is not factored into a shared load/record
method: recording writes bytes and loading reads them, so they share no method
carrying path, count and origin - they converge only on register itself. That
reasoning previously lived in a commit message, which is why the question kept
being re-opened.

The consumer MCP documentation now says the same, so users are not left
assuming a manual PUT is required.

Degrade-confirmed: making the GET handler stop surfacing registry entries turns
all five tests red. Full unfiltered core suite green - 8198 parallel and 2464
sequential - with the new global-state test registered in both pom phases and
both state guards passing.

Also carries the changelog entry for the WAR Tomcat CI wiring committed in
12758d003.

test(llm): pin the codec wire contract against something goldens cannot rewrite

The LLM codec golden files are regenerated from the codecs themselves via
-Dmockserver.updateLlmGoldens=true, so they only ever confirm that a codec
agrees with itself. A structural error bakes into its own golden and the drift
test then passes forever.

A new structural contract test reads live codec output and never reads a golden
file, so regeneration cannot reach it. The assertions are hand-authored from
each provider's published API schema - required fields, terminal markers, SSE
event-name sequences, delta reassembly, tool-envelope typing - which is the
externally-authored half the goldens were missing.

Sourcing real published payloads was considered and rejected: a provider's own
example can never byte-match our normalised output, since text, identifiers and
ordering all differ, so it collapses into structural comparison anyway at higher
cost and with more flakiness. Making regeneration harder was also rejected, as
it adds friction without verifying anything.

All seven chat providers are covered, grouped by wire family so depth goes where
the risk is rather than spreading thin: Azure delegates to the OpenAI codec and
Bedrock to the Anthropic one, so a carefully authored assertion covers its
delegate too. Rerank-only providers and the byte-identical OpenAI-compatible
aliases are excluded, matching the golden test's own exclusions.

Proven to bite, with goldens left untouched in every case: renaming
finish_reason, renaming the Anthropic content_block_delta event, dropping
Gemini's finishReason, renaming the Responses status field, and renaming
Ollama's done marker each turn it red. No codec defect was found - the
assertions were written to match output that already conforms - and no
production code changes.

The documentation now states the maintainer contract plainly: a failure here
means the codec regressed or the provider changed its API, and must not be
resolved by regenerating goldens.

docs(plans): seven coverage gaps closed, five remain and none is simply outstanding

Records what landed on 2026-08-17 and narrows the list from twelve to five.

The five that remain are all blocked or judged not worth doing, and each says
which. Three need a real k3d cluster that the corporate TLS-inspection proxy
prevents standing up locally, so they are CI-only work. The cross-cutting sweep
is bookkeeping now its named instances are fixed. The mutation smoke-gate was
rated HIGH but its value has been paid down by degrade-and-confirm-red being
performed by hand as a matter of course - every gap closed today carries that
evidence in its commit message.

Also records two things worth keeping.

A quarter of the twelve had stale premises, barely a day after the list was
written from a careful re-audit: the Node codegen typecheck was recorded as
wired to nothing when it runs under npm test; CassetteRegistry auto-registration
was recorded as an open decision when it was implemented in July; and the WAR
case was expected to run from a pipeline that only lints it. That is not
carelessness in the audit - a moving repository outruns any static catalogue.
The safeguard is that each piece of work verified its own premise first, which
is how all three were caught. Rows here are hypotheses to check, not facts.

And the gaps that mattered were not the ones with the highest severity labels.
The most valuable find was rated MEDIUM: two published client libraries whose CI
jobs passed having started no container, with python mounting the Docker socket
and then deliberately not using it. Wiring it up exposed four further defects
that would each have stopped a container starting, every one caught by the new
guard failing closed rather than by anything passing.

test(node): run the launcher tests against a jar built from this tree

The mockserver-node launcher integration tests downloaded the RELEASED
mockserver-netty jar from Maven Central, at whatever version package.json
named, and launched that. So the suite proved something about the last
release rather than about this repository: a mockserver-core fix could not
green it, and a mockserver-core regression could not red it.

That was not theoretical. The released 7.5.0 jar carries the dynamic-CA
generation race fixed on master in 4cff56e61, which permanently breaks TLS
for the process lifetime when it hits. It presented as an ~8% launcher flake
that no source change could resolve, and cost four CI retry cycles.

Build the jar in the node pipeline and launch that instead. A new build step
runs `-pl mockserver-netty -am -DskipTests package` and uploads the assembly
jar; the launcher step depends on it, downloads it, and points the launcher
at it. With the tree jar, 32 iterations of the previously-flaky file — 64
executions of the two dynamic-CA cases — passed with zero failures.

The mechanism is a real launcher feature, not a test backdoor: `jarPath` and
`MOCKSERVER_JAR_PATH` use an exact jar and skip download entirely, serving
air-gapped and corporate installs. It is symmetric with the existing
MOCKSERVER_BINARY_BASE_URL override, which covers only downloadBinary.js —
the launcher's own jar path had no hook at all.

Both layers fail closed. A configured-but-missing jar is a hard error that
names the refusal to fall back to a release, and the CI step exits 1 when the
artifact is absent, so a failed build step cannot silently revert to
downloading. Local `npm test` with neither option set is unchanged.

The jar could not come from the java pipeline: the node pipeline is a
separate Buildkite build created by API, with no access to another
pipeline's artifacts. Building in-pipeline duplicates that build when a
server change triggers both — the accepted cost of testing the tree.

test(k8s): let the Helm suite's k3d cluster start behind a TLS-inspection proxy

Three Kubernetes test-coverage gaps were deferred as impossible to verify
locally because a corporate TLS-inspection proxy "prevents standing up a k3d
cluster". That was never tested, and it is wrong.

There are two trust stores, not one. The host Docker daemon already trusts
the corporate root, so `k3d cluster create` pulls the k3s node image fine —
which is exactly what makes the misdiagnosis convincing, because creation
appears to succeed. But containerd running inside the k3s node has its own
trust store at /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt holding public roots only.
It cannot pull even the rancher/mirrored-pause sandbox image, so every pod
dies at sandbox creation with "x509: certificate signed by unknown
authority" and the cluster looks broken rather than mistrusting one cert.

Overmounting a CA bundle into the node's trust store at create time fixes it.
With that, the full Helm suite passes 7/7.

The hook is opt-in and CI-inert: when K3D_LOCAL_CA_BUNDLE is unset — always,
in CI — the k3d command is byte-identical to before, and an empty value
behaves as unset rather than producing a malformed --volume argument. Set but
missing warns rather than fails, mirroring LOCAL_DOCKER_CA_BUNDLE in
run-in-docker.sh. No CA path or proxy configuration enters a repo or pipeline
file; the variable is user/shell scope only.

The bundle must be the combined one — public roots plus the corporate root —
because the mount replaces containerd's entire trust store, so a
corporate-root-only file would break every public pull instead. The docs say
so unmissably, and record the pause-image symptom so the next person
recognises it rather than re-deriving the wrong conclusion.

ci: fail the build when a new false-green test shape appears

This repository keeps shipping tests and gates that report success while
verifying nothing: a Docker-gated suite that skipped silently in CI, a python
step that mounted the Docker socket and then ran `pytest -m "not docker"`, a
WAR case parked behind a "CI wiring is a follow-up" skip and read as green for
months. The 2026-07-21 audit named these shapes, but the naming lived only in
plan documents, so nothing stopped the next one.

Enforce the three that can be pinned down precisely. Every suite gated by
DockerAvailability.isAvailable must be paired with assert-suite-ran over its
reports, or an unusable Docker socket skips it while the build stays green.
No step may mount the Docker socket and then deselect the Docker-marked tests.
No container-integration logTestSkip may park deferred work as a green skip.

Wiring it up immediately found a live instance: the Gcs and Azure
RegistrarConfigWiringTest suites ran under a Docker socket in CI with no
fail-closed assertion, so they could have skipped on every build and reported
green. Those pairings are added here.

The coverage match is module-scoped rather than class-name-only, which matters
more than it sounds. These suite families grow by adding a same-suffix module
— S3 then GCS then Azure — so a class-name match would report a new gated
suite as covered on the strength of a different module's glob, reinstating the
exact defect inside the guard meant to catch it. The key is the module
directory basename, which assumes those basenames stay globally unique; both
the script and the doc say so, since an undisclosed limit in a guard like this
is itself a false green.

Always-on, because a false green can enter from a Java source, a pipeline
step, a client test or a container-integration script, and no single
path-filtered pipeline sees them all. Each rule fails closed on an empty
corpus, so a broken checkout cannot pass by scanning nothing. The allow-list
carries a rot check: an entry that no longer describes what it exempts fails
the build rather than silently widening.

Two shapes are deliberately not enforced — self-derived goldens and
preconditions that can fail silently are test-design properties with no
low-false-positive textual signature. docs/operations/false-green-guards.md
records that rather than implying the class is covered.

fix(helm): repair the sidecar-injection webhook, broken out of the box

Enabling webhook.enabled=true from the shipped chart defaults produced a
cluster that could not create matched pods at all. The TLS bootstrap image
default, bitnami/kubectl:1.31, no longer exists — Bitnami withdrew the tag
from Docker Hub — so both bootstrap Jobs failed, the
MutatingWebhookConfiguration's caBundle was never patched, and because
failurePolicy is Fail the webhook then rejected every matched pod CREATE.
The feature did not degrade; it blocked admission.

Swapping the image was not sufficient, and the reason is the more important
half of this fix. WebhookServer accepted PKCS#8 only and explicitly rejected
anything else, so any replacement emitting a different key format crashed the
handler. That same rigidity had already broken the cert-manager path: the
chart's Certificate requests algorithm RSA with no encoding field, which is
PKCS#1, which the handler refused. The withdrawn image had been masking a
loader that tolerated exactly one format — the one that image happened to
emit. Two shipped defects, one cause.

Parse any standard unencrypted PEM private key instead: PKCS#8, PKCS#1 and
SEC1 EC. Encrypted and non-key PEMs still fail loudly with a message naming
what was actually parsed, rather than being silently accepted. bcpkix takes
its version from the reactor-managed property, so bcpkix, bcutil and bcprov
all resolve together and DependencyConvergence holds.

Bootstrap now uses registry.k8s.io/ingress-nginx/kube-webhook-certgen, the
purpose-built tool for this exact job. It is self-contained, so it needs
neither a shell nor an openssl CLI nor an install-at-runtime step that would
fail on an airgapped or proxied cluster — which is what ruled out the
alternatives, since no durable pinnable image still bundles sh, the openssl
CLI and kubectl together. Phase 2's ClusterRole gains the update verb, which
certgen's patch step genuinely performs.

Found by writing an integration test that insisted on exercising the shipped
default rather than pinning a working image around it.

test(k8s): prove sidecar injection and JGroups DNS discovery against a real cluster

Three Kubernetes paths shipped unproven. The admission webhook had no test at
all — no helm_* case referenced webhook, inject or sidecar — so the chart's
MutatingWebhookConfiguration was never driven. JGroups DNS_PING discovery was
covered only by JGroupsKubernetesStackTest, which parses the XML and stops;
ClusteredTwoNodeTest uses loopback MPING, so the Kubernetes discovery path had
never executed. And helm_clustered_convergence recorded a result that could
not fail the suite.

All three were previously deferred as unverifiable behind a corporate
TLS-inspection proxy. That premise was wrong, and the k3d hook committed
earlier removes it.

helm_sidecar_injection drives a real labelled pod CREATE through admission and
asserts the resulting pod spec carries the injected sidecar, the iptables init
container and the injected annotation. It renders the chart's own default
bootstrap image and asserts it is pullable rather than overriding it, so the
default cannot silently rot again — this is what surfaced the withdrawn
Bitnami tag. A negative-control pod without the opt-in annotation must receive
none of the three, so a webhook that injects unconditionally fails.

helm_jgroups_dns_ping asserts the headless Service really is headless, that
JGROUPS_DNS_QUERY resolves to at least two pod IPs, that a two-node view forms,
and that state converges. The view-size assertion is the point: two pods each
forming a cluster of one would otherwise satisfy a naive convergence check.

helm_clustered_convergence becomes blocking. The swallowed image import is now
verified present in the node's containerd before deploying, and the flake it
was blamed on turned out to be something else entirely — helm install racing a
namespace still Terminating from the previous run. Guarding that took it to
3/3 green. Its Times.exactly(3) assertion no longer tolerates 2 or 4; requests
are issued sequentially against a shared atomic counter, so exactly 3 is
deterministic and the tolerance was hiding the off-by-one this test exists to
catch.

Each was proven red by degrading the behaviour it names: deleting the
MutatingWebhookConfiguration drops the sidecar, and deleting the headless
Service makes both pods form clusters of one and convergence fail.

These depend on Java-built images the CI helm step does not build, so in CI
they record an honest SKIP and run blocking only where those images exist.
The changelog and plan doc say so plainly — a gap closed locally is not the
same as a gap covered in CI, and recording it as such would be the exact
false green this work is meant to eliminate.

docs(changelog): mark the TLS-defaults change as BREAKING BEHAVIOUR, not BREAKING

This repository distinguishes the two markers by what they ship as, and the
distinction is load-bearing for release preparation. Plain `BREAKING:` appears
only in major releases — 7.0.0 and 6.0.0. `**BREAKING BEHAVIOUR:` is the form
for a behaviour break that ships in a minor; 7.5.0 carried six of them, plus
the template-sandbox RCE fix.

The TLS-defaults change is going out in 7.6.0, a minor, so the plain marker
was wrong: AGENTS.md reserves it for when a major bump is intended, and the
release-preparation rules read it as the trigger for one. Left as-is it would
have implied a major that did not happen, and misled the next release.

Only the marker and the line wrapping change; the described behaviour, the
restore instructions and the cipher-suite note are untouched.

ci: build the Kubernetes test images so the three helm cases actually run

helm_sidecar_injection, helm_jgroups_dns_ping and helm_clustered_convergence
recorded a SKIP in CI because the helm step runs with SKIP_JAVA_BUILD=true and
no JDK, so the -clustered and mockserver-webhook images never existed. A skip
that reads as a satisfied result is the false-green shape this repository has
been working to remove, and here it covered the admission-webhook and JGroups
discovery paths entirely.

Worse than recorded: the webhook image was never built by the harness at all,
only by the release and snapshot pipelines. So helm_sidecar_injection was
skipping everywhere, including on a developer machine with a JDK — not just in
CI, as the plan doc claimed.

A new producer step builds the three jars once and uploads them; the helm step
depends on it, downloads them, and does cheap COPY-into-distroless builds. The
jars travel, not the images: ~200 MB against ~1.3 GB, and the consumer rebuilds
in seconds. That is the same hand-off the WAR case and the node launcher jar
already use. The dead Maven fallback in the helm step is deleted rather than
left as a second silent path.

Two independent layers fail closed. The step exits non-zero if a jar artifact
is absent, and the harness runs with REQUIRE_CLUSTERED_IMAGE and
REQUIRE_WEBHOOK_IMAGE set, so an image that is expected but missing is recorded
as a failure rather than a skip. Proven both ways: images removed with the
flags on gives three failures and exit 1; flags off gives an honest skip and
exit 0. The expected-tests manifest declares all three, so a case producing no
result at all also reds the build.

Verified on a live cluster: 10 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped.

Costs roughly 8-12 minutes, partly offset by moving the netty build out of the
helm step into the producer where it happens once.

test(core): run the fresh-clinit tests sequentially, they reset every logger

mockserver-java #1919 failed one test of 8198:
ConfigurationValueRedactionTest expected one captured warning and saw none.
The production path is deterministic and always emits that warning, so a zero
capture never meant "no warn" — it meant the test's log handler had been torn
off the logger between its two emits.

MockServerLogger.installDefaultJavaLoggingFormat calls
LogManager.getLogManager().readConfiguration, whose reset() strips every
handler from every logger in the JVM. LogManager is a global singleton and is
NOT isolated by a child-first classloader, so a test that forces a fresh
<clinit> of MockServerLogger or ConfigurationProperties in an isolated loader
detaches the handlers of whatever else is running. Two such tests were in the
parallel phase: ClassInitializationDeadlockTest and
ConfigurationPropertiesInitializationTest.

Route both to the sequential phase. Cutting the two antagonists rather than
the victims is the smaller and more durable surface: that reset is an
irreducible JVM-global side effect, unsafe beside any handler-capturing test
present or future, and it costs ~0.003s of sequential time. The other victim,
ConfigurationDTOCredentialMaskingTest, is protected by the same move — and one
exposed assertion checks for silence, where a stolen handler would have made
it pass for the wrong reason rather than fail.

No production change. configureLogger preserving foreign handlers would be a
real behavioural change, and the product is not racy here.

Proven rather than assumed, because the window is sub-millisecond and a
passing run proves nothing: widening it gave 10/10 red with the exact #1919
signature, and the fix is green with the widening still in place, so the
antagonist can no longer co-schedule. Full suite 10662 tests, all green,
ParallelStaticStateGuardTest included. Both surefire lists updated, since that
guard requires a parallel-excluded class to appear in the sequential list.

Worth recording: -Dtest bypasses the POM excludes, so it forces excluded
classes back into the parallel phase and cannot validate a routing fix. Only a
full-suite run can.

ci: guard the two false-green paths that reviews found this session

Rule 4 — the three k3d cases only fail closed on a missing image because the
step running the harness exports REQUIRE_CLUSTERED_IMAGE and
REQUIRE_WEBHOOK_IMAGE. Delete those two lines and CI silently records a SKIP:
green, testing nothing, no guard tripped. Those exports became load-bearing
for three tests one commit ago, so assert they are there. Keyed on behaviour
rather than the filename — any step that invokes the harness without setting
SKIP_HELM_TESTS=true must export both — so a rename or a second helm-running
step is covered automatically, and the docker-only step stays exempt.

Rule 5 — a mockserver-core test that reaches
LogManager.getLogManager().readConfiguration performs a JVM-global handler
reset and must be in the sequential-includes list. This is the invariant the
flake in the previous commit violated. ParallelStaticStateGuardTest cannot
catch it: it only checks classes already excluded from the parallel phase, and
these were in neither list.

Rule 5's signatures are narrow on purpose, because a rule that gets silenced by
allow-list entries is worse than no rule. Bare logLevel(, disableSystemOut( and
disableLogging( are rejected — they match the per-instance Configuration
builder, which has no global effect, and would have falsely flagged four
legitimately parallel tests; only the static ConfigurationProperties-qualified
form counts. Bare Class.forName( is rejected too, since it matches a test
iterating already-loaded classes and another with java.lang.Runtime inside a
JavaScript template string; only the three-argument initialize=true form is the
fresh-clinit pattern, and it hits exactly the two culprits with nothing else.

Both rules fail closed on an empty corpus rather than passing having scanned
nothing, and both carry the allow-list rot check the existing rules use. Each
was proven by reintroducing the defect it targets and confirming the build reds
naming the offending file.

Rule 5 depends on the sequential registration in the preceding commit, so that
one lands first and every commit here is green in isolation. The doc records
what each rule does not catch — it has already been corrected once for
overclaiming, and a guard that oversells its coverage is the very thing these
rules exist to stop.

fix(ci): stage the clustered libs inside the reactor, not a second Maven run

The container-test image producer added in e8386bf65 broke master on the first
clean agent. It ran two Maven invocations: the first built the three modules
with -am and package, the second ran dependency:copy-dependencies standalone
for mockserver-state-infinispan. A standalone -pl run starts a fresh reactor
with no in-session siblings, so it has to resolve mockserver-core, -netty and
-client-java 7.5.1-SNAPSHOT from a cache — and package never writes them
anywhere. Result: "Could not find artifact ...:SNAPSHOT", an empty
clustered-libs, and 2 of 3 artifact sets uploaded.

Local verification passed because this machine's ~/.m2 already held those
SNAPSHOTs from earlier builds. That is the ~/.m2 pollution false green, and
the review could not have caught it — it is invisible in the diff and only
appears when the repository is empty.

Bind copy-dependencies to the infinispan module's package phase behind a
clustered-libs profile and run one reactor invocation. copy-dependencies then
operates on the already-resolved dependency set, so the siblings come from the
in-session reactor and no cache is consulted. One invocation has no
cross-invocation state to get wrong.

The profile lives in that module's own pom, which is the point: an -am second
invocation or a CLI-appended goal would run copy-dependencies for netty and
the webhook too and pollute clustered-libs with their dependencies. Switching
the first invocation to install would fix resolution by writing SNAPSHOTs into
a cache shared across builds on a reused agent — trading this bug for a
contamination source.

Proven the way the original was not: with org.mock-server absent from the
repository the pre-fix path reproduces the exact CI error, and the post-fix
single reactor succeeds with all three artifact sets and clustered-libs at 160
jars. The output matches what build_clustered_docker assembles for local dev —
same includeScope, same excludeGroupIds, module jar copied in after.

Sibling producers checked: node-launcher-build-jar.sh is a single invocation;
the java-*-test.sh steps do a self-contained in-step -am install before their
second invocation, which is not this fault.

test(core): stop the serializer tests fetching a spec over the internet

The 7.6.0 release build died here. ExpectationSerializerTest referenced the
bundled petstore OpenAPI spec by its raw.githubusercontent.com URL, and
deserializeArray() genuinely loads the spec to generate example bodies — so
this was a live network fetch on every ordinary build, not just a string in a
fixture. GitHub rate-limited it (HTTP 429), the read timed out after 18.67s,
and the release failed after prepare had already tagged and pushed.

Two methods did this, not just the one the stack trace named:
shouldAllowSingleOpenAPIObjectForArray and
shouldAllowMixedExpectationTypesForArray. Either could have red any build at
any time.

Both now resolve the byte-identical copy already on the test classpath —
verified identical by MD5 across all four in-repo copies — which is the same
local reference HttpStateTest and JsonSchemaExpectationValidatorTest already
use. The assertions are untouched and still check the generated example
bodies, so they still prove the spec was loaded and resolved.

Proven by running under sandbox-exec with network-outbound denied: 44 tests
pass with no outbound request, and a positive control confirms the sandbox
really blocks that host (curl gets nothing inside it, 301 outside). Pointing
resolution at a different local spec makes both tests fail, so they still
depend on the content they name.

Nothing intentional was lost. Neither test existed to cover remote-URL spec
loading — they are serialization tests that happened to name a URL. If that
product feature ever needs direct coverage it should use a local endpoint, not
a live one, because a test that reaches the public internet is a build that
can fail for reasons unrelated to the code.

release: versioned site 7-6.mock-server.com

Recovers the versioned-site step that did not run during the 7.6.0 release.
create-versioned-site was left at its default of no, which is correct for a
patch and wrong for a minor, so versioned-site.sh skipped creating the new
subdomain.

The consequence was worse than a missing archive. main_bucket_name resolves to
the bucket for latest_version, which was still 7-5, so the 7.6.0 docs publish
targeted aws-website-mockserver-7-5 — the bucket serving 7-5.mock-server.com.
Because website.sh syncs with --delete, the 7.5 archive was not merely
overwritten but replaced, and 7-5.mock-server.com served 7.6.0 content.

Applied by hand in the order the script would have, chosen so the main
distribution was never pointed at an empty bucket: create the 7-6 bucket and
distribution while latest_version still read 7-5, copy the content across
(24,212 objects), then move latest_version to 7-6, then invalidate.

7-5 was then restored by rebuilding the Jekyll site and syncing it back with
the same flags the release uses. The source is commit 898900420, "release:
update version references to 7.5.0" — NOT the mockserver-7.5.0 tag, which
still carries mockserver_version 7.4.0 in _config.yml because prepare tags
before update-version-references runs. Building from the tag would have
published a site labelled 7.4.0.

S3 versioning is not enabled on any site bucket, so a version restore was not
available; the rebuild is faithful because the bucket content is exactly the
Jekyll output plus the four excluded paths, which the 7.6.0 sync never touched.

Verified at the origin: 7-5 serves 7.5.0, 7-6 serves 7.6.0.

fix(release): derive create-versioned-site instead of asking an operator

The 7.6.0 release ran with create-versioned-site=no — the input's default.
The operator left it alone, which is correct for a patch and destructive for a
minor.

main_bucket_name follows latest_version, which was still 7-5, so "main"
resolved to the bucket serving 7-5.mock-server.com and the docs publish went
there. website.sh syncs with --delete, so the 7.5 archive was not shadowed but
destroyed, and that subdomain served 7.6.0 docs until it was rebuilt by hand.
Nothing failed. The pipeline was green.

The correct value is fully determined by RELEASE_VERSION and OLD_VERSION, so
asking a human for it adds a failure mode and no information. Derive it in
require_release_inputs, the one chokepoint every release script passes
through, and default the Buildkite input to auto so leaving the dropdown alone
— exactly what happened — now does the right thing.

An explicit yes or no is still accepted, but only as a confirmation: it must
agree with the derived value or the run fails closed, naming the consequence.
That covers both destructive directions, a major/minor with no and a patch
with yes. The one-directional guard in prepare.sh becomes dead code and is
removed. The check runs before the pom bump, the tag and the push, on every
entry point including a standalone component run used for recovery.

Also adds the regression test the guard did not have. test-all.sh could only
assert exit 0, so the contradiction guard — the entire defence against this
incident — was covered by nothing. Four must-fail cases are now asserted
directly. Proven by disabling the contradiction branch: the three contradiction
cases go red and the unknown-value case stays green, so the assertions
discriminate rather than merely pass.

The release-process runbook now says to verify the PREVIOUS version's
subdomain still serves the OLD version. A checklist that only confirms the new
subdomain exists would not have caught this. Its worked examples were also
internally inconsistent (next-version below release-version) and are now a
coherent 7.5.0 to 7.6.0 set.

build(deps): stop Dependabot proposing TypeScript 7 for the UI

typescript-eslint pins its peer range to `typescript >=4.8.4 <6.1.0`, so a
TypeScript 7 bump fails at `npm ci` with ERESOLVE before lint or typecheck can
run. Nothing else in the tree raises that ceiling — the npm group PR does not
touch typescript-eslint, and bumping typescript alone cannot resolve it. The
upgrade is unmergeable until typescript-eslint ships support for the new
native-compiler major, which is substantial upstream work with no date.

Ignoring 7.x stops a guaranteed-red PR being reopened on every 7.x release.
The comment records why, and the specific condition to revisit under, so this
is a decision someone can re-evaluate rather than a rule with no rationale —
an ignore whose reason is lost becomes permanent by accident.

Closes #2547. Note that closing a Dependabot PR makes it skip that exact
version permanently, which is why it is right only for an indefinite block
like this one and wrong for anything merely waiting on a rebase.

test(llm): pin the published provider contract to the server enum

Community PR #2545 added a working LLM provider, wired every server-side
registration point correctly, and still left the published contract behind —
the OpenAPI spec and the Node client's type union both said 14 providers while
the server had 15. Every gate stayed green, so it took a human review to spot.

Nothing could have caught it. ProviderSchemaEnumParityTest pins only the
internal schema, and the Node drift test compares mockServer.d.ts against the
OpenAPI spec. Since a contributor naturally updates neither consumer file, the
two drift from the server together, agree with each other, and pass. Comparing
two copies only proves they match, not that either is right.

So the authority here is the compiled Provider enum, read by reflection, and
both consumer artefacts are checked against it independently and in both
directions. There is no shared intermediate file, so lock-step drift cannot
hide. Pinning the .d.ts against the spec in the Node suite would have rebuilt
the same hole one layer along.

Both extractors fail closed on an empty parse — the specific way a parity test
passes while comparing nothing, which this repo has shipped before. The
messages are written for an outside contributor: they name the provider, the
file, the structural location and the fix, and deliberately carry no line
numbers, which would go stale as the files grow.

Only the website copy of the spec is pinned; OpenApiSpecSyncTest already
asserts the embedded copy is byte-identical, so the other cannot drift alone.

This is the gate that should have failed instead of a review comment, and I
have told the contributor it is being added.

build(deps): take examples out of the reactor so Dependabot can parse it again

mockserver/pom.xml declared <module>../examples/java</module>. There is no
repo-root pom, so that module escaped Dependabot's directory: "/mockserver".
During grouped update creation Dependabot re-parses a scoped file subset, found
no top-level pom, and aborted with "No pom.xml!".

Zero grouped Maven PRs have ever been created for the core reactor. Not one
since 2026-06-03, when the examples were unified; the self-contained
mockserver-maven-plugin sibling produced them normally throughout, which is why
a full-looking PR list hid it. Core Java minor and patch bumps have not been
proposed for two and a half months. Alerts were unaffected — the dependency
graph submission is separate and healthy — so this is about updates not being
offered, not vulnerabilities going unseen.

Examples now build standalone. Their parent is already
../../mockserver/pom.xml, so a second Maven invocation resolves them once the
reactor is installed; that invocation lives in the same container as the
reactor build, gated on it having passed, with its exit folded into the build
result. Examples ceasing to be built silently was the main risk of this change,
so that gate is the point of it. examples/java also gains its own Dependabot
block — those dependencies have never had coverage.

BREAKING BEHAVIOUR: org.mock-server:mockserver-examples is no longer published
to Maven Central. It was, every release — GPG-signed, with a documented JPMS
automatic module name — because it was a reactor module and the release deploys
the whole reactor. Removing it from the reactor stops that, so the unpublish is
made explicit rather than accidental: skipPublishing=true guards a future
re-add, and the changelog states the impact and the remedy. Previously
published versions stay resolvable on Central forever.

That guard has to be skipPublishing, not maven.deploy.skip. This project
publishes with central-publishing-maven-plugin, whose lifecycle participant
disables maven-deploy-plugin and binds its own goal to the deploy phase.
Verified against the pinned 0.11.0 jar: no reference to maven.deploy.skip
anywhere in it, ${skipPublishing} is the only skip gate, and it filters
per-artifact so it cannot abort the wider release.

Six review iterations, five of them blocked, and every block was a false
premise rather than faulty logic: that the job broke yesterday (June), that
examples was never shipped (published every release), that maven.deploy.skip
prevented publication (wrong plugin), that the false mechanism had been purged
(one file still carried it), and a .snyk "fix" resting on a cause nobody had
checked. Each was plausible, written into comments and docs, and reused as
justification. The .snyk change is reverted and its documentation now states
only what was observed.

ci: give fork pull requests a test signal, in an environment with nothing to steal

Community PRs got no automated tests at all. Buildkite sets
build_pull_request_forks: false, and must keep it: those agents hold IAM roles,
the Docker socket and Secrets Manager access to the Maven Central signing key,
Docker Hub, npm, PyPI, RubyGems, the GitHub token and the release TOTP seed.
Building a fork PR there runs a contributor's code beside all of it. This came
up on #2545, where the author had no way to know whether their change worked
and reviewers had nothing to look at.

The fix is not to relax that setting but to run the tests somewhere empty. A
GitHub Actions workflow triggered by pull_request runs fork code with a
read-only token and no repository secrets, so there is nothing in the
environment worth attacking. Never pull_request_target, which runs
attacker-controlled code in the base-repo context with secrets.

An isolated Buildkite agent pool was considered and rejected as not-easy rather
than not-better. Two holes make "an agent without secrets" insufficient: the
pipeline definition is uploaded from the branch, so a fork controls the script
that emits every step's queue routing; and all queues share one cluster and one
agent token, so Docker-socket access on any agent reaches release jobs. Doing
it properly needs a separate cluster, token, ASG and a pipeline defined outside
the repo. Worth revisiting if fork contributions become common; the failure
mode if rushed is a leaked signing key.

Scope is completeness over speed, because slow feedback beats none: the whole
reactor, unit and integration tests, plus the standalone examples build,
1.5-3h. Every Docker-gated suite genuinely runs, since they are all
emulator-backed rather than cloud-credentialed.

Only the three privileged transparent-proxy suites are excluded, and the
exclusion is real rather than asserted. An earlier draft claimed
RUN_TRANSPARENT_PROXY_E2E gated them; that variable is read only by a Buildkite
shell step, and Maven honours nothing of the sort, so they would have run and
plausibly false-red on a hosted runner. They now go through
-Dfailsafe.excludesFile, which augments the POM includes and leaves Surefire
alone. Not -Dit.test: measured, it ran 856 classes of which 855 were unit
tests, and it silently disables excludesFile as well.

A fail-closed assert-suite-ran step covers the case that matters most here — if
a runner image ever lacked Docker the Testcontainers suites would assumeTrue-
skip and the job would otherwise go green having tested far less.

test(netty): stop asserting a socket is open against a server built to close it

The fork-PR workflow went red on its first run: one failure in 2231, in
ThirdPartyStreamingClientConformanceIntegrationTest. Buildkite passed the same
commit, so the suite looked environment-specific. It is not. It is a real race
the hosted runner merely lost.

Java-WebSocket's connectBlocking returns connectLatch.await(...) &&
engine.isOpen(), and that latch is counted down by BOTH onWebsocketOpen and
onWebsocketClose. Line 333 was the only websocket handshake site whose server
is configured withCloseConnection(true) — so it asked "is the socket still open
right now?" of a connection designed to close right now. The server delivers
"bye" and closes, exactly as promised; if that lands before isOpen() is read,
connectBlocking returns false and a bare assert fails in ~12ms. Buildkite has
been winning that race, not avoiding it, and would have started flaking.

Assert the observable outcome instead: the opened latch, counted down in onOpen
and never un-set by a later close. The handshake always precedes the close when
it succeeds, so this is race-free by construction rather than by timing. The
assertions that do the real verification — the message arrived, the close was
orderly, not an abnormal drop — are unchanged. The assert also gains a message;
a contributor previously got a bare AssertionError with nothing to act on.

Proven by forcing the losing interleaving: isOpen() reads false while the
opened latch reads true, reproducibly. Worth recording that the obvious proof
does not work — forty iterations of the real connectBlocking won 40/40 on this
machine, so a loop would have shown nothing and could easily have been mistaken
for evidence.

Also stops one failure producing three red steps. The standalone-examples step
and the Docker-gated suite assertion now run only when the reactor succeeded.
Previously a reactor failure left examples unable to resolve SNAPSHOTs that
were never installed, and made assert-suite-ran report "the suite did not run"
for mockserver-blob-s3 — which has a test-scope dependency on the failed netty
module and so was simply never built. That pointed contributors at a Docker
problem they did not have. Fail-closed is preserved: with no Docker the suites
assumeTrue-skip, Maven still exits 0, the reactor succeeds, the assertion runs
and reds.

test(blob): stop the s3 registry leaking between classes in a shared fork

The fork-PR workflow went red a second time, on a different test that the
first failure had been hiding: mockserver-blob-s3 has a test-scope dependency
on mockserver-netty, so when netty failed the whole module was skipped and this
never ran. Fix one, reveal the next.

S3ExpectationPersistenceReloadTest starts a real server with
blobStoreType("s3"). That makes StateBackendFactory discover and register the
s3 factory in a JVM-global registry, and the teardown stopped the server and
the MinIO container without resetting it. Every class in the module shares one
reused fork, and surefire's default filesystem run order is not stable across
machines, so whenever that class landed first S3BlobStoreRegistrarTest's
"s3 should not be registered before register()" precondition read inherited
state and failed. Buildkite has been getting a lucky order.

Both halves are wrong, so fix both. The leaker resets the registry on teardown
and leaves the JVM as it found it. The registrar tests scrub on ENTRY as well
as exit, so the precondition holds whatever ran before — defending only on the
way out protects the next test, not yourself.

The gcs and azure registrar tests are byte-for-byte the same shape and were
passing only because their modules contain no equivalent leaker. Both get the
same entry scrub rather than waiting for someone to add a full-server test
there and rediscover this.

Not fixed by pinning runOrder. An order-dependent test that passes because the
order suits it is the thing that keeps being found here; the defect is trusting
inherited global state, not the order that exposed it.

Reproduced locally before fixing: forcing the losing order with
-Dsurefire.runOrder=reversealphabetical reproduces the exact CI failure, and
the same command passes with the fix. All three modules green in both orders —
33, 26 and 32 tests.

build(deps): stop two Dependabot ceilings silently suppressing every update

Two open PRs failed for real reasons, and chasing them found two ignores that
had quietly stopped Dependabot proposing anything at all.

#2554 offered checkstyle 13, which ships Java 21 bytecode against this
project's Java 17 floor and can never pass. A checkstyle ceiling already
existed for /mockserver, but the PR came from /examples/java. That pom
declares the reactor as its parent, so Dependabot scanning the child directory
resolves up, edits the parent pom, and escapes an ignore written only for the
parent's own block. Mirror the parent-declared ceilings into both blocks that
reach the parent, and record why they must stay in sync. infinispan-core is
deliberately not mirrored: it lives in a module pom, off that chain, so
copying it would suppress updates nobody meant to freeze.

#2555 (guava 33.6.0 -> 33.7.0) trips DependencyConvergence: guava-parent
33.7.0-jre declares jspecify 1.0.1 while graphql-java 26.0 and its
java-dataloader 6.0.0 declare 1.0.0, and nothing managed the version. Pin
jspecify 1.0.1 so the two paths converge whenever either side moves. Verified
by reproducing the collision — guava 33.7.0 without the pin fails with #2555's
exact error, with the pin it converges, and the pin is a no-op on today's tree.
guava itself is left alone for Dependabot to land.

The suppressions are the more valuable find. graphql-java was ceilinged at
>=25.0.0 while the pom had moved to 26.0, so the in-use version sat above its
own ceiling and no candidate could ever be proposed — no patches, no security
fixes. And the typescript >=7.0.0 ignore added two days ago went onto the npm
block shared by the UI and the published Node packages, freezing
mockserver-client-node, which was already on 7.0.2 and carries no
typescript-eslint, so the peer conflict behind that ignore never applied to it.

Both were invisible. A ceiling that blocks everything and a ceiling that works
produce exactly the same observable: no pull requests. That invariant is now
written where each ignore lives — keep the ceiling above the version in use,
and keep directory-specific constraints in directory-specific blocks, which is
why mockserver-ui now has its own block just as mockserver-vscode already did.

A sweep of every remaining versioned ignore against its in-use version found no
others. The stale prose that helped hide this is corrected too: the pom claimed
graphql-java was "pinned to the 22.x line" while pinning 26.0, and security.md
documented the old ceiling and a java-dataloader version four majors out of date.

ci: auto-merge Dependabot minor and patch updates, fail-closed, in dry-run

Around 2.6 Dependabot PRs land a day, spiking at 8. Merging them by hand is
the kind of repetitive judgement that gets rubber-stamped, which is worse than
automating it deliberately.

GitHub's native auto-merge was rejected, and the reason is the whole design.
Native waits only on the checks named in branch protection's required list.
Add a scanner tomorrow, rename a job, restructure a pipeline, and unless
someone updates that list it merges past the new check silently. Two live
instances of exactly that shape were found in this repo yesterday: a
graphql-java ceiling sitting below its own in-use version, and a typescript
ignore covering a package it was never meant to reach. Both looked like
working controls. Both produced silence.

So this reads the checks that actually exist on the head commit and requires
them to pass. No list to maintain, and a check added next year is covered the
day it appears.

It reads BOTH APIs, which is the detail that matters. Check runs carry CodeQL;
commit statuses carry buildkite/mockserver and both Snyk scans. A workflow
calling only /check-runs sees six green results and merges past the build and
the vulnerability scanner while looking entirely correct.

Skipped and neutral check runs are non-blocking — the fork-only test workflow
is always skipped on an in-repo branch, so demanding literal success from every
run would merge nothing, ever. That leniency is safe because it cannot reach
the checks that matter: commit statuses have only error, failure, pending and
success, so Buildkite and Snyk are structurally incapable of reporting a
non-blocking state. The docs record that assumption and what to revisit if
either ever migrates to the Checks API.

Everything else fails closed: zero checks found, any pending or failed or
unrecognised result, an API error, unknown mergeability, a draft, a fork head,
an author who is not dependabot[bot]. Majors are excluded structurally rather
than by parsing a title — every Dependabot group here contains only minor and
patch, so majors arrive ungrouped and cannot match the group branch pattern.
Security updates arrive ungrouped too and are deliberately left for a human.

Runs on a schedule with no PR-controlled input, checks out nothing, uses no
third-party actions, and merges by PR number pinned to the SHA it validated.
A write-scoped workflow is only acceptable while no PR content influences what
it executes.

Ships with dry-run ON. It logs what it would merge and why it declined the
rest; flip DEFAULT_DRY_RUN when the decisions look right. A merge bot's first
act should not be merging.

ci: let Dependabot's distroless digest bumps auto-merge, on two signals

The dry-run against ten live PRs refused six of them: distroless digest bumps
like "bump distroless/java17 from `1c6329f` to `90003c9`". A digest has no
semver, so it matches neither minor nor patch, falls outside the group, and the
structural major-exclusion correctly rejects it. Behaving as designed, but the
design excluded the highest-volume and most routine class there is — a pinned
tag being rebuilt upstream, usually to patch it.

Grouping them in dependabot.yml was built first and then abandoned, and the
reason is worth recording: Dependabot's digest grouping is inconsistent. A
distroless digest has previously landed inside docker-minor-and-patch, while
today's six arrive ungrouped despite being group-eligible. So a new group might
or might not capture them, and that could not be demonstrated without running
Dependabot for real. Its failure direction was always safe — refuse — but
shipping a control we cannot verify is the thing this workflow exists to avoid.

Instead, a second acceptance path requiring two independent Dependabot-generated
signals together: the branch shape, and a title carrying a backticked hex pair.
Scoped to distroless, which is the load-bearing part rather than belt-and-braces
— the title signal alone is not sufficient, because a date-tagged bump such as
"from 20240115 to 20240220" is all hex and matches it. Only the branch scope
rejects that.

The scope is safe on evidence rather than habit: all nine gcr.io/distroless
FROM lines in this repo pin non-semver tags (nonroot, debug-nonroot, latest), so
a from-hex-to-hex title on a distroless PR can only be a digest. A tag move
would fail the hex-tail branch pattern regardless, and the author and fork gates
run before either path is reached.

Deliberately narrower than "docker digests auto-merge": only distroless
qualifies, and any other digest-only image stays manual. The docs say so, along
with the grouping-inconsistency finding, so the scope is not widened later by
someone assuming it was meant to be general.

dependabot.yml is untouched. Dry-run stays on.

ci: guard the auto-merge gate's four properties, then arm it

This is the change that removes the human from the merge path: from here a
scheduled sweep merges Dependabot PRs into master every three hours. Everything
else in it exists to make that safe.

The gate's safety rests on four things, and each looks like clutter to someone
tidying up later: the /distroless/ scope on the digest branch pattern, a
trailing hex-run floor of at least seven, the title cross-check that keeps
path B a two-signal AND, and update-types staying within minor and patch for
every group whose name path A accepts. Drop any one and more merges than
intended, silently. Rule 6 turns each into a red build.

The scope is the one people will assume is redundant. It is not: a datetime-
tagged bump like "from 202401151200 to 202402201200" satisfies the title regex,
because a long enough date token is indistinguishable from hex. Only the scope
rejects it.

Rule 6 was reviewed and one fail-open found: the group parser recorded a group
only when the name line ended in a colon, so a group written inline as
`name: {}` was never checked — and `{}` defaults to every update type, majors
included. The other groups kept the empty-sweep guard quiet, so it passed.
Inline empty mappings are now recorded with no types and fail. Proven by
rewriting a real group that way: caught, named, and green again on restore.

Also corrects an example I had repeated in three files. "from 20240115 to
20240220" does not match the title regex — an eight-digit token leaves nothing
for the closing-backtick position, so the illustration did not demonstrate the
property it claimed. I first "verified" it by adding backticks Dependabot only
writes for digests, which made it appear to match. The reviewer was right and
the check was wrong. Nine or more characters is the real threshold, so the
example is now a datetime tag.

Armed by flipping DEFAULT_DRY_RUN, with the workflow_dispatch input still
defaulting to dry-run, so a manual probe stays safe while the schedule merges.

fix(rust): stop the clippy gate failing on unchanged source after a rust:1 toolchain drift

The mockserver-rust pipeline lints in a container pulled from the floating
`rust:1` tag. That tag moved to clippy 1.98.0, whose `needless_late_init` now
also flags late-initialised `let` chains assigned across an `if`/`else if`
sequence. `resolve_platform()` had two (`os_name`/`ext`, and `arch`), so under
`-D warnings` the crate stopped compiling on code nobody had touched: master
build #638 passed this exact source, #639 fifteen hours later did not, and it
also failed an unrelated Dependabot PR that only changed a Java dependency.

Both chains become initialising `if`/`else` expressions — a tuple for the
jointly-assigned `os_name`/`ext` pair — which is the rewrite clippy suggests.
The diverging `else` arms still `return Err(...)` and coerce as `!`. Behaviour
is identical: same platform tokens, same error messages, same `Platform`.

Verified under the real clippy 1.98.0 inside `rust:1` (original reproduces as
exit 101 with two errors, the fix is clean) plus `cargo test --all-targets`.
A locally-installed clippy older than 1.98 cannot see this lint, so the
container is required to reproduce it.

fix(llm): emit a valid cost-budget 429 body on comma-decimal locales

`LlmCostBudgetMonitor` hand-builds the `cost_budget_exceeded` JSON body and
formatted its numeric fields with `String.format("%.6f", ...)` and no explicit
`Locale`, so it followed the JVM default. On a comma-decimal locale — de, fr,
es, it, pt-BR, ru, and a container inherits the host/env locale — it emitted

    "cumulative_cost_usd":1,500000,

which is not valid JSON. Clients parsing the 429 got a parse error rather than
a structured budget signal, so the feature silently failed for a large part of
the world. The same defect rendered the optimisation report's saving text as
`$0,00` and mis-grouped token counts, and made
`LlmOptimisationBriefRendererTest.matchesGoldenFile` fail on whichever agent
had a non-US locale — which is how it surfaced, after red-herring-failing an
unrelated Dependabot pull request.

All ten locale-sensitive `String.format` sites now pass `Locale.ROOT`, matching
the convention already in `LlmOptimisationBriefRenderer`. `%x` sites are left
alone: `java.util.Formatter` does not localise `o`/`x`/`X`.

`LocaleInsensitiveNumberFormattingTest` forces `Locale.GERMANY` and asserts the
429 body parses and that `cumulative_cost_usd`/`budget_usd` are JSON numbers;
without the fix it fails with `JsonParseException`. It mutates the JVM-global
default locale, so it is registered in both the parallel-excludes and the
sequential-includes.

fix(templates): read request header names case-insensitively in templates

HTTP field names are case-insensitive (RFC 9110 §5.1) and MockServer's matchers
already treat them so, but response and forward templates reached the headers
through plain map semantics: Velocity's Uberspector turns $request.headers.host
into get("host"), Mustache's fetcher calls containsKey then get, and a
JavaScript template receives a JSON.parse'd plain object where
request.headers.host is a native property lookup. A template asking for
$request.headers.Host therefore missed a header the client sent as host, and
vice-versa — and which one you got depended on the protocol, because HTTP/2
lower-cases field names on the wire while HTTP/1.1 preserves the client's
casing, so one template silently produced different output over the two
protocols (issue #2575).

Two additive mechanisms, one per engine family:

- Velocity and Mustache go through CaseInsensitiveHeaderMap, a LinkedHashMap
  subclass. An exact-case hit is returned unchanged; only a miss falls back to
  a case-insensitive resolution. Iteration keeps the original wire casing in
  arrival order, so loop-over-headers templates and Jackson serialisation are
  unaffected — unlike a TreeMap with a case-insensitive comparator, which would
  reorder alphabetically.

- JavaScript templates get a pure-JS Proxy over request.headers with get/has
  traps, installed in PolyglotRunner's generated prelude for all three template
  shapes. It wraps the parsed plain object, not a host object, and scans only
  Object.keys(target), so it exposes no prototype member and creates no new
  route to Java.type/Function/eval. ownKeys is deliberately not trapped, so
  Object.keys, JSON.stringify, spread and for-in still enumerate exactly the
  original keys with no duplicates.

The map resolves the case-insensitive match by scanning the live entries rather
than maintaining a lower-case index. An index refreshed only from an overridden
put goes stale: HashMap routes putAll, putIfAbsent, merge and compute* straight
at its internal storage without calling put, and the keySet/entrySet views
mutate it directly. Probed against a compiled index-based version, six lookups
desynced — a header inserted via any of those paths was invisible to
case-insensitive lookup, and one removed through a view still reported as
present, which is precisely the failure this change exists to fix. The class is
public and Velocity's Uberspector invokes public methods from template
expressions, so that was reachable. Deriving from the entries cannot go stale by
construction; the scan runs only on a miss and header counts are tens.

One behaviour deliberately changes: when two differently-cased spellings of one
name arrive as separate fields, their values now combine into the first-seen
entry per HTTP's same-name-field rule instead of one silently overwriting the
other, so headers.host[0] gives the first spelling rather than the last.

Headers only — cookie, query-string-parameter and path-parameter names stay
case-sensitive, as their specifications require.

CaseInsensitiveHeaderMapTest locks the four casing combinations, containsKey /
getOrDefault agreement, order and casing preservation, the merge, exact-case
overwrite, remove-by-any-casing, the put-bypassing mutation routes above, and
ordinary-Map equality. Forcing the resolution to never match reds 5 of its 9
cases. Full mockserver-core suite green (8212 parallel + 2472 sequential, no
crashed forks).
