fix(testcontainers): wait on the port-count-independent part of the startup banner

The reported regression in #2580 — that the `started on port:` readiness line is
no longer printed by newer Docker images — could not be reproduced. Running
5.15.0, 7.4.0, 7.5.0, 7.6.0/latest and 7.6.1-SNAPSHOT each emits an identical
`started on port: 1080` that satisfies the reporter's
`Wait.forLogMessage(".*started on port:.*", 1)`. The banner is still produced by
`LifeCycle.startedServer()` and is covered by existing tests. So the server's
logging is deliberately left unchanged here.

Investigating it did surface two real problems, which this fixes.

The banner's wording depends on how many ports were bound:

    started on port: 1080
    started on ports: [1080, 1090]

so a readiness check written against the singular form INCLUDING its trailing
colon silently stops matching the moment a second port is configured. The caller
then blocks until its wait times out, with nothing in the log to say why.

`testcontainers-mockserver` (Rust) hard-coded exactly that string, so it would
hang for any multi-port user. It now waits on `started on port`, the prefix both
forms share. Widening the match is safe: the only other startup lines containing
it are the DNS mock server's, which is disabled by default and bound after the
main port, and HTTP/3's, which reads "started on UDP port" and does not contain
the prefix at all — so this cannot report readiness before the server is
listening. The Rust module is the only consumer in the repository that keys
readiness off the log at all; every other Testcontainers module, and the Docker
HEALTHCHECK, already wait on `PUT /mockserver/status`.

Guarded on both sides. A Rust unit test asserts the readiness string matches real
single- and multi-port banner samples, and fails if the colon is restored.
`JarWithDependenciesLoggingIntegrationTest` now boots the executable jar on two
ports and asserts the prefix survives; asserting the colon form instead makes it
fail on the 60-second timeout, reproducing the downstream hang exactly. Its two
ports are now taken from sockets held open simultaneously, so they cannot collide
and produce a spurious `-serverPort P,P` bind failure.

The Testcontainers documentation now describes both readiness signals and
recommends the status endpoint over the log line, because the banner is logged at
INFO and disappears entirely when `MOCKSERVER_LOG_LEVEL` is raised to WARN —
verified: the line is absent at WARN while `PUT /mockserver/status` still returns
200. That is the most likely explanation for the single-port symptom reported.

Fixes #2580

fix(core): stop concurrent expectation creation silently dropping expectations

Creating expectations in parallel could lose some of them. Every
`PUT /mockserver/expectation` returned 201 with a unique id, yet roughly a
quarter of runs left one or more of those expectations permanently absent from
`retrieveActiveExpectations` — and therefore unmatchable — with nothing logged.
Setting `nioEventLoopThreadCount=1` made the loss disappear entirely, which is
what pointed at the write path rather than the store.

`RequestMatchers.add` was a non-atomic read-modify-write. It inserted the
compiled matcher into the node-local structures (`matcherCacheById`, the
`CircularPriorityQueue`, `expectationRequestDefinitions`) first, then wrote the
backend key-value store, then ran an eviction reconcile. That reconcile,
`trimEvictedFromBackend`, infers "the backend evicted something" purely from a
size comparison and deletes every cached id missing from a backend snapshot.

Control-plane adds genuinely run in parallel — one per connection, across the
`nioEventLoopThreadCount` Netty worker threads (default 5) — despite a contract
comment asserting they were externally serialized. So one thread's trim could
observe a second thread's just-inserted local matcher before that thread's
backend write had landed, conclude it had been evicted, and delete it from every
node-local structure. The victim's own later trim then saw `local <= backend` and
never rebuilt it. `reconcileFromBackend` was already synchronized, but the local
mutation and the backend write sat outside that monitor, so the synchronized trim
was reading torn state.

The fix restores a real single-writer contract: every node-local cache mutator —
`add`, `update`, `reset`, the `clear` family, `clearByNamespace`,
`applyConfigurationCapacity` and `removeHttpRequestMatcher` — is serialized on
the same instance monitor `reconcileFromBackend` already used, so no mutator can
observe another's half-applied state, including against a clustered backend's
cross-node invalidation callback. Reusing that monitor rather than introducing a
new lock is what keeps the backend's synchronous same-thread re-entry safe, and
avoids creating a second lock ordering. `add`, `update` and `reset` fire their
listener notifications after releasing the monitor so the file-persistence write
lock and its disk I/O do not run underneath it. The read and matching hot path is
deliberately left unsynchronized, so per-request throughput is unaffected. The
stale contract javadoc has been rewritten to describe what is now guaranteed.

Patching only the size heuristic would have been wrong: the heuristic is the
trigger, but the non-atomic local-then-backend-then-trim sequence would have
stayed racy against the invalidation callback.

`RequestMatchersConcurrentAddTest` covers it both ways: a deterministic seam that
parks one add between its local insert and its backend write while another runs
its trim, and an 8-thread x 64-expectation hammer. Both fail against the pre-fix
code with a dropped expectation and pass after it. The absence of any test
creating expectations concurrently is why this shipped.

Verified with the full mockserver-core two-phase suite (8214 + 2472, no failures)
and the mockserver-state-infinispan suite (115 tests), the latter including the
two-node cross-invalidation cases that exercise the clustered callback path.

Fixes #2579

Revert "fix(core): stop concurrent expectation creation silently dropping expectations"

This reverts commit 98ab5d8de.

It deadlocks the clustered backend. Serializing the node-local mutators on the
`reconcileFromBackend` monitor means `add` now holds that monitor across
`expectationBackend.put`, which for Infinispan is a blocking distributed call
that must round-trip to the other node — while this node's own invalidation
listener needs the same monitor to make progress. `ClusteredTwoNodeTest` and
`ClusteredExpectationPersistenceReloadTest` hang in
`RequestMatchers.add -> InfinispanKeyValueStore.put -> Cache.compute` and are
killed by the 60-second test timeout: 8 errors on master build 1997.

The local run that cleared this suite (115 tests) did not reproduce it, and the
pre-commit review reasoned that holding the monitor across the backend put
introduced no new lock ordering because `reconcileFromBackend` already held it
while reading the backend. That reasoning was wrong: reading under the monitor
is not the same as blocking on a distributed write under it.

Reverting to get master green rather than fixing forward, because the correct
fix is a design change — the local cache mutation must be made atomic with
respect to the eviction reconcile WITHOUT holding a lock across a network call —
and that deserves proper work rather than a follow-up patch on a red master.

Issue #2579 is genuinely broken and is being reopened; the diagnosis in the
reverted commit message stands and the regression test comes back with the
redesigned fix.

fix(core): stop concurrent expectation creation silently dropping expectations

Creating expectations in parallel could lose some of them. Every
`PUT /mockserver/expectation` returned 201 with a unique id, yet roughly a
quarter of runs left one or more permanently absent from
`retrieveActiveExpectations` — and so unmatchable — with nothing logged.
`nioEventLoopThreadCount=1` made the loss vanish, which pointed at the write
path rather than the store.

`trimEvictedFromBackend` infers "the backend evicted something" from a size
comparison and then deletes every cached id missing from a backend snapshot.
Control-plane adds genuinely run in parallel, one per connection across the
Netty worker threads, despite a contract comment claiming they were externally
serialized. So one thread's reconcile could see a second thread's just-inserted
local matcher before that thread's backend write landed, conclude it had been
evicted, and delete it. The victim's own later reconcile saw fewer local entries
than backend entries and never rebuilt it.

The fix corrects that inference rather than serializing around it. Ids are
registered in a reference-counted in-flight registry before any local mutation
and deregistered once their backend write returns, and both reconcile paths
exclude registered ids from eviction. The registry is reference-counted, not a
set, so two concurrent writers of the same id both hold protection until both
complete — otherwise the first writer's failure could lift protection while the
second's write was still outstanding.

Both `trimEvictedFromBackend` and `reconcileClusteredScan` snapshot in the order
cachedIds, then in-flight ids, then backend ids, and compute evictions over the
cachedIds snapshot rather than the live map. That order is load-bearing: if an
id is in cachedIds its registration preceded that snapshot, so by the in-flight
snapshot it is either still registered, or was deregistered — which happens only
after its backend write returned, hence before the backend snapshot, so it
appears there. Either way it cannot be evicted. Each method carries its own
proof rather than cross-referencing the other.

The node-local structures are mutated only inside short critical sections that
contain no backend call, no listener notification and no blocking I/O, which
also fixes concurrent corruption of the non-thread-safe CircularHashMap and
CircularPriorityQueue. The read and matching path stays unsynchronized, so
per-request throughput is unaffected.

An earlier attempt at this fix was reverted. It serialized the mutators on the
reconcile monitor, which made `add` hold that monitor across the backend write —
a blocking distributed call on the clustered backend — and deadlocked against
the node's own invalidation listener, hanging the two-node suite on CI. The
design here deliberately never holds a lock across any backend call; a
regression test asserts that directly by using a backend whose put blocks until
a concurrent add completes, which deadlocks under the reverted approach.

Guarded by `RequestMatchersConcurrentAddTest`: a deterministic drop
reproduction, an 8-thread by 64-expectation hammer, the deadlock guard above,
and a clustered-path test that parks a reconcile holding a pre-add backend
snapshot while an add completes. All four fail against the code they guard.
Verified with mockserver-core (8216 + 2472) and mockserver-state-infinispan
(115, no timeout signature).

Fixes #2579

feat(retrieve): filter /mockserver/retrieve by expectation id

PUT /mockserver/retrieve now accepts an expectation id ({"id": "..."}) in the
request body in place of a request matcher, matching what PUT /mockserver/clear
and PUT /mockserver/verify have always accepted. Retrieve was the only one of
the three control-plane matchers that could not be pointed at a single
expectation.

Behaviour by type:

- active_expectations returns ONLY the expectation with that id. It filters on
  the id itself rather than on the request definition the id resolves to:
  matching by request definition would also return every other expectation
  whose matcher matches the same request, and would miss expectations (OpenAPI,
  JSON-schema or regex matchers) whose own request definition does not match
  their own matcher.
- requests, request_responses, recorded_expectations and logs return the
  entries matching that expectation's request, exactly as verify by expectation
  id matches them.
- An unknown id is rejected with 400 "No expectation found with id ...". The
  resolution path is fail-closed: a filter that resolves to nothing raises
  rather than degrading into "match everything".

The id body and the request-matcher body are unambiguous, because both JSON
schemas set additionalProperties: false and only the expectation id schema
allows (and requires) an id property. The id is therefore parsed BEFORE the
body reaches RequestDefinitionSerializer, which rejects {"id": "..."} on schema
validation. clear() and retrieve() now share that parsing in one
parseExpectationId(body) helper rather than duplicating it.

Also updated: the OpenAPI specification (both byte-identical copies) and the
Postman/Bruno collections generated from it, the consumer docs, the internal
request-processing doc, and all nine client libraries, which gain calls
alongside their existing clear-by-id: Java retrieve*ById, Node retrieve*ById,
Python/Ruby/Rust retrieve_*_by_id, Go Retrieve*ByID, PHP retrieve*ById and
.NET Retrieve*ById.

Fixes #2591

fix(control-plane): repair the four broken published examples the collection gate excused

The collection gate (scripts/collections/test_collections.py) fires every example in the
generated Postman collection at a live MockServer. Five endpoints sat in its KNOWN_FAILING
ratchet. Four of them were real defects rather than untestable examples, and are now fixed;
the list shrinks to the one genuinely state-dependent entry.

MediaType.isString() did not recognise application/yaml (RFC 9512), application/x-yaml or
application/graphql. All three are UTF-8 text with neither a "text" type nor a "+json"/"+xml"
suffix, so the body was stored as a BinaryBody and getBodyAsString() handed back base64. That
silently corrupted every YAML specification and GraphQL SDL document sent with its natural
content type — PUT /mockserver/graphql rejected its own documented example this way, and
PUT /mockserver/openapi did the same for a YAML spec — and it applied to user request matchers
just as much as to the control plane.

PUT /mockserver/verifySLO answered 400 when SLO tracking was disabled, the same status as
malformed criteria. A caller could not tell a typo in its criteria from a server with the
feature switched off, and every client library papered over it with a combined "invalid
criteria (or SLO tracking disabled)" message. It now answers 403, matching
PUT /mockserver/loadScenario/start, which is the same situation, and the feature-disabled error
the clients already model. All nine clients now distinguish the two.

Three published OpenAPI examples did not work as published: /mockserver/asyncapi/http declared
no requestBody example at all (so the generated collections sent an empty body), and
/mockserver/loadScenario/generateFromOpenAPI and /mockserver/contractTest fetched their
specification from a remote URL, so they failed anywhere without egress. All three now carry an
inline specification.

Separately, PUT /mockserver/contractTest reported allPassed for a run that verified nothing:
"passed == results.size()" is vacuously true for an empty result set, so a contract test whose
operationId filter was mistyped or had gone stale against a renamed operation returned
{"totalOperations": 0, "allPassed": true}. This is what made the endpoint look healthy against
one server and fail against another; an empty run is now allPassed:false with an error naming
why nothing ran.

/mockserver/loadScenario/generateFromRecording stays in KNOWN_FAILING: its body is well-formed
and the handler parses it, but a freshly-started container has no recorded traffic to convert.
Clearing it needs the harness to record traffic first, not a change to the example.

fix(loadgen): answer 409, not 400, when there is no recorded traffic to convert

PUT /mockserver/loadScenario/generateFromRecording returned 400 when the event log held
nothing to convert into a load scenario. The request body was well-formed and had parsed
cleanly — only the state was missing — so 400 told the caller its request was malformed and
gave it no way to tell that apart from "record some traffic through the proxy first". It now
answers 409, and 400 is reserved for a genuinely malformed request (missing name, an invalid
mode, or a scenario that fails validation).

LoadScenarioFromRecording throws a dedicated NoRecordedTrafficException rather than a bare
IllegalArgumentException, so the handler can distinguish the two without string-matching the
message. It extends IllegalArgumentException, so any caller already catching that keeps
working, and every client library reports the endpoint's errors generically by status, so none
needed changing.

This was the last entry in the collection gate's KNOWN_FAILING ratchet
(scripts/collections/test_collections.py), which is now empty: all 106 examples the published
Postman and Bruno collections carry are accepted by a default container. The list is left in
place with a note that adding to it is a last resort — four of the five entries it once held
looked like "this example cannot work in a bare container" and every one of them turned out to
be a real defect.

test(httpclient): de-flake HttpForwardConnectionPool idle-eviction timing tests

shouldNotEvictBeforeTheIdleTimeoutElapses and shouldRescheduleEvictionOnEachRelease
intermittently failed on loaded CI agents (e.g. Buildkite master build 6812) with
"channel must survive until the full idle timeout".

Root cause: EmbeddedChannel.advanceTimeBy() does NOT freeze the embedded clock and
timeFrozen defaults to false (see io.netty.channel.embedded.EmbeddedEventLoop$
FreezableTicker in Netty 4.2.17). When not frozen, advance() only shifts an offset
while nanoTime() keeps reading the REAL system ticker. The idle-eviction deadline is
captured at release() as nanoTime + IDLE_TIMEOUT_MILLIS (30000ms); after
advanceTimeBy(IDLE_TIMEOUT_MILLIS - 1) only a 1ms margin remains, so any real
wall-clock stall (GC pause / scheduler jitter) greater than 1ms between release() and
runScheduledPendingTasks() leaks into that margin and fires the reaper early.

Fix: call channel.freezeTime() in the shared newChannel() helper so nanoTime() advances
ONLY via advanceTimeBy(). The before/at-timeout boundary is still asserted at exact
millisecond granularity, now deterministically. This also makes the class-level Javadoc
("uses a frozen embedded clock") actually true.

The property under test is preserved: with production eviction temporarily broken to
ignore the timeout, exactly these two "before timeout" tests fail (degrade-and-confirm-
red), so the fix is not a false-green. Verified stable over 25 consecutive runs.

ci: make Buildkite resilient to transient Maven Central failures

A single transient failure from repo.maven.apache.org (a "Connection reset" /
timeout / 5xx while resolving one artifact or plugin) was reddening whole builds,
including builds that had already passed every test and child pipelines that only
touch Maven to build the mockserver jar before their own language tests (e.g.
Dependabot PRs #2625/#2623). Three layered, defence-in-depth mechanisms address it;
each covers a failure window the others do not.

1. In-Maven retry (mockserver/.mvn/maven.config)
   Add aether.connector.http.retryHandler.count=5, requestSentEnabled=true and
   connectionMaxTtl=120. These are the NATIVE Maven Resolver transport property
   names: Maven 3.9 defaults to the native HTTP transport, which IGNORES the legacy
   maven.wagon.http.* properties (setting those would be a silent no-op). Every
   invocation runs with its working directory inside the mockserver/ reactor, so
   all inherit these through this one file. Proven with a blackhole server: with
   the flags a Connection reset is retried exactly 5 times (1+5 = 6 attempts);
   the wagon names leave the native default of 3.

2. Warm local repo (S3 maven cache)
   Restore the maven dependency cache before the jar build in the python, ruby,
   node and ui pipelines (restore-only; the java and maven-plugin pipelines remain
   the sole savers so a partial subset never overwrites the full cache). Add
   --cache maven to build-local-mockserver-image.sh, whose jar build previously
   mounted no maven cache at all and went straight to Central. Degrades to a cold
   build (empty mount) when no cache was restored.

3. Step re-run (Buildkite retry on a sentinel exit code)
   Buildkite retry.automatic matches only exit codes, and a transient Central
   failure exits 1 -- the same code as a genuine test/compile failure -- so
   retrying on 1 would silently retry real regressions into green. Instead
   run-in-docker.sh (CI only, BUILDKITE=true) inspects the build output and remaps
   the exit to sentinel 42 ONLY when a Maven RESOLUTION phrase AND a NETWORK cause
   appear on the same line; jar-only steps opt in with `- exit_status: 42`
   (limit 2). A test that logs "Connection reset" carries no resolution phrase on
   that line and is not remapped; a genuine missing-artifact/404 has no network
   cause and is not remapped.

What a retry can and cannot mask: it CAN re-run a transient-infra window that
outlasts Maven's own retries; it CANNOT mask a test/compile/asset regression on the
opted-in steps -- each isolates a -DskipTests Maven build in its own run-in-docker
invocation, separate from the invocation that runs its tests, so a real test failure
exits 1 in a log with no resolution line and can never reach 42. The java :maven:
build step is deliberately NOT opted in: it runs resolution AND the full test
reactor in one classified invocation (under -T 1C a transient line can co-occur with
a real test failure), so it relies on layers 1+2 only.

Also correct a stale docs claim: the dependency_cache IAM policy IS attached to the
default and release queues (terraform main.tf), not detached as ci-cd.md stated.

Docs updated: docs/infrastructure/ci-cd.md (new Transient Maven Central Resilience
section + corrected cache activation state) and docs/operations/build-system.md
(the native-transport retry flags).

docs(terraform): correct the stale dependency-cache status comment

The header claimed "The IAM policy is DETACHED from all agent roles" and that
the runtime wiring "was reverted". Both were false and had been for some time:
the policy is attached to the default and release roles (main.tf
managed_policy_arns), and cache-restore.sh / cache-save.sh run in the java,
maven-plugin, node, python, ruby, ui and website pipelines.

This is the same failure shape as the #2579 root cause -- a safety claim living
in the descriptive layer while the operative layer does something else -- so the
replacement states the verified status and points readers at main.tf and the
pipeline YAML as the authority rather than the comment.

It also records what the old comment gated on and never got: cache entries are
plain lockfile-keyed tarballs, unsigned and not content-addressed, so a build on
the default queue can write an entry a later build on that queue trusts. Fork
PRs cannot reach these agents and the release pipelines do not restore the cache,
so there is no path into a published artefact today -- but that containment is
incidental rather than enforced, and is recorded as such.

Comment-only; no resource, policy or plan change. terraform fmt clean.

   onData", but Http3MockServerHandler.channelRead copies bytes, calls onData,
   then releases the frame in the finally block AFTER onData returns. The
   safety property (flow-control window not pinned) still holds because onData
   dispatches asynchronously; the mechanism description was wrong and is now
   corrected. The HTTP/2 path (GrpcBidiStreamHandler.handleData) has the same
   finally-block structure and is already correctly described.

2. ai-protocol-mocking.md — Name the enforcing test in the exemplar.
   "A test pins the inequality" now reads
   "shouldSizeThePendingBoundAboveTheAdvertisedStreamLimit in
   GrpcToHttpResponseHandlerTest pins the inequality", matching the target
   shape: claim + mechanism + named enforcing test + diagnosability.

3. BreakpointMatcherRegistry.java — Kill "exactly as in findMatch" cross-
   reference. Replace with a direct statement of the property so the javadoc
   is self-contained and no longer inherits correctness by assertion.

4. request-processing.md — Qualify the collision-free rotationCount invariant.
   Note that AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is the enforcing mechanism, and
   that MockServerMatcherSequentialResponsesTest covers single-threaded
   behaviour only; no concurrent test currently pins this property.

test(core): parameterise reconcile eviction parity over clustered + non-clustered backends

Close the #2579 clustered-branch coverage blind spot: bind both
reconcileFromBackend siblings (trimEvictedFromBackend and
reconcileClusteredScan) to one set of add/update/remove-sync and
maxExpectations eviction assertions via a parameterised test, so the
clustered leg can no longer drift from its non-clustered twin untested.

The 2026-08-22 survey that prompted this predates the final #2579 fix and is
stale: the chaos registries and the cross-protocol bus are already covered
clustered-side by ClusteredTwoNodeChaosTest and
ClusteredTwoNodeCrossProtocolBusTest against a real two-node Infinispan
backend, so no core-side duplicates were added. What was genuinely missing
was parity -- the behaviours the two siblings must AGREE on were asserted
only against the non-clustered leg.

Document per-claim which test enforces each reconcile ordering guarantee,
replacing prose that asserted the ordering applied to both paths while the
clustered leg actually read the live cache last.

test(examples): de-flake SOCKS/HTTP proxy end-to-end tests by binding the backend race-free

The BooksPage*ProxyEndToEndIntegrationTest suites intermittently errored with
"502 Bad Gateway" from MockServer-as-proxy (e.g. build 6815). Root cause was in
the example backend fixture, not the proxy: BookServer.startServer() fired
serverBootstrap.bind(httpPort) and ignored the returned ChannelFuture, then slept
3 seconds. When the port (chosen earlier via PortFactory.findFreePort()) was
claimed by another process between selection and bind — a TOCTOU race PortFactory
itself documents — the BindException was silently swallowed: nothing listened on
the backend port, so the proxy could not reach the upstream and returned 502. The
proxy's 502 for a genuinely-unreachable upstream is correct behaviour, so the fix
belongs in mockserver-examples.

Fix:
- BookServer now binds to an ephemeral port (0), .sync()s the bind (failing loudly
  on BindException and giving real readiness in place of the fixed sleep), reads
  the actual OS-assigned port from channel.localAddress() and publishes it as the
  "bookService.port" system property; the channel is closed in @PreDestroy. This
  removes the find-then-bind race entirely.
- BackEndServiceConfiguration passes port 0 and no longer pre-allocates a racy
  free port; the redundant findFreePort() pre-seed in BooksPageEndToEndIntegration
  Test @BeforeClass is removed.
- The eight backend-exercised BookService clients (jetty, apache, jersey, spring
  rest template, google http+socks, java http+socks) now read "bookService.port"
  lazily at request time instead of caching it in @PostConstruct, so correctness
  no longer depends on Spring bean-initialisation ordering.

Verified: SOCKS/HTTP E2E suites green across repeated sequential runs and isolated
concurrent runs with zero 502s; degrade-and-confirm-red (pointing the SOCKS client
at a wrong backend port) reproduces the exact 502 and turns the suite red,
confirming it still catches a genuine proxy-path defect.

test(core): cover HttpState clustered chaos + cross-protocol-bus listener wiring

The two clustered-only addInvalidationListener blocks in HttpState -- the
chaos-registry reconcile listener and the cross-protocol-bus reconcile listener
-- had no test. The infinispan ClusteredTwoNode* suites hand-wire equivalent
listeners in their own setup and never construct HttpState, so deleting either
block left every suite green while a clustered node would silently stop
rebuilding node-local chaos and bus state on remote writes.

Cover both with one parameterised test driving the real HttpState constructor
through the StateBackendFactory seam, asserting listener registration counts
and, behaviourally, that firing the registered listeners drives a reconcile
read of the chaos-service and cross-protocol-bus stores when clustered and of
neither when not. Each block was removed in turn to confirm the clustered rows
go red on that specific block while the non-clustered rows stay green.

Constructing HttpState mutates process-global singletons, so the class is wired
into both the surefire parallel-excludes and sequential-includes lists,
matching HttpStateReadinessTest.

fix(core): honour keep-alive at end of stream instead of always closing (#2641)

Streaming responses (httpSseResponse, and httpLlmResponse with
completion.streaming:true) closed the connection at end of stream even
though the response head advertised Connection: keep-alive.

finishStream tested `getCloseConnection() == null || getCloseConnection()`,
so the unset default meant "always close", and it never consulted
request.isKeepAlive(), the explicit close opt-out, or
alwaysCloseSocketConnections. Two symptoms followed from that one line:

  * HTTP/1.1 clients that reused the connection the response had just
    promised they could keep got RemoteDisconnected on the next request.
  * On HTTP/2 the ctx.close() tore down the whole connection. Every
    non-gRPC HTTP/2 stream is multiplexed onto a single connection
    channel (HttpToHttp2ConnectionHandler, streams carried by
    x-http2-stream-id, no per-stream child channels), so finishing one
    stream emitted GOAWAY and killed its siblings.

The end-of-stream decision now mirrors the non-streaming path in
NettyResponseWriter: an explicit closeConnection still wins on HTTP/1.1,
otherwise the request's keep-alive intent decides, and
alwaysCloseSocketConnections still forces a close. An HTTP/2 request
never closes the shared parent connection - its terminal frame ends only
that stream - and this holds even for closeConnection:true, because
tearing down a shared connection to satisfy one expectation would
re-introduce the sibling-kill for every concurrent stream. The Connection
header now reports the decision actually taken rather than always
claiming keep-alive.

Fully-interleaved concurrent HTTP/2 streaming remains a separate
pre-existing limitation of the single-connection HTTP/2 path.

ci: let Dependabot security PRs auto-merge via an explicit semver gate

Dependabot security updates never auto-merged. The sweep accepts only a
*-minor-and-patch group branch (path A) or a distroless digest bump
(path B), and every groups: entry in dependabot.yml omits applies-to,
which defaults to version-updates. Security fixes are therefore raised
ungrouped and matched neither path, so they sat open indefinitely - four
fully-green security PRs (#2640, #2645, #2646, #2647) had accumulated.

Grouping cannot fix this: update-types is not supported for
applies-to: security-updates, so a security group named *-minor-and-patch
would let a MAJOR bump ride a branch that path A accepts. Rule 6d already
fails the build on exactly that shape.

Path C instead derives major-exclusion from an explicit semver
comparison. It accepts only when Dependabot's own security-fix marker is
present in the body, the title yields exactly one dotted-numeric
"from X to Y" pair, and the majors are equal - plus equal minors when the
major is 0, since 0.x minors are breaking. Every generic gate still
applies unchanged: dependabot[bot] author, in-repo head, mergeable, and
the full check-runs + commit-statuses green aggregation. The dotted-numeric
requirement keeps path C disjoint from path B's backticked hex digests,
and a grouped multi-update title yields no parseable pair and is refused.

Rule 6e guards path C, binding each refuse to its own comparison: a first
attempt grepped the whole block for `return 1`, which the npairs check
alone satisfied, so gutting the major-exclusion body still passed green.
It now extracts each comparison's if...fi and requires a live return 1
inside it, and fails closed when either sub-block cannot be located.

test(core): run the FileWatcher tests sequentially to fix a shared-static race

FileWatcherTest.shouldReloadWhenFileReappearsAfterBeingUnreadable
intermittently observed 0 updates, reddening master builds 6914 and 6918
and Dependabot PR #2655. It is not a JVM WatchService latency problem.

FileWatcher polls on a shared scheduler, and its poll period is a STATIC
mutable field defaulting to 5 seconds, read once when scheduleAtFixedRate
captures it, so the first poll lands one full period after construction.
Both FileWatcherTest and ExpectationFileWatcherTest shorten that static to
500ms in @BeforeClass and RESTORE it in @AfterClass, and both were running
in the parallel phase. Whichever class finished first therefore put the
5-second default back while the other was still running, leaving that
class's later watchers polling every 5s against a ~4.9s retry budget. That
near dead-heat is why it passed on an idle machine and failed under CI
load, and why an npm-only commit could "fail" a Java test.

FileWatcherTest's javadoc had reasoned about this and reached the wrong
conclusion: it argued the classes were safe to run concurrently because
they set the same value. They do, but it is the restore that collides.

Both classes now run in the sequential phase, alongside the other tests
that mutate JVM-global state. As defence in depth the two retry budgets
widen to ~15s so they exceed the 5-second DEFAULT period rather than only
the shortened one, should any future test leave the static at its default.

ParallelStaticStateGuardTest keeps the parallel excludes and sequential
includes in step, and passes.

fix(core): replace the static FileWatcher poll period with a configuration property

The initialization-file watch interval was a process-wide mutable static
(FileWatcher.pollPeriod, default 5 SECONDS) with public static accessors
and no supported configuration route. Four test classes shortened it in
@BeforeClass and restored it in @AfterClass, and two of them ran in the
parallel Surefire phase, so whichever finished first reinstated the
5-second default under the other, leaving it polling every 5s against a
~4.9s retry budget. That near dead-heat reddened master builds 6914/6918
and PR #2655. Commit 1c1f37ae5 moved those two classes to the sequential
phase, which stopped the bleeding; this removes the hazard itself.

The period is now watchInitializationJsonPollPeriodMillis, a first-class
property resolvable by system property, environment variable, properties
file, the Configuration instance setter and PUT /mockserver/configuration,
defaulting to 5000 so behaviour is unchanged. FileWatcher takes it as a
constructor argument and ExpectationFileWatcher reads it from the
Configuration it already holds; the statics and all four accessors are
deleted. A property was needed rather than a constructor argument alone
because MainCliTest drives the server through Main.main, which no
constructor parameter can reach.

The tests also did not all set the same value - MainCliTest used 200ms
while the others used 500ms - so the original "safe because both set the
identical value" reasoning was never true, not merely incomplete.

GlobalStateMutationGuardTest should have caught this and did not: all
seven of its detection patterns named specific classes, making it an
allow-list in which every new offender was invisible by construction. It
now also matches a static setter on any capitalised type, which is precise
in Java because instance calls go through lower-case receivers. That
immediately surfaced five further genuine global mutators already sitting
in the parallel phase - two calling Locale.setDefault, three mutating
static tracer/listener/supplier fields - all now sequential. Netty's
HttpUtil.setTransferEncodingChunked mutates its argument rather than
global state and is the one justified benign entry.

The guard's javadoc now records what it still cannot see - a mutator
reached through a static import has no receiver to match, and a direct
public-static-field assignment has no setter - so a green run is not
mistaken for proof that a test touches no global state. Reading it that
way is what let this through the first time.

build(deps-dev): bump vitest and @vitest/coverage-v8 to 5.0.0 together

Dependabot raised these as two separate pull requests, #2662 for vitest and
#2663 for @vitest/coverage-v8, because majors are excluded from the
npm-minor-and-patch group. The two are peer-locked to the same exact
version - @vitest/coverage-v8@5.0.0 requires vitest "5.0.0", not a range -
so each pull request on its own left a mismatched pair and npm ci failed
with ERESOLVE. Neither could ever go green alone, and retrying them was
pointless.

That single install failure surfaced in three places. It broke the UI lint,
typecheck and test steps directly; it broke the Maven reactor, because
mockserver-netty bundles the dashboard and so runs npm ci in mockserver-ui;
and through that same reactor build it also failed CodeQL's Analyze (java)
job, which is why a JavaScript-only change appeared to break Java analysis.

Bumping both together resolves the pair. The suite is unchanged at 192
files and 3044 tests, and coverage thresholds still pass.

Vitest 5 removed the top-level bench export - it is now a test-context
fixture - which broke the typecheck on the three benchmark files. They now
register through the fixture and run each OLD/NEW pair with bench.compare,
so the two variants are still measured and reported in one comparison
table. Scenario names and bench labels are unchanged so historical results
stay comparable.

fix(core): keep whole-number doubles intact when serializing a JsonBody (#2658)

An expectation built through the Java client with JsonBody.json(...) was
silently corrupted before it ever reached the server: a body containing
275.0 was stored as 275, so a byte-identical request no longer matched and
the client got a 404. The reporter saw the corruption in the server's own
"creating expectation" log, with 275 already in place before any request
arrived.

Both client-side body serializers enable USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS, so
readTree builds a DecimalNode. Jackson's STRIP_TRAILING_BIGDECIMAL_ZEROES,
which has defaulted to true since 2.15, then normalises that node as it is
constructed - 275.0 becomes 275, 0.00 becomes 0, 100.0 becomes 1E+2. The
server re-reads the stripped value with the default mapper as an IntNode
while the incoming request's 275.0 is a DoubleNode, and json-unit does not
consider those equal. Setting an exact-BigDecimal node factory on the two
private mappers stops the stripping, so what the user supplied is what is
stored.

The matcher is deliberately left alone. json-unit treating 275 and 275.0 as
different is defensible behaviour; the defect was that a lossless value was
made lossy during serialization, so the fix belongs there.

This also completes the fix for #1740, which introduced
USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS to stop 0.00 collapsing to 0.0. That commit
already ran on Jackson 2.21.3, where the stripping default was true, so it
never achieved its own goal - it turned 0.00 into a bare 0 - and regressed
whole-number doubles at the same time. It also shipped without a test,
which is why this went unnoticed.

Numbers now round-trip verbatim in persisted expectations, the REST API and
the dashboard, so a stored body shows 275.0 rather than 275. Integers are
unaffected and stay integers.

The gap that let this ship was that nothing covered the client-side
round-trip; the bug is invisible when the same JSON is PUT directly to
/mockserver/expectation, bypassing the client serializer. The new matcher
tests serialize through ExpectationDTO, deserialize, and then match a
byte-identical body, for both STRICT and ONLY_MATCHING_FIELDS.

test(core): guard against enabling big-decimal parsing without exact BigDecimals

Enabling USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS makes Jackson build a DecimalNode, and
STRIP_TRAILING_BIGDECIMAL_ZEROES - default true since 2.15 - then normalises
that node as it is constructed, so 275.0 becomes 275, 0.00 becomes 0 and
100.0 becomes 1E+2. The feature is only safe when paired with an exact
BigDecimal node factory.

That pairing was missing from the two JSON body serializers between
11561ad28 and bdf1eb4d2, which silently corrupted expectations built through
the Java client (issue #2658) and meant the earlier fix for issue #1740 never
achieved its own goal. It survived because 11561ad28 shipped with no test.

The behavioural tests added with bdf1eb4d2 protect the two mappers that exist
today: delete the pairing from either and they fail. What they structurally
cannot see is a third mapper added later with the same unpaired shape, which
is exactly how the original defect entered. This guard covers that vector: it
walks every module's main sources and fails the build if a statement enables
the feature without pairing it, in that same statement, with exact
BigDecimals. Any of the three legitimate spellings satisfies it - an exact
node factory, disabling the strip feature, or configuring it false - so a
future refactor is not forced into one form, and qualified type names are
accepted as well as imported ones.

The pairing is checked per statement rather than per file, so a second
unpaired mapper added to an already-compliant file is still caught, and the
suppression marker is likewise scoped to the statement it sits on rather than
blinding the whole file.

The guard is a text scanner and is deliberately not exhaustive; its javadoc
records what it cannot see, and separates shapes that fail open from those
that fail closed, so a green run is not mistaken for proof. The two real
paired mappers double as a live anchor: if the detection pattern ever stopped
matching them they would fall to the unclassifiable branch and fail the build,
so the guard cannot quietly stop working while they exist. Self-tests pin the
patterns independently of those two call sites.

fix(core): address streamed HTTP/2 chunks to their own stream (#2667)

Two concurrent streaming responses on one HTTP/2 connection could leave one
of them hanging forever. A chunk belonging to the stream that arrived first
was written to whichever stream had most recently sent a response head, and
if that stream had already finished the write failed with "Stream no longer
exists". The client received the head and the first chunk and then waited
indefinitely, with nothing but a warning in the server log.

Every non-gRPC HTTP/2 stream shares one HttpToHttp2ConnectionHandler, and
that handler chooses the target stream for an outbound write from a single
mutable field which it updates only when an HttpMessage head passes through
it. Content frames are not HttpMessage and carry no headers, so a chunk
written after another stream's head went by is routed to that other stream.
Stamping the id onto the chunk is not possible: the codec never looks at
content for one. The id has to travel out of band and the data write has to
name its stream.

Streamed chunks are now wrapped so they carry their originating stream id
and an end-of-stream flag, and a HttpToHttp2ConnectionHandler subclass
writes them with encoder().writeData addressed to that id rather than to the
shared field. The wrapping happens only for a request that arrived over
HTTP/2, so HTTP/1.1 writes the same objects it always did, and gRPC is
untouched because it runs on the multiplexed child-channel path where the
channel already is the stream.

The hang had a second cause worth naming. The failed write was reported as a
warning and the error path then wrote the terminal frame, which was itself
mis-routed, so the stream never ended. Addressed writes fix that, and a
failed streaming write now also resets its own stream so a client is never
left waiting on a stream that cannot make progress. Only that stream is
reset; the shared connection is left alone, which is the invariant #2641
established.

httpLlmResponse streaming builds an HttpSseResponse and runs through the
same handler, so it had the same defect and is covered by the same fix.

The comment in finishStream claiming the codec propagated the stream id onto
trailing content was wrong. It held only while a single stream was in flight
at a time, which is why the sequential test added with #2641 passed while
concurrency did not.

fix(core): give the LLM completion a serialization boundary so timeToFirstToken loads (#2668)

An expectation setting streamingPhysics.timeToFirstToken was rejected with a
400 and an error naming org.mockserver.model.Delay, a type the user never
wrote. The client serialized it happily and the server then refused to read
it back, so nothing client-side could catch it.

Delay has only multi-argument constructors and no creator, so Jackson cannot
construct one. Everywhere else a Delay crosses the wire it goes through
DelayDTO, but HttpLlmResponseDTO held the completion as the model class
rather than a DTO and StreamingPhysics had no DTO at all, so this one field
reached the wire as a raw Delay.

Completion and StreamingPhysics now have DTOs, with timeToFirstToken wrapped
in a DelayDTO like every other Delay. The emitted JSON is unchanged - a raw
Delay already serialized to exactly what DelayDTO produces - so stored
expectations and existing clients are unaffected; only the read path
changes.

Delay is the only model type in the graph reachable from these DTOs without
a creator, and this was the only place one reached the wire unwrapped, so
the fix is complete rather than one instance of a wider fault. The seven
other model subtrees HttpLlmResponseDTO still holds raw contain no such
type.

Adding a creator to Delay would have been the smaller change but was
rejected: it would state Delay's wire contract in a second place, taking a
raw DelayDistribution and bypassing DelayDistributionDTO, which is the drift
the DTO layer exists to prevent.

The round-trip tests exercised StreamingPhysics but never set
timeToFirstToken, while the only test that set it built the object in memory
and never crossed the wire. The new cases round-trip it for real, including
a Delay carrying a distribution, and assert the neighbouring fields survive
so a DTO that quietly drops one is caught.

test(core): guard against a model type reaching the wire without a Jackson creator

Issue #2668 was an expectation the client happily serialized and the server
then refused to read: HttpLlmResponseDTO held the completion as the model
class rather than a DTO, so StreamingPhysics.timeToFirstToken reached the
wire as a raw Delay, which Jackson cannot construct.

Two things kept it hidden. Serialization never failed - a raw Delay emits
exactly what DelayDTO emits - so any test asserting the generated JSON
passed while the feature was unusable. And the coverage inverted: the wire
round-trip tests exercised StreamingPhysics but never set timeToFirstToken,
while the only test that set timeToFirstToken built the object in memory and
never crossed the wire.

Round-trip tests only cover fields somebody remembered to populate, so they
cannot close that gap on their own. This guard is structural instead. It
walks the type graph from ExpectationDTO through Jackson's own serialized
property view and asserts every org.mockserver.model type it reaches can
actually be constructed, reporting the path by which an offender is
reachable rather than just its name. Reverting the #2668 fix makes it name
the completion, the streaming physics and the delay in order.

That matters because HttpLlmResponseDTO still holds seven other model
subtrees raw. They are safe today only because nothing creator-less lives
under them, which is a property of the current code rather than a rule
anyone is enforcing.

Its couplings fail loudly rather than quietly. Breaking the deserializer
introspection collapses the walk, which the minimum-types-walked tripwire
turns into a build failure, and the self-test pinning Delay as
non-constructible fails if the exception wording it keys on ever changes.
A Jackson upgrade therefore breaks this visibly instead of leaving it
passing over nothing.

The javadoc records what it cannot see - Object-typed and raw properties,
serializer-driven shapes, subtrees owned by a custom deserializer,
polymorphic subtypes - so a green run is not read as proof.

fix(testcontainers): wait until MockServer is serving before start() returns

MockServerContainer waited on the container's port being listenable, which
is satisfied the moment the mapped port accepts a TCP connection. Docker
binds that port as soon as the container is created and MockServer's own
listener binds early too, but it accepts and then resets connections until
initialisation finishes. start() therefore returned inside that window and
a request issued straight afterwards could be reset, surfacing as "Channel
handler removed before valid response has been received".

Measured against the released image the port accepted TCP at 0.145s, PUTs
were reset until 0.491s, and only then did the server answer - a window of
roughly a third of a second at rest, and wider on a loaded host, which is
why it showed up as an intermittent CI failure rather than a constant one.

The wait is now an HTTP probe for PUT /mockserver/status returning 200,
which only happens once the request pipeline is serving, so start()
returning means ready. withServerPort re-installs the probe against the
port it selects. /mockserver/status is deliberate: it is unauthenticated,
so enabling control-plane authentication does not stall the probe, and it
exists in every MockServer version, whereas /ready arrived in 7.2.0 and
this container accepts arbitrary images. It answers before initialisation
JSON has been seeded, which the javadoc now says plainly.

The startup ceiling is set explicitly rather than left at the framework
default of a minute. With every core saturated this test took 51.9s and
55.8s against about 4s idle, so a minute was closer to the edge than it
looked, and a larger ceiling costs nothing on the happy path because the
wait ends as soon as the probe answers.

The integration test pinned mockserver/mockserver:latest, so its result
depended on whatever had last been pushed and could change with nothing
changing here. It now pins a released tag.

Verified with ten consecutive runs at rest and further runs under full CPU
saturation, all passing.

chore(agents): refuse edits to the main checkout

Every session is meant to work in its own linked worktree. An agent that
edits the main checkout instead fails quietly rather than loudly: that tree
is usually on an older commit, so the edit is written against stale content,
never passes through the session's own verification, and another session can
rebase or reset it away. This repository has already lost committed,
gate-passed work that way, recovered only from the reflog, and two agents
made the same mistake again in a single session. Both caught it themselves;
nothing else would have.

A PreToolUse hook now refuses an edit whose target resolves inside the main
checkout, and says what to do instead. It asks git which worktree a path
belongs to rather than hard-coding anything: in the main worktree
--show-toplevel is the directory holding --git-common-dir, and in a linked
worktree the two differ. So it holds for any clone or layout. Paths are
canonicalised first, so .tmp/../ does not walk out of the allowed scratch
areas. Scratch under .tmp/ and .worktrees/ stays allowed, since that is
where worktrees are made.

It fails open, like the halt hook beside it. A gate that runs before every
tool call must never be able to wedge a session because the gate itself
broke, and failing closed on a transient git lock would be a worse and far
more frequent failure than the one being prevented. Where that silence could
be permanent rather than momentary - git too old to answer, no python - it
now says so, so the guard cannot quietly stop working.

It only sees the edit tools. A write through bash still gets past it,
because guessing target paths out of arbitrary shell would block ordinary
read-only commands. The script and the docs say that plainly: this narrows
the mistake, it does not remove it.

docs(netty): point the HTTP/2 multiplex TODO at its tracked issue

The migration to Http2MultiplexHandler for the non-gRPC HTTP/2 path lived
only as a comment here. Every issue that motivated it is now closed - #2641
and #2667 - so nothing outside this line remembered the work was still
outstanding. It is tracked as issue #2669, which records why it is still
worth doing now that #2667 has removed the correctness pressure, and the
blast radius already scoped while fixing that.

fix(netty): carry the HTTP/2 stream id onto the dashboard response

The dashboard was unreachable over HTTP/2. The client received nothing at
all and waited until it timed out.

DashboardHandler writes straight to the channel rather than going through
ResponseWriter, so nothing had copied the request's stream id onto the
response, and the response mapper reads that field rather than a header.
With it absent, the shared-connection HTTP/2 path routes the response head
onto a fresh server-initiated stream instead of the client's, so the client
never sees its own answer. MetricsHandler already did this correctly; the
dashboard was a one-line divergence from it.

The two early path-traversal rejections bypass the mapper in the same way
and are stamped too, so no write in this handler is left unaddressed.

Http2StreamIdAuditHandler exists to warn about exactly this shape, which is
what made it findable.

The test drives a real HTTP/2 client and asserts END_STREAM on the client's
own stream rather than only checking the body, because a response routed to
the wrong stream produces no END_STREAM at all - which is the actual
symptom. It uses the synthetic dashboard fixture so it runs without the UI
build profile.

fix(netty): carry the HTTP/2 stream id onto the remaining direct writes

Four more responses were written straight to the channel without the
request's stream id, so each hung over HTTP/2 the same way the dashboard
did: the OpenAPI spec at /mockserver/openapi.yaml, the 503 that tells a
client to retry elsewhere while the server drains, the 200 answering /stop,
and the 407 demanding proxy authentication.

These share one cause. A handler that writes through ResponseWriter or the
gRPC bridge gets the stream id carried across for it; a handler that writes
to the channel itself does not, and the response mapper looks for the model
field rather than a header. So the omission is silent, and the symptom is a
client that waits rather than an error anyone would notice.

The drain 503 and the proxy 407 are the worse two: both exist to tell a
client something it needs in order to act, and both were being routed
somewhere the client was not listening.

Every remaining direct write in the netty module was checked; the rest
already carried the id.

refactor(netty): hold the websocket handshaker per channel, not per handler

CallbackWebSocketServerHandler is annotated Sharable but kept the
handshaker in an instance field. That is safe only because one instance
currently exists per pipeline, which is a property of how it happens to be
wired rather than of the handler itself. Sharing one instance across
channels would let concurrent handshakes overwrite each other.

The handshaker genuinely outlives a single call - it is created during the
HTTP upgrade and read again later when a close frame arrives - so a local
will not do. It now lives in a channel attribute, alongside the upgrade
marker this class already keeps there.

The close path also tolerates the handshaker being absent instead of
throwing, which the instance field would have done in the same situation.

No behaviour change on HTTP/1.1, which is the only protocol this handler
serves: websocket callback upgrades are refused over HTTP/2.

fix(netty): give HTTP/2 stream channels the connection state they read

A multiplexed HTTP/2 stream gets its own child channel, and Netty gives that
child none of the parent connection's attributes. Only the local-host
headers were being copied across, so every other piece of connection state a
handler reads was simply absent on a stream.

Four things broke as a result, all of them silently, and all of them only
when gRPC bidi streaming is enabled - which is why no test caught them:

  - the negotiated protocol was unreadable, so a request arriving on a
    stream was not recognised as HTTP/2. It never captured a stream id,
    withProtocol(HTTP_2) did not match it, and the logs said HTTP/1.1.
  - the websocket handlers could not tell the connection was HTTP/2, so
    instead of refusing the upgrade with 501 they began a handshake over a
    stream, and the client got no usable response at all.
  - the client certificates were gone, so anything reading them live - MCP
    control-plane auth, the dashboard websocket path - saw an unauthenticated
    caller. The REST control plane was unaffected: it is handed the
    certificates when the child pipeline is built.
  - a proxied request no longer looked like one.

Connection state is now copied onto each child as it is created, once, by
value. The list is the attributes that are set while the connection is
established and read on a stream; each is referenced through the constant
its owning class declares, so a rename cannot leave the reader and this list
disagreeing. Attributes a stream initialises for itself - the trace context,
the websocket registry, CORS - are deliberately not inherited, since sharing
those across streams is the cross-talk this is meant to prevent.

The remote socket address is copied along with the proxying flag. They are
set together and mean nothing apart: with only the flag, a proxied stream
knows it should forward but not where to, and falls back to rebuilding the
target from the Host header - which silently reaches a different server
whenever the CONNECT target and the Host header disagree. That is a worse
outcome than the original bug, and it is what the accompanying test pins
down, by pointing the two at different servers and asserting which one is
reached.

fix(netty): emit GOAWAY on the connection when asked from a stream

On the multiplexed HTTP/2 path the request handlers run on a per-stream
child channel, and the connection handler lives on the parent. The emitter
looked for it in the local pipeline only, found nothing, and returned false.
Both callers treat that as "nothing to do" and carry on, so the two signals
that depend on it were quietly lost whenever gRPC bidi streaming was on:
the GOAWAY that tells clients the server is draining and they should go
elsewhere, and the http2GoAway chaos experiment.

Losing those silently is the bad part. The server believes it has told the
client something the client needs in order to act, the client never hears
it, and nothing is logged.

The emitter now walks to the parent connection's pipeline when the local one
has no connection handler, and writes there. GOAWAY carries stream id 0 and
concerns the whole connection, so the connection channel is where it
belongs - which is also why the stream reset in HttpErrorActionHandler
deliberately does the opposite and writes on the child.

A stream child channel shares its parent's event loop, so reaching across
to the parent's context does not cross threads.

Behaviour is unchanged anywhere the connection handler is already in the
local pipeline, and a channel with no parent and no handler still returns
false rather than throwing, so HTTP/1.1 is untouched.

The javadoc and netty-pipeline.md said multiplex support was deferred. It no
longer is.

fix(netty): end the stream when a streaming response finishes on a multiplexed HTTP/2 child

Turning on gRPC bidi streaming switches the whole HTTP/2 connection to Netty's
multiplex model, and that applies to every stream on it, not just the gRPC ones.
An ordinary SSE, NDJSON or Bedrock event-stream response - so every streaming
LLM response - is served on a per-stream child channel too.

The streaming handler marks its last frame as ending the stream. On a child
channel that frame passes through Http2StreamFrameToHttpObjectCodec, whose only
branch for a bare content chunk emits a DATA frame with the end-of-stream flag
hard-coded to false. The marker was dropped on the floor.

So the client received every event and then waited for an end that never came,
until it gave up. The server thought it had finished, logged nothing, and failed
nothing. Silence on both sides is what made this worth fixing carefully.

The fix translates the frame into the object the codec already maps correctly:
the terminal frame becomes a LastHttpContent, which the codec emits with the
end-of-stream flag set even when the payload is empty, and a mid-stream chunk
stays a plain content chunk. The buffer moves to the new carrier without a
retain or a release, so ownership stays single.

On a child channel the stream id is implicit - the channel is the stream - so
only the end-of-stream flag needed carrying across. The shared-connection
pipeline is untouched: it still receives the wrapper intact, because it needs
the stream id that the child channel gets for free.

Proven by degrading the handler and watching the stream hang: the terminal
frame arrives without the flag and the client times out with all events
collected.

fix(netty): treat requests on a multiplexed HTTP/2 child like every other request

Turning on gRPC bidi streaming moves the whole HTTP/2 connection onto Netty's
multiplex model, and every stream on it goes there - ordinary requests included.
Two things that hold everywhere else did not hold on that path.

A compressed request body was never decompressed. It reached the matchers as
gzip bytes, so an expectation written against the body did not match and the
caller got a 404, with the recorded request showing unreadable bytes. The
connection-level pipeline decompresses via its frame listener and HTTP/1.1 via
HttpContentDecompressor; the child pipeline had neither. It has one now, in the
same position HTTP/1.1 puts it - after the codec, before aggregation.

A request carrying an odd header value - a leading space, an embedded DEL, a
control character - was rejected outright with a stream error before it reached
the matchers, so nothing matched and nothing was recorded as received. That is
the wrong answer from a mock server: driving one with malformed traffic to see
how your client copes is a reason people use it. The connection-level pipeline
accepts these; this path now does too.

The second fix needed care. Netty's stream-frame codec has one validation flag
governing both directions, so simply turning it off would also have stopped
validating the response header names we send. Requests and responses do not
deserve the same latitude: being liberal about what we accept is the point,
while putting an illegal header name on the wire is a defect. So the codec
subclass here is lenient inbound and re-asserts the strict check outbound,
performing the same conversion Netty would have performed with validation on
rather than restating the rule and risking drift from it.

Only names are validated outbound, never values, and only on response heads and
trailers - never per chunk, so streaming responses pay nothing.

The malformed value in both tests is written as a \u007F escape rather than a raw
DEL byte. A raw byte is invisible in a diff and reads as though the test
exercises nothing, which already caused one wrong conclusion about it. A guard
test now asserts the character is really there, because the tests that depend on
it cannot themselves tell the difference.

fix(netty): make the mid-response reset fault abort the connection, not one stream

resetMidResponse exists to simulate a server that dies mid-reply, so the client
sees a connection reset. On the multiplexed HTTP/2 path the response is written
on a per-stream child channel, and resetting that only ends the one stream.

Worse, it failed quietly. Setting SO_LINGER on a stream child does not throw -
the config returns false for an option it does not recognise - so there was not
even an exception to swallow. The fault reported success, the client got a tidy
end-of-stream, and nobody was told the abort never happened.

The fault now walks up to the parent connection and resets that, killing the TCP
connection and every stream on it. That is the point of the fault: a real socket
abort takes everything with it, and one that spares the siblings is not the
thing being simulated.

The walk is guarded on the channel TYPE, not on having a parent. An ordinary
HTTP/1.1 socket also has a parent - the server's listening socket - so guarding
on parent() alone would set SO_LINGER on the listening socket and close it,
shutting the server down on the first fault. There is a test for that, and it
was confirmed by making the mistake deliberately: every test in the class then
failed, because the server was gone.

Closing is left alone. closeSocket, closeChannel and the slow-close fault still
end just the stream: ending one stream is what closing means in HTTP/2, and one
expectation should not be able to destroy other people's in-flight requests.
Aborting is the exception because aborting is inherently connection-wide.

If SO_LINGER cannot be applied to whatever we resolved, that is now a warning
rather than silence, since the alternative is a destructive fault that politely
does nothing.

feat(netty): give every HTTP/2 stream its own channel

MockServer served all of an HTTP/2 connection's streams through one shared
pipeline. Netty offers a multiplexed model instead, where each stream is its own
channel, and this switches to it for all HTTP/2. There is no flag: two pipelines
would mean two sets of behaviour to keep honest, which is how the bugs below
survived as long as they did.

The multiplexed pipeline was already here, used only when gRPC bidi streaming
was on. That made it a quiet corner - anything connection-level that does
nothing useful on a per-stream channel failed there and almost nowhere else.
Fixing those was the bulk of this work and each one landed on its own: stream
channels not inheriting the connection's state, GOAWAY never reaching the
connection, streaming responses never ending, request bodies never being
decompressed, malformed request headers being refused, and the reset fault
resetting a stream instead of the socket. Every one of them was silent. The
server believed it had acted; the client waited for something that never came.

With those fixed the two pipelines agree, so the old one goes.

What a user notices: nothing, for a well-behaved client. Requests match the same
way, responses come back the same way, expectations are written the same way.
Under load the difference is that one stream can no longer disturb another -
which was the point of the exercise.

Two things this turned up late, both caught by review rather than by the tests:

The gRPC request handler lost its Configuration when it moved. It has a
constructor that takes one and a constructor that does not, and the frame codec
quietly falls back to the static property store when the field is null - so a
message-size limit set on a Configuration instance stopped being enforced over
HTTP/2, while HTTP/1.1 carried on honouring it. There is now a test that sets
the limit the way an embedding user would and fails if the argument goes missing
again.

Decompressing request bodies removes the content-encoding header, so an
expectation matching on that header stopped matching. HTTP/1.1 has long kept a
copy of the headers Netty removes, for exactly this reason; the stream pipeline
now does the same, in the same place. That fault is already reachable today by
anyone running gRPC bidi streaming, so this is a fix and not just a precaution.

The old connection-level handlers are now unreferenced but still present; they
are removed separately so this change is only a change of behaviour.

refactor(netty): remove the shared-connection HTTP/2 handlers

Nothing reaches these any more. Every HTTP/2 stream now has its own channel, so
the handler that routed frames onto a stream id by hand, its builder, and the
handler that warned when an outbound head had no stream id all describe a
pipeline that no longer exists.

The audit handler is worth a note. It existed to warn when a response head went
out without a stream id, because the old codec would then quietly invent a new
stream and the client would hang. On a per-stream channel the channel is the
stream, so there is nothing to get wrong and nothing to warn about. Its test
goes with it - it asserted only that the warning was logged.

Kept, despite looking equally dead: the wrapper that carries the end-of-stream
flag on streaming responses and the handler that translates it, which are what
stop SSE and LLM streams hanging; and the inbound stream-id capture, which is
what makes protocol matching work. The stream id the wrapper carries is
arguably redundant now that the channel identifies the stream, but that is a
change to a path that was hard to get right, and this is a deletion.

Comments in the streaming, dashboard and stream-id code described the removed
handlers as though they were still doing something. Those are corrected rather
than left to mislead the next reader. One unreleased changelog line said a
failed streaming write resets its stream; it ends it, which is a different frame
and the wording is now accurate.

ci(perf): measure what a channel per HTTP/2 stream costs under concurrency

Giving every stream its own channel allocates a channel, a pipeline and a set of
handlers per stream where before there was one set per connection. The tests say
it is correct; nothing said what it costs, and the honest answer was that we did
not know.

Two attempts to find out on a laptop failed. The first reported a million
requests a second and a 95 nanosecond p95 - faster than the hardware can move a
packet - because it stopped its timer on a per-stream latch and then divided a
request count it had assumed rather than counted. It recommended shipping. The
second was honest enough to refuse, and was then killed for memory.

So this runs on a quiet agent instead, sweeping one, ten and a hundred streams
over a single connection and recording throughput and percentiles.

It records; it does not judge. There is no threshold, because nobody knows the
run-to-run spread on the build agents yet, and a number invented today would
either never fire or fire at random. Once there is history a threshold can be
set against something real.

The one thing it will fail for is not measuring properly. The harness checks
that every response it counted actually arrived and was a 200, that the latency
is not impossibly small, that the throughput is not impossibly large, and that
time moved forwards. Any of those failing is a red build, and it says
HARNESS VALIDATION FAILED so nobody mistakes it for a slow server. A self test
runs first and deliberately trips each check, because a measurement that cannot
fail is not a measurement and would quietly certify that all is well for years.

None of this touches a pull request, a master build or a release.

docs(changelog): call out that closeSocket now ends a stream, not a connection

Over HTTP/2 a per-expectation closeSocket used to take down the whole TCP
connection and every request in flight on it. It now ends only the stream that
asked, which is what closing means when a connection carries many requests at
once, and what the same expectation already did over HTTP/1.1.

That is the one thing in this work a user can notice without having hit a bug,
so it belongs under Changed with the reason and the alternative, rather than
buried among the fixes. Anyone who actually wanted the connection torn down -
to see how their client recovers - should reach for the mid-response reset
fault, which still does exactly that.

The same entry under Fixed was written while this only happened with gRPC bidi
streaming turned on. That qualifier stopped being true when the multiplexed
pipeline became the only one, so it is gone.

fix(deps): take the js-yaml fix in the node client

GHSA-2883-xcg3-v3hh: merge keys with empty sources are not counted against
maxTotalMergeKeys, so the limit meant to bound the work does not, and a crafted
document can burn CPU. Fixed in 4.3.2.

The other node packages were moved to 4.3.2 already; this one was left on 4.3.1
and no update was in flight for it, so it would have gone out with the release.

The caret range already allowed 4.3.2 - it was the lockfile holding the old
version - so both the range and the lock are updated and npm ci resolves 4.3.2.

The four high advisories npm audit still reports here are lodash and minimatch
reached through the deprecated nodeunit and jshint test tooling. Those were
looked at before and set aside for want of time rather than because they are
harmless, and they are dev-only. npm now says a fix is available for each, so
that decision is worth revisiting - but replacing that tooling is its own piece
of work, not a dependency bump.
