fix(python): ship the py.typed marker so the annotations are actually used

The Python client is annotated almost everywhere - 675 of 679 definitions - and
none of it reached anyone. Without the marker PEP 561 asks for, mypy declines to
read a library's inline types at all:

  Skipping analyzing "mockserver": module is installed, but missing library
  stubs or py.typed marker

so every import came through as Any and no call into the client was checked.
The annotations were being written and then thrown away at the boundary.

The marker alone is not enough. setuptools puts non-Python files in a
distribution only when they are declared, so the package-data entry matters as
much as the file; without it the marker sits in the source tree and never
reaches the wheel. Both are here, and both artefacts were unpacked to confirm
the marker is inside rather than assumed.

Checked against the reported symptom: with the marker, reveal_type gives
mockserver.client.MockServerClient instead of Any, and mypy immediately caught a
missing argument in the snippet used to test it - which is the point. Removing
just the marker from the installed package brings the reported error back
verbatim.

The Testcontainers module had the same gap and is fixed the same way.

The release now refuses to publish if the marker is not in the built artefacts.
A packaging declaration is one line and nothing fails when it goes missing - the
package just quietly stops being typed, which is how it was shipped this way in
the first place. twine check does not look for it.

fix(test): pull MinIO from quay.io, Docker Hub no longer serves it

minio/minio has stopped being pullable from Docker Hub. Not the pinned tag -
the repository. The registry answers 401 for every tag including latest, the
Hub API reports the repository itself as not found, and docker pull says the
repository does not exist or needs a login. bitnami/minio and other images
resolve fine through the same calls, so this is not a local or method problem.

Master went red on it twice, on two dependabot commits that had nothing to do
with S3 - a posthog-js bump and an aws-sdk bump - which is what made it look
like flaky dependency failures rather than something that will fail every time
from now on.

quay.io is MinIO's other official registry and serves this exact tag with the
same manifest digest, so the image under test does not change. Both pins move
there; the S3 suite that was failing passes, 21 tests.

Left as a tag rather than pinned to the digest to match how every other
testcontainers image here is referenced. Worth noting that pinning a mutable
tag on a registry we do not control is what made this a surprise, and the same
exposure remains for the other images.

fix(netty): propagate channelReadComplete so HTTP/2 flow control can flush

Seven handlers overrode channelReadComplete as `ctx.flush()` only, never
calling `ctx.fireChannelReadComplete()`. That is harmless for a handler at
the end of a pipeline, but on the CONNECT-tunnel path three of them sit
ahead of the TLS and HTTP/2 layers, so the event never reached Netty's
HTTP/2 connection handler — whose channelReadComplete exists precisely to
flush flow-control-pending writes.

The result: an h2 response served through the HTTPS forward proxy stopped
at exactly the peer's initial flow-control window. The client's
WINDOW_UPDATE was read and the window credited, but the queued DATA was
never written, so anything over 64 KiB hung until the client timed out.
Direct h2 (h2c and TLS+ALPN) and HTTP/1.1-through-CONNECT were unaffected,
as were bodies that fit in one window and clients announcing a large
initial window.

Every affected handler now propagates the event.

The existing tests missed this because every HTTP/2 test used a response
body smaller than the 65,535-byte window — including the one named "large
body", at 50,000 bytes. The regression tests here use 300,000-byte bodies
over the CONNECT tunnel (mocked and forwarded) and, as isolation controls,
over direct h2c and direct TLS+ALPN.

Fixes #2683

fix(cli): record the port MockServer actually bound, not the one requested

Main.startServer recorded the REQUESTED port values, so starting the CLI
with `-p 0` recorded 0 rather than the ephemeral port the OS assigned.
A user running on port 0 could not discover their port, and the `ui` and
`demo` subcommands printed a dashboard URL ending in `:0`. It now records
the actual bound port from the MockServer instance. Explicit non-zero
ports resolve to the same value as before, so nothing else changes.

That also lets the tests stop guessing. PortFactory.findFreePort() draws
its candidates by bind(0) on the same ephemeral pool every other bind(0)
in the JVM uses, then closes them and returns a number; because surefire
reuses one fork per module, another bind could claim the port before the
server bound it. The test then failed as `hasStarted() == false`, because
Main swallows the startup exception, so the visible symptom pointed at
the code under test rather than at a stolen port.

The start tests now request port 0 and read back the real port, which
removes the race by construction instead of retrying around it. The one
test that must distinguish a CLI port from a system-property port keeps
an explicit port and retries only on a bind conflict.

MainTest + MainCliTest went from 20 failures in 30 runs to 2, with no
BindException in roughly 130 runs. The remaining intermittent failures
are a separate pre-existing problem — they occur in baseline runs with
no BindException at all — caused by these tests sharing a JVM and
mutating global configuration. Isolating them is left as its own change.

test(netty): lock HTTP/2 conformance with an independent client and real bodies

Four HTTP/2 defects reached users in recent releases (#2641, #2667, #2669,
#2683) and they share one shape: a connection-level concern is dropped as
it crosses a channel boundary, the failure is silent, and a user finds it.
They also share one reason the suite missed them — every HTTP/2 test used
a response body smaller than the 65,535-byte flow-control window, so the
WINDOW_UPDATE-driven flush was never exercised on any transport. The test
named "large body" was 50,000 bytes, fifteen short of the only threshold
that mattered.

This suite closes that gap. It drives MockServer with java.net.http's
client rather than the Netty client MockServer itself uses, so a bug
cannot be shared between the two sides, and every body is 300,000 bytes.
It covers direct h2 over TLS, h2 through the CONNECT proxy both mocked and
forwarded, and concurrent streams on one connection whose bodies differ
per stream, so a response delivered on the wrong stream fails rather than
matching on length.

Two constants carry the whole suite and are commented as such. The body
size is the obvious one. The other is a pin of the client's receive window
to the RFC default: the JDK client's own default window is far larger and
it enlarges the connection window straight after the preface, which made
the CONNECT case pass against the unfixed code until the window was
pinned. The pin is restored afterwards so it does not follow later tests
through the reused fork.

Reverting the handler fix from abbc36c18 makes both CONNECT cases hang
rather than fail an assertion, which is the behaviour they exist to catch.

Prior-knowledge h2c is deliberately absent: this client negotiates
cleartext h2 by upgrade and falls back to HTTP/1.1 rather than sending the
preface, so the test would assert HTTP/1.1 while appearing to cover h2c.
H2cMockingMatrixIntegrationTest already covers that transport at size.

fix(netty): negotiate the tunnel protocol before wiring the SOCKS relay

An HTTPS request that negotiated HTTP/2 through the SOCKS proxy failed
outright — the client got nothing at all, at any body size.

The relay wires up its loopback connection when MockServer sends the SOCKS
success reply, and a SOCKS client only sends its ClientHello after that
reply arrives. So at wiring time no TLS had happened and no ALPN result
existed, and the relay assumed HTTP/1.1. The client's TLS was then
terminated further along by the PortUnificationHandler the SOCKS path
leaves in place, which happily negotiated h2 — leaving a client speaking
HTTP/2 to a loopback provisioned for HTTP/1.1. The forwarded frames were
unparseable, fell through to the binary proxy, and the connection died.
HTTP/1.1 survived only because its forwarded bytes are self-describing
text that protocol detection still recognises downstream.

A SOCKS target on a port ending in 443 now sets the upstream TLS flag as
well as the downstream one, so the relay terminates the tunnelled TLS
itself and waits for that handshake's ALPN before wiring anything up —
the path the CONNECT proxy already took. The relay also removes the
leftover PortUnificationHandler first, so it is the only thing
terminating that TLS rather than racing a second SNI handler.

The port heuristic remains the only signal available before the
ClientHello, so a tunnel to TLS on a port not ending in 443 is still
wired as HTTP/1.1. The changelog says so, and points at the CONNECT proxy.

Covered by SOCKS5 and SOCKS4 HTTP/2 tests, both of which fail without
this change, plus an HTTP/1.1 test guarding the flow that has moved onto
the newly shared branch.

Fixes #2685

fix(netty): reply to a SOCKS4a client instead of throwing while writing

A client that used SOCKS4a — the extension that sends a hostname rather
than an IPv4 address, as curl's socks4a:// does — hung forever against
MockServer. Cleartext and TLS alike, on every released version.

Nothing was wrong with detecting or decoding SOCKS4a. The reply was the
problem: the destination was echoed straight back into Netty's
DefaultSocks4CommandResponse, whose address field must be an IPv4
literal, so a hostname made it throw. It threw while the grant reply was
being written, so the client received nothing at all and sat waiting
until it timed out, which is why this looked like a hang rather than an
error.

The destination is now echoed back only when it really is an IPv4
literal; for a hostname the reply omits it and the encoder writes
0.0.0.0:0. Those fields carry meaning only for BIND, and clients ignore
them for CONNECT, which is the only command MockServer accepts here.
Classic SOCKS4 replies are unchanged. The failure reply is built the same
way, since it took the same destination and would have thrown just as
readily.

This went unnoticed because Netty's Socks4ProxyHandler sends classic
SOCKS4 whenever it is given an IPv4 literal, so the existing SOCKS4 test
never sent a hostname. The new test speaks SOCKS4a on the wire and
asserts the grant reply byte for byte.

test(netty): make an HTTP/2 test body cross the flow-control window by default

Four HTTP/2 defects reached users because every HTTP/2 test in the
repository used a response body smaller than the 65,535-byte flow-control
window, so the WINDOW_UPDATE-driven flush was never exercised anywhere.
The fixes so far have been point fixes: individual tests raised to a
300,000-byte literal, which works only for as long as everyone who writes
the next HTTP/2 test knows that history.

Http2FlowControlBodies offers named sizes instead, so an author picks
OVER_WINDOW without needing to know the number or the reason. Bodies are
stamped with a caller-supplied marker throughout, so a body delivered on
the wrong stream or truncated fails an equality assertion rather than
slipping past a length check. Shrinking OVER_WINDOW to the window or
below fails at class load with a message naming the four issues it would
bring back, so the blind spot cannot quietly return through a single
edited number.

The tests that were point-fixed now take their bodies from it, across
direct TLS, h2c, and both the mocked and forwarded CONNECT paths, and so
does the third-party conformance suite, which had grown its own copy of
the same constant and generator. Of these, the two CONNECT cases are real
locks — reverting the handler fix from abbc36c18 hangs them — while the
direct cases pass either way and say so, since that defect lived on the
CONNECT pipeline. The remaining HTTP/2 tests are left alone; sweeping
them would add risk without adding cover.

fix(cli): exit non-zero when the server fails to start

A failed port bind threw out of bindPorts, was rethrown by MockServer, and
was then swallowed by the run command's catch-all. picocli saw no failure,
so the CLI exited 0 and a shell or CI caller had no way to tell that the
server never came up. The only trace was an ERROR line in the log.

The run command now reports exit code 1 from that path, and the ui, demo,
proxy and openapi subcommands report the code of the run they delegate to,
which otherwise would have kept returning 0 on a failed start. A usage or
validation error still exits 0, as before: a bind failure arrives as a
plain RuntimeException and never reaches that branch.

This also removes a trap for anyone reading a test failure here. A stolen
port made the server fail to bind, the failure was swallowed, and the test
reported only that the server had not started — which reads as a fault in
whatever the test was exercising rather than in the environment.

test(cli): restore the log-entry cap a dev-mode test borrows

The build caps mockserver.maxLogEntries at 1000 in test JVMs because each
event log pre-allocates a disruptor ring buffer of that size rounded up to
a power of two, and the tests create many of them in one reused fork. The
dev-mode test has to clear that cap to observe what dev mode defaults to,
and afterwards restored "production defaults" by recomputing them from the
heap — up to 100000, so a 131072-entry buffer per server, for every server
started later in the fork.

The effect was a flake that looked like nothing to do with this test: a
later, unrelated test would occasionally time out or read an empty body,
because the fork was under memory pressure by then. It now captures both
the system property and the resolved cache value for each key it borrows
and puts back exactly what it found.

Over 30 runs this takes the failure rate from 4 to 2, and the failures
that remain look nothing like the ones it removed: no read timeouts, no
empty bodies, just a readiness poll occasionally missing its budget on a
loaded machine with no exception behind it. That residue is contention,
not this leak, and isolating these classes into their own fork is a
separate question about the build rather than about this test.

build(gradle): stop a distribution download from failing the whole build

A Maven reactor of roughly twenty-five minutes failed because the Gradle
wrapper could not finish downloading the distribution:

  Downloading https://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-8.14-all.zip
  Caused by: java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out

Nothing was wrong with the build. The agents cache .gradle/caches but not
.gradle/wrapper/dists, so every build fetches the distribution afresh from
an external service, and a stall on that one download takes everything
with it.

The wrapper now fetches the binary distribution rather than the one that
also carries sources and documentation for IDE completion, which this
harness has no use for: 131MB instead of 214MB. It waits a minute on a
read rather than ten seconds, and retries the download three times.

The wrapper jar had to be regenerated for any of that to take effect. The
one checked in predates Gradle 7.6 and hard-codes the ten-second timeout,
so setting the property alone would have changed nothing while looking
like a fix. The new jar is what Gradle's own wrapper task produces; the
distribution it fetches is still 8.14. The retry it gained applies to the
download step only, before Gradle starts, so it cannot hide a failing test.

While pinning the download path, the distribution is now pinned by
checksum too, so a substituted or truncated archive fails rather than
executing. Verified by a cold download into an empty Gradle home.

The jetbrains wrapper gets the longer timeout for the same reason. It is
left on its own jar, which predates the retry property, so setting that
there would be a no-op.

The durable fix is for the agents to keep the distribution between builds,
or to serve it internally. That lives in the agent image rather than here.

BREAKING: publish only MockServer's own modules in the BOM

Importing mockserver-bom took over a consumer's third-party dependencies.
The published BOM managed 221 artifacts, of which only 24 were ours: the
flatten plugin was expanding the whole inherited parent dependencyManagement
into what we publish. Four of those inherited entries carried a scope. A
project declaring com.nimbusds:oauth2-oidc-sdk without one got MockServer's
internal test-scoped pin, so a dependency its production code needed landed
on the test classpath and the build failed.

Nothing about the BOM changed to cause that. An OIDC fix added the library
to the parent for MockServer's own tests, and the BOM picked it up on its
own. Adding a test dependency rewrote a published contract.

The BOM now publishes the 24 MockServer modules and nothing else.

The scope is correct where it is, in the parent, and removing it there
would put test-only libraries on MockServer's compile classpath and ship
them to everyone. The problem was never that entry; it was republishing
other people's libraries at all.

Consumers who imported the BOM to align MockServer's transitive versions,
typically to satisfy dependencyConvergence, no longer get those pins and
should manage the versions themselves or import each project's own BOM.
The changelog says so.

The module had no tests and, being pom packaging with a single file,
nothing that could observe what it published — which is why a change
elsewhere could rewrite it unnoticed. A consumer project now builds
against the BOM during the build and asserts both that it keeps its own
version and scope, and that every entry we publish is ours. Reverting the
flatten mode fails it.

feat(test): let tests pick ports from a band the OS will not hand out

PortFactory finds a free port by binding port 0, which draws from the
operating system's ephemeral range — the same range every other program on
the machine draws from. On a developer machine with unrelated services
listening in it, a test can be handed a number that something else takes
first, or worse, connect to whatever is already there. Both were seen this
week: binds failing on ports adjacent to a running application, and tests
receiving a JSON body and an HTTPS handshake error that exist nowhere in
this repository or its dependencies.

Setting mockserver.testPortRangeStart and mockserver.testPortRangeEnd now
makes PortFactory bind candidates inside that band instead. Leave them
unset and nothing changes. Both must be set, and a reversed, unparseable
or too-narrow range fails loudly rather than quietly reverting.

This is worth being precise about, because it fixes less than it might
appear to. It helps only where a port is chosen ahead of binding. Tests
that start on port 0 and read back the port never go through here and are
unaffected — they were already immune to losing the port, and their
occasional failures are a loaded machine, not a stolen one. Measured over
thirty runs the CLI tests did not improve to any degree worth claiming.
What did change is the one test that must name a port in advance: it
reached a foreign listener without the band and never did with it.

The properties are read inside the test JVM, so a surefire run needs them
passed through to the fork rather than to Maven, which the changelog
spells out.

PortFactoryTest joins the sequential phase in both lists, since it sets
these properties globally and the negative cases set invalid ones — a
concurrent findFreePort on another thread would read those and throw.

ci(gradle): cache the Gradle distribution between builds

A build lost a twenty-five minute Maven reactor to a timed-out download of
the Gradle distribution. The wrapper was hardened afterwards so a slow
download retries rather than failing, but it was still fetching 131MB from
services.gradle.org on every single build, because nothing kept it.

The cache type already existed and was never used by any step. It also
mounted the wrong directory: Gradle's dependency cache lives in
.gradle/caches, but the distribution lives beside it in
.gradle/wrapper/dists, which was never mounted. Both are now mounted, as
two named subdirectories rather than the whole of .gradle, which also
holds daemon state and logs that should not follow a build around.

The key is the content of every gradle-wrapper.properties, so it turns
over exactly when a Gradle version is bumped and holds still otherwise.
A cached distribution cannot outlive its pin: the same file carries the
checksum the wrapper validates against, so a changed pin is a changed key,
and a corrupted archive fails the wrapper's own check rather than running.

Only the java pipeline saves this cache, and that is load-bearing rather
than tidiness. The key has no pipeline dimension, saves are first-write
wins, and the two wrapper files in the repository pin different Gradle
versions. A second pipeline saving first would store its own distribution
and leave the java reactor restoring a cache without the one it needs,
re-downloading it every build and quietly undoing the point of the cache.
The documentation now says so, and says what would have to change before
another pipeline can use it.

Cold builds are unaffected: every step soft-fails, and a miss or absent
credentials leaves a build exactly as slow as it is today.

fix(netty): decide a SOCKS tunnel's protocol by looking at the bytes

MockServer guessed whether a SOCKS tunnel would carry TLS from the
destination port: ending in 443 meant TLS, ending in 80 meant cleartext.
The guess was wrong in both directions. HTTP/2 over TLS to any other port
was wired as HTTP/1.1, so the client negotiated h2 and the frames arrived
somewhere that could not read them; cleartext to a port like 8443 had TLS
termination forced onto it.

The decision is now made from the first bytes of the tunnel rather than
from the port. When the SOCKS handshake completes the relay defers the
choice, hands the connection to a one-shot detector, and that detector
classifies the first record header the way Netty's own OptionalSslHandler
does before routing to the TLS or cleartext branch and stepping out of the
way. Both branches are the ones that already existed and are already
proven; only the decision moved.

The detector replaces the leftover SOCKS decoders rather than sitting
behind them, because the port unification handler is left in place on this
path and would otherwise see the same bytes. The client cannot send
anything until it has the SOCKS reply, and the reply listener is where the
swap happens, so there is no window where both are live.

The CONNECT path keeps assuming TLS, since a CONNECT to a proxy always is.
Its termination code is now shared with the SOCKS path rather than
duplicated; nothing about its behaviour changed.

Still unchanged: cleartext HTTP/2 with prior knowledge through a SOCKS
tunnel is wired as HTTP/1.1, exactly as it always has been. The detector
looks for a TLS record, not an h2c preface.

Verified against curl across the grid: h2 over TLS through SOCKS5 and
SOCKS4 to 443, 8443 and 9999; HTTP/1.1 over TLS; cleartext to 80 and to
443; and CONNECT unchanged.

docs(build): say how to keep local tests off the OS ephemeral range

The test port band added alongside PortFactory is opt-in, which means
nobody will use it unless they are told it exists and what it is for.

The failures it prevents do not look like port problems. A server fails to
bind for no apparent reason, or a request comes back answered by another
program entirely — a .NET service on this machine returned a control-plane
500, and a test once received a JSON body containing a string that appears
nowhere in this repository or any of its dependencies. The natural reading
of all of that is a bug in whatever the test was exercising.

Two full runs of core and netty on the same commit, with and without the
band, are recorded here: the bind failure and the three cascaded failures
behind it disappear, and sixty-nine more tests run because the classes that
used to die during setup now get as far as running.

The limits are written down too, because the band is easy to over-trust.
It only helps where a port is picked before it is bound, so tests that
start on port zero are untouched, and it covers TCP rather than the UDP the
HTTP/3 suites use. The properties also have to reach the forked JVM;
passing them to Maven alone looks right and does nothing.

ci: pull the test container images before running the suites

The cloud blob-store step failed two of the last three builds. MinIO moved
to quay.io because Docker Hub stopped serving it, pulls from the agents
started stalling, and Testcontainers reported it five minutes later from
inside the suite as a ContainerFetchException with a timeout underneath.
Nothing about the tests was wrong and the message did not say so.

The images are now pulled before Maven starts, so a registry that is slow
or throttling fails the step in seconds and says which image and which
registry. The same applies to the broker step, which pulls Kafka, RabbitMQ
and Mosquitto from Docker Hub and has the same exposure to a rate limit.

The retry covers the pull and nothing else. These steps already assert that
their suites really ran rather than trusting an exit code, because a Docker
guard that silently skips everything looks exactly like success, and a
retry wrapped around the test run would undo that. An image already on the
daemon is left alone rather than re-pulled, which is what Testcontainers
itself would do and stops an outage failing a build that would have run
perfectly well from the cache.

Raising the Testcontainers pull timeout instead was considered and is
weaker: the suite would still spend five minutes getting to an error that
does not explain itself.

What this does not do is remove the dependency on other people's
registries. Caching them in ECR would, and is worth doing separately.

ci(gradle): give the cache a scope so a second pipeline can use it

The Gradle cache added for the java pipeline could not be extended to the
JetBrains one, because the key is derived from the content of every
gradle-wrapper.properties in the checkout and has no pipeline dimension.
The two files pin different Gradle versions, so both pipelines computed
one key and would have shared one tarball. Saves are first-write-wins, so
whichever ran first would have stored its own distribution and left the
other restoring a cache without the one it needed, re-downloading it every
build. The documentation warned against exactly that.

The key now takes a scope, and the java and editors pipelines each own
theirs. Gradle without a scope no longer falls back to a shared key: it
declines to use the cache at all, so a third consumer that forgets one
gets a cold build rather than somebody else's distribution. The warning is
now a property of the script instead of a paragraph people have to read.

Other cache types are untouched and keep their existing keys. The java
gradle cache moves under a scope, which costs one cold download before it
re-caches.

What the editors pipeline gains is the Gradle distribution and the
dependency cache, including the IntelliJ platform it compiles against.
What it does not gain is the Plugin Verifier's IDE downloads, which are
the larger part: they land outside GRADLE_USER_HOME because the verifier's
own caching is off by default. Turning that on means much bigger tarballs
against the existing timeout, so it is left alone and written down rather
than half-done.

feat(netty): serve cleartext HTTP/2 through a SOCKS tunnel

A client using HTTP/2 with prior knowledge through the SOCKS proxy was
served HTTP/1.1. The relay's detector classified the first bytes as TLS or
not, and anything that was not TLS took the cleartext branch, which only
ever wired up HTTP/1.1. That predates the byte-driven detection and was
documented rather than fixed.

The detector now also recognises the HTTP/2 connection preface once it has
ruled out a TLS record, and wires both relay legs for cleartext HTTP/2 when
it finds one. The branch it selects is the one that already existed and is
already exercised; only the condition that reaches it is new.

Detection waits while the bytes so far could still become a preface, and
the preface begins with a method reserved for exactly this purpose, so no
real HTTP/1.1 request can be mistaken for one or left waiting: anything
that diverges is HTTP/1.1 from that byte onward. Nothing is consumed while
deciding, so the bytes reach whichever codec is chosen, once.

The decision is tied to the same http2Enabled setting the listener reads,
so the tunnel and the server it forwards to cannot disagree about whether
the preface means anything — a client speaking HTTP/2 to a leg wired for
HTTP/1.1 is how this whole family of bugs has gone wrong before.

The wire constant lives in one place now and both detectors read it. The
pipeline test keeps its own literal deliberately: it feeds the preface in
and asserts the switch happens, so sharing the constant would let a wrong
constant satisfy itself.

CONNECT is untouched, and cleartext HTTP/2 with prior knowledge through it
is still HTTP/1.1, as it always has been.

ci: cache the test container images in ECR instead of pulling upstream

The suites pull six images from three registries on every build. When
MinIO moved to quay.io those pulls started timing out and cost two builds
in three; the pre-pull added afterwards made the failure fast and legible
but still left every build depending on someone else's registry being
reachable and unthrottled.

An ECR pull-through cache now sits in front of Docker Hub and quay.io.
The first build to want an image fetches it through the cache; later ones
pull it in-region. Storage is a few pence a month and same-region pulls
are free.

Microsoft's registry cannot be cached — ECR refuses it as an upstream —
so azurite still comes from mcr.microsoft.com and still depends on that
registry being up, with the pre-pull as its only guard. That is written
down rather than left to be found out. It was found out here: the paper
design had all three registries supported, and only applying it and
asking AWS proved otherwise. The transform would have rewritten azurite
to a cache repository that cannot exist, so every Azure test would have
failed to pull the moment caching was switched on; it now passes that one
registry through untouched, while any registry nobody has mapped is
rejected rather than guessed at.

Image names live in one properties file that the tests and the pre-pull
script both read, so the two can no longer drift apart — they had already
been duplicated in two places.

None of this is on yet. Without MOCKSERVER_ECR_PULL_THROUGH nothing sets
a registry, every image resolves to the name it does today, and a failed
ECR login falls back to the public names rather than half-configuring the
build. Local machines and forks, which have no access to this registry,
are unaffected either way.
